file: 1996/1996-05-01_alice slams wally_fast forwarded_harrasment_ignore sexy_mandatory video_sext_sexual harassment_video_evolution.gif
title: Harassment Video Fast-Forward Backfires on Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just watched the mandatory video on sexual harassment. It worked!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In only thirty minutes, that video corrected a billion years of evolution. Do something sexy and watch me ignore it!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I probably shouldn't have fast-forwarded through the boring parts.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Alice that the mandatory sexual harassment video has completely cured him of any inappropriate impulses. He boasts that she can try to be sexy and he will ignore it. In the last panel Wally is embedded in a cracked wall, having apparently been slammed there by Alice, and he admits he should not have skipped the boring parts of the video.
punchline: Wally's smug claim that a thirty-minute video fixed his behavior is undone when his provocative remark gets him violently thrown into a wall, showing he skipped the very parts that would have taught him better.
summary: After bragging that compliance training has transformed him, Wally ends up smashed into a wall because he skimmed the lesson.

file: 1996/1996-10-30_award_tim_incredible accomplishments_two years stonewalling_hired.gif
title: Award for Finally Doing His Job

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This award goes to Tim for his incredible accomplishment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: After two years of stonewalling all progress, Tim finally agreed to do the work for which he was hired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We look forward to working with Tim in the coming year.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: As if I'd have time for that.

situation: The Boss presents an award to Tim and explains that it is for finally agreeing to do the work he was hired for after two years of blocking all progress. Dilbert watches from the audience. As the Boss says he looks forward to working with Tim next year, Tim cheerfully says he won't have time for that.
punchline: Management rewards an employee for merely doing his job, and the employee, having been rewarded for obstruction, has no intention of continuing to do it.
summary: A staffer who obstructed everything for two years gets honored for reluctantly starting his actual duties, then promptly signals he won't keep it up.

file: 1996/1996-12-20_ratbert the consulatant_existing computer_new one_new system_devastating_paid exactly the same.gif
title: Consultant Paid Regardless Of Outcome

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: ...Then we'll turn off the existing computer systems and fire up the new one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if the new system doesn't work on the first try? Won't the economic impact be devastating?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Let me check my contract... Nope. I get paid exactly the same.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, same here.

situation: Ratbert, working as a consultant, explains a plan to switch off the company's existing computer systems and start up a new one all at once. Dilbert asks what happens if the new system fails and the economic damage is huge. Ratbert checks his contract and cheerfully reports his pay is unaffected, and Dilbert says the same applies to him.
punchline: Neither the consultant nor the employee faces any personal consequences if the risky cutover fails, so nobody has a real incentive to worry about the company's losses.
summary: A cat consultant discovers that a catastrophic system failure wouldn't cost him a cent, and his colleague admits the same is true for him.

file: 1996/1996-06-28_day care facility_free range day care_roam free_economical_powerpoint lsides.gif
title: Free Range Day Care Plan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my final plan for the company's day care facility.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call it free range day care. The children are allowed to roam free among the cubicles. It's very economical.

transcript.speaker: Child
transcript.text: I don't believe he's really an evil troll.

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: Look at the "PowerPoint" slides he's making. It's not human.

setting: The Boss's office, then the cubicle area
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, presents The Boss with his final plan for a company day care facility: let the children roam loose among the cubicles. Meanwhile two children in the cubicle area watch a balding, bespectacled employee making PowerPoint slides and conclude from his output that he can't be human.
punchline: Making PowerPoint slides is so soul-deadening that the kids take it as proof the employee must be an evil troll rather than a person.
summary: A cut-rate day care scheme that turns kids loose in the office ends with them judging a coworker inhuman because of his slide decks.

file: 1996/1996-02-16_expect_new employment agreement_first born_dna_derivative works.gif
title: Employment Agreement Claims Your DNA

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't believe they expect us to sign these new employment agreement forms.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: According to this, anything we even think of becomes the company's property. I'm surprised they don't claim our firstborn sons!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What do you suppose it means when they copyright our "DNA and all derivative works"?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They'd make an exception for you.

setting: Office, with the three coworkers standing together reading papers
situation: Dilbert, Wally and Alice read their new employment agreement forms and complain about how much the company claims to own. Wally notes that even their thoughts become company property, then wonders what it means that the company copyrights their DNA and derivative works. Alice replies that they would exempt him.
punchline: Alice insults Wally by implying that his DNA is so worthless that not even the grabby company would want to claim ownership of any of his offspring or derivative works.
summary: Coworkers balk at an overreaching employment contract that claims ownership of their ideas and genetic material, until one is slyly told his own offspring would be exempt.

file: 1996/1996-05-09_dogbert_career counselor_expect employer_don't expect raises_trained pension_sourball_marbles_cellophane.gif
title: Dogbert Sells Marbles as Sourballs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Career Counselor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't expect your employer to take care of you forever, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't expect raises, don't expect to be trained and don't expect a pension.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's depressing. I need a sourball.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Those are marbles wrapped in cellophane.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a career counselor, tells Wally he can't count on his employer for raises, training or a pension. Wally says the news is depressing and reaches for a sourball from the candy jar on the desk. Dogbert reveals the candies are actually marbles wrapped in cellophane.
punchline: Dogbert's bleak career advice extends to his own office, where even the comforting candy is a fake, reinforcing that you can't expect anything from anyone.
summary: A counselor dog warns a worker that employers owe him nothing, then lets him learn the candy dish is a trick too.

file: 1996/1996-10-03_document_job process_requirements_anticipate_shifting political winds_relevant buzzwords_achieve_importance_adding value_process design.gif
title: Documenting a Buzzword-Wrapped Non-Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to document your job processes to satisfy our ISO 9000 requirements.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I try to anticipate the shifting political winds. Then I wrap myself in the relevant buzzwords and try to achieve importance without adding value.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your job title?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Director of ISO 9000 quality process design.

situation: Dilbert sits at a table with a laptop, interviewing a coworker so he can document the man's job processes for ISO 9000 compliance. The coworker candidly explains that his work consists of reading office politics, using buzzwords, and appearing important without adding value. When Dilbert asks for his job title, it turns out he is the Director of ISO 9000 quality process design.
punchline: The man describing a useless, politically driven job is himself the director of the very quality-process program that is documenting everyone's work, so the quality bureaucracy is exposed as the example of valueless busywork.
summary: A process-documentation interview reveals that the interviewee's role is pure political posturing, and that he happens to head the quality-process initiative itself.

file: 1996/1996-02-07_biggest offices_file cabinet_least need_living monument_proprietary documents_stacks full_storage psace_efficiency.gif
title: Biggest Offices, Least Storage Need

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Why is it that the people with the least need for storage space have the biggest offices?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I know! You're using your office as kind of a living monument to inefficiency!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is this because I wouldn't let you get a file cabinet?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Where would I put it? My cubicle is full of stacks of proprietary documents.

setting: The Boss's large office and the doorway of Carol's cubicle
situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, walks into his spacious office and complains that the people who need the least storage space get the biggest offices. She jabs that his office is a monument to inefficiency. The Boss guesses she is still sore that he denied her a file cabinet, and she retorts that her cramped cubicle is already overflowing with documents.
punchline: Carol's complaint about the unfair distribution of office space is really a dig at the Boss's refusal to approve a simple file cabinet, leaving her buried in paper while he enjoys a huge, mostly empty office.
summary: A frustrated assistant mocks her boss's oversized, underused office while explaining she has nowhere to put the paperwork he wouldn't let her file.

file: 1996/1996-05-05_square pattern_move cubicle_random pattern symetry_waste of time_5 people_downsized_formed pentagon.gif
title: Moving Cubicles for Square Symmetry

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to move you one cubicle down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That way my people will be in a square pattern.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're in a random pattern now. The symmetry is bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want me to waste two days of work to move...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have no phone and no network connection for a week...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have to order new business cards and update my cubicle address on dozens of records.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you still won't have a square because there are five of us.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I got downsized. Apparently somebody complained that I formed a pentagon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That can happen.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he must move one cubicle down so his team sits in a square pattern. Dilbert objects that the move wastes days of work, cuts off his phone and network, and creates paperwork. He points out that five people can't form a square, and in the last panel a coworker carrying a box of belongings says he was laid off for forming a pentagon.
punchline: Management's absurd obsession with cubicle geometry is so strong that an employee was fired simply for making the layout a pentagon instead of a square.
summary: A manager's quest for a perfectly square seating arrangement ends with a worker being fired for spoiling the shape.

file: 1996/1996-03-15_business plan_start up_provide venture capital_lost of media_afraid of dogs_media hype_greeting investors_prospectus.gif
title: Dogbert's Venture Capital Investor Scam

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The business plan for your start-up is idiotic but I'm going to provide the venture capital funding anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll generate lots of media hype, go public and make millions by shafting greedy and ignorant investors.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Latin word for "close your eyes and open your mouth" is "prospectus."

transcript.speaker: Bald man
transcript.text: This is exactly why I'm afraid of dogs.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a venture capitalist, tells a start-up founder that he will fund the company despite its idiotic business plan. His plan is to generate media hype, take the company public and profit by fleecing greedy, ignorant investors. He then jokes about the Latin meaning of 'prospectus', prompting a nervous bald man at the table to say this is why he fears dogs.
punchline: Dogbert cynically admits that the funding is a scheme to exploit gullible investors, and the 'prospectus' wordplay frames investing as being fed something unpleasant while blindly trusting.
summary: A scheming canine financier bankrolls a hopeless start-up purely to hype it, float it and fleece the gullible people who buy shares.

file: 1996/1996-07-10_engineer up_management support_meeting_boss ego_master at work_promised customer_full management support_sales meeting_business.gif
title: Sales Promises Impossible Product by Thursday

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll need your full management support in this meeting with sales.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just watch the master at work.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I promised a customer a product that we don't make. You need to engineer-up a thousand units by early next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is Thursday okay?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait until he finds out that Thursday isn't "early next week." Hee hee!

setting: Conference room and corridor in the office
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for management support at a meeting with sales, and the Boss brags that he will handle it. In the meeting, a salesman admits he promised a customer a product the company doesn't make and demands a thousand units by early next week. The Boss cheerfully offers Thursday, which Dilbert gleefully notes is not actually early next week.
punchline: The Boss thinks he is skillfully negotiating, but he misunderstands the deadline and misses that Thursday is late in the week, so he is making the situation worse while Dilbert quietly gloats.
summary: A boss who boasts of his negotiating skill fumbles a sales demand for an unmade product by misreading what early next week means.

file: 1996/1996-01-25_troublesome customers_service costs_eliminated.gif
title: Eliminating Customers Who Actually Use Product

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've asked Dogbert to help us get rid of our most troublesome customers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Grrr

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ten percent of your customers account for ninety percent of your service costs. They must be eliminated.

transcript.speaker: Woman in meeting
transcript.text: Is that the same group of customers who actually use our product?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Plus the ones who were injured unpacking it.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces that Dogbert, acting as consultant, will help the company get rid of its most troublesome customers. Dogbert explains that a small share of customers drive most service costs and must be eliminated. A female executive points out these are the people who actually use the product, and Dogbert adds that it also includes those hurt while unpacking it.
punchline: The company wants to cut the customers who cost the most to support, but those are simply the people who really use the product, and some are so troublesome because the product is dangerous even to unbox.
summary: A consultant recommends dumping the customers who generate the most support costs, only to reveal they are the ones genuinely using, and being hurt by, the shoddy product.

file: 1996/1996-04-01_laptop computers_its to program_training program_rectangle plastic thing_boost sales_sales force.gif
title: Salesman Pitches Laptop as Plastic Thing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In an effort to boost sales, laptop computers have been given to every member of the sales force.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That could be a problem, given the recent cuts to the training budget.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile, in the field

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: And if you order today, I'll throw in this rectangular plastic thing.

setting: Conference room, then a customer's office in the field
situation: The Boss announces that every salesperson has been issued a laptop to boost sales, and Dilbert warns that training budget cuts could be a problem. Cut to a salesman in the field who, not knowing what the laptop is, offers it to a customer as a free bonus item.
punchline: Without training, the salespeople don't know what a laptop is, so they treat it as a throw-in gift, showing the folly of buying technology while cutting training.
summary: Handing out computers to sellers while slashing their training leads one of them to peddle his laptop as a mystery freebie.

file: 1996/1996-02-06_proprietary documents_cubicle_competitors_utilize synergy.gif
title: Competitors Laugh at Our Plans

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you've got to lock up these proprietary documents you have in your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If our competitors see our plans, it could be very dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: For us or for them?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Competitors

transcript.speaker: Competitor
transcript.text: Ooh! Look! They're planning to "utilize synergy." We're in trouble now!

transcript.speaker: Competitor
transcript.text: Ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Competitor
transcript.text: Stop! You're killing me!!

setting: Office cubicle, then a competitor's office
situation: The Boss tells Alice to lock up the company's proprietary documents so competitors can't see the plans and cause danger. Alice asks whether the danger would be for us or for them. Cut to the competitors, who are reading the stolen plans and laughing hysterically at the buzzword-filled content.
punchline: The company's secret plans are so full of empty buzzwords like 'utilize synergy' that competitors would find them hilarious rather than threatening, so the real danger is to the company's own reputation.
summary: A manager frets about rivals seeing confidential plans, but the rivals who read them just collapse in laughter at the corporate jargon.

file: 1996/1996-07-17_action plan_solve problems_problems_demented_expense_demented plat_lift veil_ignorance.gif
title: Dilbert's Problem-Solving Date Gets Misread

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's date
transcript.text: Um... when I've shared my feelings with you, I wasn't hoping you'd design an action plan to solve all of my problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why else would you tell me all of your problems... unless it's some demented plot to make yourself feel better at my expense?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You were right. It was all a demented plot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to gradually lift your veil of ignorance.

setting: A park bench outdoors, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert's date explains that when she shares her feelings she doesn't want him to craft an action plan to fix her problems. Dilbert, baffled, concludes she must be plotting to feel better at his expense. At home he reports to Dogbert that Dogbert's cynical advice was right, and Dogbert says he is slowly lifting Dilbert's ignorance.
punchline: Dilbert, who only understands sharing problems as a prompt to solve them, has been coached by Dogbert into a paranoid worldview, and Dogbert cheerfully admits he is deliberately making Dilbert's social understanding worse while claiming it is enlightenment.
summary: A man who cannot grasp that venting isn't a request for solutions treats his date's confiding as a scheme, thanks to his dog's cynical coaching.

file: 1996/1996-08-27_boost morale_more reviews_hear employees_300% more criticism_working in box.gif
title: Quarterly Reviews Mean More Criticism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news, Alice. I'm going to have quarterly performance reviews to boost morale.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wow! In addition to working sixteen hours a day in this big box, now I'll get 300% more criticism!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll have a chance to hear employee concerns four times a year.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I assume comprehension will remain on the bicentennial plan.

situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Alice he is introducing quarterly performance reviews to boost morale. Alice points out that this only means working long hours in a cubicle and receiving four times as much criticism. The Boss says he will get to hear employee concerns more often, and Alice replies that he will still fail to understand them.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that although the boss will hear employee concerns four times a year, he will only truly understand them once every 200 years, so the reviews are just extra criticism.
summary: A manager touts more frequent reviews as a morale booster, but his sharp-tongued employee sees them as extra scolding that won't make him any more understanding.

file: 1996/1996-09-11_team building_exercise_solve problems_working sundial_pencil_donut_make any differnce_health.gif
title: Sundial Teambuilding Ends in Donut Eating

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Teambuilding exercise

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: This next exercise will challenge your ability to solve problems as a team.

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Build a working sundial using only a pencil and a donut.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Four hours later...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: One more bite isn't going to make any difference.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sob

setting: A corporate teambuilding workshop in a meeting room
situation: A small, odd-looking facilitator stands on a table and assigns a teambuilding challenge: build a working sundial using only a pencil and a donut. Four hours later the group sits around the table, exhausted and distraught, with the donut nearly eaten and only crumbs left. One of them rationalizes eating another bite.
punchline: The team, instead of solving the problem, has eaten nearly the whole donut, rationalizing it bite by bite and proving that the exercise has defeated them and wrecked any chance of success.
summary: A pointless group challenge to craft a sundial from a pencil and a pastry ends with hungry, sobbing colleagues devouring the key material.

file: 1996/1996-05-02_connection_network_broken_token ring_wind beneath my wings_ethernet.gif
title: Token Fell Out of the Network

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's your problem. The connection to the network is broken.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. It's a "token ring" LAN. That means the token fell out and it's in this room someplace.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You are the wind beneath my wings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll wait a week then tell him the token must be in the "Ethernet."

setting: Office of a network user with a computer on a desk
situation: Dilbert fixes a network connection for the Boss, who sits in a blue chair, and tells him the broken link is because the token fell out of a token ring LAN and is somewhere in the room. While the Boss crawls on the floor searching, Wally praises Dilbert for his brilliant con. Dilbert plans to wait a week, then claim the token is in the Ethernet.
punchline: Dilbert exploits the Boss's technical ignorance by inventing a physical 'token' that fell out of the network, sending him on a pointless search and planning to repeat the trick with another bogus explanation.
summary: A tech support worker fools his clueless manager into hunting the floor for a nonexistent network part, to the admiration of a coworker.

file: 1996/1996-08-12_catbert_evil hr director_big layoffs coming_secret_cats don't keep secrets.gif
title: Catbert Leaks Layoff List Secretly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil HR Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hey, Wally... Big layoffs coming.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I've seen the list. I know more about your future than you do. But it's a secret.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Sadly, cats don't keep secrets very well.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nice chair.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, peers over a cubicle wall and tells Wally that big layoffs are coming. He hints that he has seen the list and knows Wally's fate, but claims it's a secret, then admits cats are bad at keeping secrets. In the last panel a coworker approaches Wally and says 'Nice chair,' implying he already assumes Wally will be laid off and wants his furniture.
punchline: Catbert deliberately leaks the layoff rumor to spread panic, and the coworker immediately eyeing Wally's chair shows everyone now assumes Wally is doomed.
summary: The HR cat taunts an employee with hints about a secret layoff list, and a colleague promptly starts coveting the doomed worker's furniture.

file: 1996/1996-03-11_new product deal_alert in effect_danger new idea_crush o matic.gif
title: Inspiration Alert: Idea Crush-O-Matic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally and I came up with a great new product idea!

transcript.speaker: Speaker box
transcript.text: Inspiration alert in effect!!

transcript.speaker: Lamp
transcript.text: Danger! New idea!

transcript.speaker: Speaker box
transcript.text: State your idea now.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Um, you tell him.

situation: Dilbert announces that he and Wally have a great new product idea. The boss's office erupts with alarms and a warning lamp, and a giant mallet labeled Crush-O-Matic descends above him. Wally nervously pushes Dilbert to be the one to state the idea.
punchline: The company has installed an automated system to smash new ideas, showing that management actively fears and suppresses innovation, and Wally wisely avoids being the one to get crushed.
summary: Management has rigged an alarm-and-hammer contraption to destroy any employee suggestion the moment it is announced.

file: 1996/1996-06-29_employee satisfaction survey_department dismal_assigning satisfaction_task force_problem solved.gif
title: Satisfaction Task Force As Punishment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The results of the employee satisfaction survey are in. Scores for my department are dismal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm assigning you to the satisfaction task force until the problem is solved.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please... anything but that...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How satisfied are you now?

situation: The Boss announces that his department scored terribly on the employee satisfaction survey. He assigns Alice to the satisfaction task force until the problem is solved. When she begs to be spared, he asks how satisfied she is now, treating her misery as a measure of progress.
punchline: The Boss uses the unpleasant task force assignment as a punishment that makes employees even less satisfied, then smugly cites her distress as proof of how bad things are.
summary: After poor morale scores come in, a manager hands out a dreaded committee assignment and taunts the unhappy recipient about her current contentment.

file: 1996/1996-04-09_stupid machine_taken coins_sunny disposition_nothing_dignity_career_drawing line_soda machine.gif
title: Dilbert Rages at Soda Machine

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stupid machine, you've taken my coins and with them my sunny disposition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's nothing left to give!!! You've taken it all!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, you got my dignity and my career, too... but I am drawing the line here, buster!

setting: Office break area beside a soda vending machine
situation: Dilbert angrily jabs the buttons of a soda machine that has swallowed his coins and rants that it has taken his good mood. He keeps escalating, shouting at the machine as colleagues, including The Boss and Alice, stare at his outburst. By the end he has lost his dignity and career in front of them, yet insists he is drawing the line at the machine.
punchline: Dilbert's public tantrum over a lost soda purchase has already cost him his dignity and career, so his declaration that he is 'drawing the line' is absurdly too late.
summary: A man yelling at a vending machine that ate his money humiliates himself in front of coworkers while claiming he'll stand his ground.

file: 1996/1996-07-21_love_strongest force_stupidity_cousin ignorance_morning breath_selfhiness_lust_fear_money_luck_relationships.gif
title: Dogbert Ranks Forces Stronger Than Love

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, do you think love is the strongest force in the universe?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, I'd have to go with stupidity.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Followed closely by its cousin ignorance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Morning breath is number three. Thanks for reminding me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then you've got selfishness, lust, fear, money and luck.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But love is in the top ten, right?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's fourteenth, right after foolish optimism.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Someone needs his little round back scratched.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where's love now?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's down and to the left...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Left!! Left!! Left!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oowahh...

setting: Outdoors on a walk through hills and a fence, starting at a doorway at home
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert whether love is the strongest force in the universe while the two take a walk. Dogbert cynically ranks stupidity, ignorance, morning breath, selfishness, lust, fear, money and luck above love, placing it fourteenth. At the end Dilbert gets his back scratched by Dogbert and asks where love is now.
punchline: After Dogbert cynically ranks love far down the list of universal forces, Dilbert is reduced to blissful moaning when his back is scratched, suggesting that simple physical pleasure beats romance.
summary: A walk becomes a cynical countdown of the forces that rule the world, with affection landing near the bottom until a good back scratch steals the show.

file: 1996/1996-01-04_promoted ted_new manager_new beard_grow from forehead_wrong_punish them_bad opinions.gif
title: Ted's Forehead Beard Promotion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I promoted Ted to be your new manager. I used to think he looked boyish, but his new beard changed that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are either of you the least bit concerned that Ted's beard is growing from his forehead?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: She made it sound as if it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can punish them for having bad opinions.

situation: The Boss announces that he has promoted Ted to be the new manager of Alice and Dilbert, praising Ted's new beard. Alice points out that the beard appears to be growing from Ted's forehead. Ted complains that she made it sound wrong, and the Boss reminds him that as manager he can punish people for their opinions.
punchline: The newly promoted manager is immediately taught that his main new power is to punish employees for disagreeing with him, even when the observation about his odd beard is plainly true.
summary: A freshly promoted manager with a strangely placed beard learns that his new authority lets him retaliate against anyone who points it out.

file: 1996/1996-06-15_diagnose mental health_exercise regulalry_looking depressed_prescription_anti depressant.gif
title: Garbage Man Prescribes Antidepressants

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Dilbert, I notice you've been looking depressed lately.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Here's a prescription for an antidepressant drug. Be sure to exercise regularly and don't skip meals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What makes you think you're qualified to diagnose my mental health?!!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I'd better double it.

situation: A garbage man emptying a trash can tells Dilbert he has seemed depressed and writes him a prescription for an antidepressant, along with health advice. Dilbert angrily asks what qualifies him to diagnose mental health. The garbage man responds by saying he should double the prescription.
punchline: Dilbert's angry reaction to being diagnosed by a garbage man is treated as further proof of his instability, so the unqualified diagnoser doubles the dosage.
summary: An unqualified trash collector hands Dilbert a drug prescription and, when challenged, decides the objection means a bigger dose is needed.

file: 1996/1996-03-14_director of marketing_annoying_illogical_whack_better owner_salary to earnings.gif
title: Ratbert's Annoying Marketing Director Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, we'd like you to be the Director of Marketing for the company we're starting.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Okay! What do I do?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Be as annoying and illogical as you can. We'll whack you in the head with balled-up socks to make you shut up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's definitely better to be an owner than an employee.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's link his salary to earnings! Hee hee!

situation: Dilbert and Wally recruit Ratbert to be Director of Marketing for their new company. Their only job description is to be as annoying and illogical as possible, and they plan to whack him in the head with balled-up socks whenever he needs to be quieted. After remarking that owning beats being an employee, Wally gleefully suggests tying Ratbert's pay to the company's earnings.
punchline: Having cast themselves as owners, Dilbert and Wally cheaply exploit Ratbert by linking his salary to earnings, which for a startup likely means paying him nothing.
summary: Two would-be founders hire a small rodent as their marketing chief, hand him a ridiculous job description, and then hatch a scheme to underpay him.

file: 1996/1996-04-04_cronies_dumpsetr_flies_hire a rat_need experience_proctor and gamble_technology industry_vice president.gif
title: Dumpster Experience Qualifies Rat for Marketing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mister Ratbert, I don't think I can hire a rat to be our Vice President of Marketing. You need experience in the technology industry.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I spent a week in a dumpster at Procter and Gamble.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Close enough! Welcome to the team!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll bring some cronies with me. They're flies.

setting: The Boss's office, during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews Ratbert for a Vice President of Marketing position and objects that Ratbert lacks technology industry experience. Ratbert offers that he spent a week in a Procter and Gamble dumpster, and the Boss happily accepts this as close enough. Ratbert then announces he will bring along his cronies, who are flies.
punchline: The Boss's hiring standards are so low that dumpster-diving at a consumer goods company counts as technology industry experience, and he'll hire a rat and his flies as executives.
summary: A rat talks his way into an executive marketing job by stretching a stint in a corporate dumpster into relevant experience.

file: 1996/1996-11-05_dogbert consulting_credibility_money_better spent consulting_downsizing_analysis_upgrade deluxe service_science.gif
title: Dogbert's Analysis Is Magazine Page

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert Consulting Company to add credibility to my decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As my analysis shows, it's much better to give your money to me than to waste it on future downsizees such as yourselves.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What analysis? This is a page ripped out of the magazine in our lobby.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Perhaps you should upgrade to my deluxe service.

situation: The Boss announces he has hired Dogbert's consulting firm to lend credibility to his decisions. Dogbert presents an 'analysis' concluding that employees should give their money to him rather than waste it on their own future layoffs. An employee examines the handout and discovers it is just a page torn from the lobby magazine, and Dogbert suggests upgrading to his deluxe service.
punchline: Dogbert's expensive consulting analysis is a ripped-out magazine page, and he responds to the exposure by upselling a pricier service.
summary: A consultant's supposedly rigorous report turns out to be pilfered reading material, and he blithely tries to sell a premium version.

file: 1996/1996-07-30_reform tax code_idiots_have pets_define idiots_pay taxes.gif
title: Dogbert's Idiot Tax Reform Campaign

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Vote for me and I will reform the tax code so that only idiots have to pay taxes!

transcript.speaker: Crowd
transcript.text: Yahoo!! Dogbert Dogbert Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I hope nobody asks me to define "idiots."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So, under your plan I wouldn't pay any taxes, right?

setting: A political rally, then Dilbert's living room couch
situation: Dogbert stands on a podium and promises a crowd that only idiots will have to pay taxes under his reform plan. The crowd cheers wildly and chants his name. Later, Dogbert sits on the couch worrying about defining idiots, while Dilbert, hugging a toy-like object, asks whether he will be exempt from taxes.
punchline: Dilbert's confident assumption that he wouldn't be an idiot (while sitting there asking such a naive question) suggests he is exactly the sort of person who would end up paying, and the cheering crowd is too foolish to notice the vague promise.
summary: A candidate dog wins over a roaring crowd with a tax pledge aimed at idiots, then privately frets over the definition while a hopeful Dilbert asks if he's exempt.

file: 1996/1996-09-18_review 80 million lines_computer code_system_probelm_year 2000_all zeros and ones.gif
title: Ratbert Reviews Code for Y2K

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, your job is to review eighty million lines of computer code in the company's systems.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're looking for any reference to the current year. Those pieces of code will be a problem when the year is 2000.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Gotcha.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Six months later

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm happy to report that the date did not show up once. In fact, it was all just zeros and ones!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oops.

setting: Dogbert's office with a computer on a desk
situation: Dogbert assigns Ratbert the enormous task of reviewing eighty million lines of code for references to the current year, which will break at the year 2000. Six months later Ratbert proudly reports that he never found a date, because the code was all just zeros and ones. Dogbert realizes the instructions were not specific enough.
punchline: Ratbert took the task literally and examined the raw binary, where no date could ever appear, proving he completely missed the point of the Y2K review.
summary: A tiny rodent hired to hunt for date bugs in a mountain of software returns half a year later with a useless, literal-minded finding.

file: 1996/1996-06-20_quality college_clown college_prerequisite_secretaries day_angry clown.gif
title: Quality College Becomes Clown College

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I asked you to enroll me in the Quality College, but the confirmation says Clown College.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's a prerequisite course.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: This is gonna cost me on Secretaries Day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope it's okay to be an angry clown.

situation: The Boss holds a confirmation slip and complains to his secretary Carol that she enrolled him in Clown College instead of the Quality College he requested. Carol deadpans that it is a prerequisite course. She privately thinks the stunt will cost the Boss on Secretaries Day, while the oblivious Boss wonders whether it is acceptable to be an angry clown.
punchline: Carol deliberately enrolled the Boss in Clown College as a jab at his foolishness, and he is too clueless to notice he is being insulted, accepting the absurd 'prerequisite' explanation.
summary: A secretary quietly gets back at her boss by signing him up for the wrong school and passing it off as a required first step.

file: 1996/1996-04-07_boss zone_no time_no logic_urgent work_relax_work smarter_not harder_angel of cynicism_inspirational moral_freedom_not caring_quality of work.gif
title: Boss Zone: Relax But Work Urgently

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go home, Dilbert. Relax! You're working too hard!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You told me to finish this by tomorrow. You said it's urgent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Relax! Go home! Shoo!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Suddenly Dilbert is sucked into the "Boss Zone" where time and logic do not apply.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I relax AND do urgent work at the same time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Work smarter, not harder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaeeii!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mercifully, the Angel of Cynicism appears.

transcript.speaker: Angel of Cynicism
transcript.text: Slap something together in the morning. He won't look at it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The inspirational moral...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Freedom's just another word for not caring about the quality of your work!

setting: Office cubicle, then a surreal swirling 'Boss Zone'
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to go home and relax because he is working too hard, even though he previously demanded an urgent deliverable by tomorrow. Dilbert is pulled into the illogical 'Boss Zone' where he cannot reconcile the contradictory instructions. An Angel of Cynicism advises him to slap something together since the Boss won't check it, and Dilbert cheerfully adopts that as his moral.
punchline: Faced with a boss's contradictory orders, Dilbert finds freedom by simply no longer caring about the quality of his work, since nobody will review it anyway.
summary: A manager's self-contradicting instructions trap an engineer in a nonsensical limbo until a cynical angel shows him that indifference is the way out.

file: 1996/1996-06-16_downsize wally_downsized_economic neccessity_exercise didn't work_salary_stressful job_team builkding_value of stock options_afford movies_money.gif
title: Downsized So Boss Can Afford Movies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I've decided to downsize you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's nothing personal, just an economic necessity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I calculated how much your salary was dragging down the value of my stock options.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Without you, I can afford to go to the movies one additional time per year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And let's face it: recreation is important when one has a stressful job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, why don't you downsize Wally instead. You'll save enough in office supplies to buy popcorn too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sheesh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mmm...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How'd it go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know that team-building exercise we did last week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It didn't take.

setting: The Boss's office and a cubicle area
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being downsized, explaining that his salary was lowering the value of the Boss's stock options and that the savings will let the Boss see one more movie per year. Dilbert angrily suggests downsizing Wally instead, and the Boss considers it. Afterward Dilbert tells Wally that last week's team-building exercise didn't work.
punchline: Dilbert's willingness to sacrifice Wally to save his own job shows the team-building exercise failed, while the Boss's trivial reason for the layoff exposes how callous corporate downsizing can be.
summary: A manager lays off an employee to fund a few extra film outings, and the worker promptly tries to pass the axe to a colleague, proving that workplace bonding exercises achieved nothing.

file: 1996/1996-09-05_administrative task_beg for asisiatnace_network administrator_new password_upgrading network_forgotten password.gif
title: Network Admin Berates Password Seeker

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Network administrator

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have forgotten my password. I humbly beg for assistance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have no time for boring administrative tasks, you fool! I'm busy upgrading the network!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could have given me a new password in the time it took to belittle me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, but which option would give me job satisfaction?

situation: Dilbert goes to Dogbert, the network administrator, and humbly asks for help because he has forgotten his password. Dogbert scolds him for interrupting important network upgrade work. Dilbert points out that resetting the password would have been faster than the insults, and Dogbert replies that berating him is more satisfying.
punchline: The network administrator deliberately wastes more time insulting users than it would take to do the simple task, because belittling people gives him more job satisfaction than helping them.
summary: A tech support gatekeeper would rather spend his time humiliating a petitioner than quickly fixing a trivial problem, simply because it's more fun.

file: 1996/1996-05-18_talk of diversity_smart creatures endure_surrounded by dolts_hold secret meetings_constant struggle.gif
title: Smart Creatures Suffer Among Dolts

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: With all this talk of "diversity" there's no mention of the pain we smart creatures endure while surrounded by dolts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good point. I don't know how we do it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It looks like I'll have to hold secret meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, our lives are a constant struggle.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, at his desk and computer
situation: Dogbert complains that corporate talk about diversity ignores the suffering of intelligent beings who are surrounded by fools. Dilbert agrees, and Dogbert announces he will have to hold secret meetings for smart creatures. Dilbert, now humming happily with musical notes, cheerfully says their lives are a constant struggle.
punchline: Dilbert and Dogbert claim to be suffering victims of the stupidity around them, but their smug, cheerful tone shows they enjoy feeling superior, and their 'secret meetings' mock the exclusive nature of diversity programs.
summary: Dogbert proposes a clandestine support group for the brilliant minority tormented by their dim-witted coworkers, and Dilbert cheerfully signs on to the self-pity.

file: 1996/1996-07-07_performance review_daughter_cub girl cookies_volume level_downsizer_low performer_fast tracker_united way chairperson.gif
title: Boss Ties Review to Cookie Sales

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be writing your performance review this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But this morning I'm helping my daughter sell Cub Girl cookies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For your shopping convenience I have assigned a name to each volume level.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Zero to four boxes is the "Downsizer" volume...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Five to eight boxes is the "Low Performer" volume level.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's say six hundred boxes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ahh... the "Fast Tracker." An excellent choice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your daughter's name?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh... Gotta go.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I only bought twelve boxes. Now I'm the "United Way" chairperson.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just signed your name for six hundred more.

situation: The Boss announces he will write Dilbert's performance review that afternoon, but first he pitches his daughter's Cub Girl cookies, attaching career-themed labels to each purchase volume. Dilbert cheekily orders six hundred boxes to earn the 'Fast Tracker' label, then asks for the daughter's name so he can place the order, and the Boss hurries away. Wally, who bought only twelve boxes and got made United Way chairperson, tells Dilbert he signed Dilbert's name for six hundred more.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to game the Boss's coercive cookie sales is undone by a bigger consequence: his gaming of the system ends with him on the hook for six hundred boxes, while the Boss escapes the moment anyone asks for his daughter's name.
summary: A manager leverages an upcoming review to pressure an employee into buying fundraiser cookies, and the employee's clever overbuying backfires on him.

file: 1996/1996-11-03_chocolate bar_smell_wallet_impatience.gif
title: Dilbert Steals Purse for Chocolate

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmm... soon you will be mine, little chocolate bar.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: I think I have exact change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can smell it through the wrapper.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Here's a nickel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I rub it on my arm to get the total body experience.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: No, that's a breath mint.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am transported to another dimension.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Ooh, a roll of pennies...

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: No, lipstick.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: I'll give you a check.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Where's that checkbook?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Snatch

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stomp stomp stomp stomp stomp stomp

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What a funny day to forget my wallet.

situation: Dilbert is fixated on buying a chocolate bar, savoring its smell and rubbing it on his arm while the cashier slowly digs through her purse for exact change. When she fumbles around without finding the money, Dilbert snatches her purse and stomps in anger. In the end he calmly admits he forgot his wallet while the cashier glares at him holding her ruined purse.
punchline: Dilbert spends the whole transaction impatiently mocking the cashier's slowness, then reveals he has no wallet and cannot pay himself, making his impatience hypocritical.
summary: A chocolate-obsessed customer grows frustrated while a cashier rummages through her purse, only to confess he has no money of his own.

file: 1996/1996-06-22_employee suggestions_harmless_stupud_theorym_replace pencils.gif
title: Harmless and Stupid Suggestions Get Approved

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The only employee suggestions that get accepted are the ones that are harmless and stupid.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I submitted some harmless and stupid ideas to test my theory.

transcript.speaker: Suggestion (read by The Boss)
transcript.text: Suggestion: Replace all #2 pencils with #4 pencils. The hard lead lasts longer yet costs the same.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That could work.

setting: Office hallway, then a conference room and the boss's office
situation: Wally tells Dilbert that the only employee suggestions management accepts are the harmless and stupid ones. He says he submitted a few deliberately dumb ideas to test this theory. The Boss reads one of them, a pointless pencil swap, and thinks it could work.
punchline: The Boss approving a trivial, pointless pencil suggestion proves Wally's theory that management only adopts ideas that are harmless and stupid.
summary: A cynical employee's experiment with deliberately silly ideas shows his manager will only ever approve suggestions that change nothing.

file: 1996/1996-09-13_abandon startegy_making good products_ours strategy mergers_business spin offs_random reorgozations_accelerate_stock price_fruitless partnerships.gif
title: Company Abandons Good Products, Stock Rises

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: The company announced that we will "abandon our strategy of making good products..."

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: From now on we'll "pursue a desperate strategy of mergers, business spin-offs, fruitless partnerships and random reorganizations."

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: "And we'll accelerate our program of paying the good employees to leave."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stock price?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Up three points.

situation: A coworker reads aloud a company announcement to Dilbert and Wally while Alice listens over the cubicle wall. The announcement admits the company is giving up on making good products in favor of desperate mergers, spin-offs, and random reorganizations, and will pay good employees to leave. Alice asks about the stock price, and Wally reports it is up.
punchline: The company's openly self-destructive strategy is rewarded by the stock market, showing that investors cheer for corporate dysfunction rather than actual quality.
summary: A frank memo confesses a ruinous corporate plan, and the only thing anyone cares about is that shares are climbing.

file: 1996/1996-01-14_little talk_finish project_estimate resource requirements_endorsement_uninpsired_incompetence_incessant demands_strangled prodcutivity_performance_expectations.gif
title: Wally Blames Boss for Late Project

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We need to have a little talk...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You told me to finish my project in a week but it's taken two months.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This doesn't look good for your ability to estimate resource requirements.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Frankly, it's not much of an endorsement of your leadership either. I was uninspired the whole time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And don't even get me started about your incompetence at budgeting. I spent way more than you predicted!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your incessant demands for status reports were like a rope that strangled my productivity!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Bottom line, your performance did NOT meet my expectations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, Wally, do you still think the best defense is a good offense?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It seemed like such a good idea.

situation: Wally storms into the Boss's office and delivers a performance review of the Boss, blaming him for a project that took two months instead of one week. He criticizes the Boss's estimating, leadership, budgeting and demands for status reports. In the last panel Wally is battered and bandaged, and Dilbert asks whether his strategy worked.
punchline: Wally's tactic of attacking his boss pre-emptively to deflect blame for his own slow work clearly backfired, leaving him injured.
summary: Hoping to dodge blame for a late project, a lazy employee turns the tables and critiques his boss, only to end up bruised and regretful.
keywords: best defense is a good offense

file: 1996/1996-10-04_iso 9000 certified_product looks good_internal porcess_well documented_documented porcess_ace_double price.gif
title: ISO 9000 Process Doubles the Price

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Your product looks good, but you can't be our supplier unless your company is ISO 9000 certified.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... you don't care how bad our internal processes are, as long as they're well-documented and used consistently?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our documented process says I must now laugh in your face and double our price.

situation: A customer tells the Boss that his company can only become a supplier if it is ISO 9000 certified. The Boss checks that the standard only demands well-documented, consistently used processes, regardless of quality. He then cites his own documented process as the reason to laugh at the customer and double the price.
punchline: ISO 9000 only requires following documented procedures, not good ones, so the Boss's documented process of gouging the customer is perfectly compliant.
summary: A supplier exploits a quality certification's fixation on paperwork by following a documented procedure that mocks the buyer and inflates the bill.

file: 1996/1996-07-29_supreme ruler_universe_next movie_the show_embraced you_befor ehsow_no visible mouth.gif
title: Dogbert Poses as Sharon Stone

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Larry, I'm here to announce my candidacy for Supreme Ruler of the Universe.

transcript.speaker: Larry
transcript.text: That's funny! Tell us about your next movie, Sharon.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm not Sharon Stone. I said that to get on the show.

transcript.speaker: Larry
transcript.text: So... when I embraced you before the show...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think we're both glad I have no visible mouth.

situation: Dogbert has talked his way onto a late-night talk show by pretending to be actress Sharon Stone, then announces he is running to be Supreme Ruler of the Universe. The host assumes it is a joke and asks about his next movie, so Dogbert admits the deception. The host then realizes he hugged Dogbert backstage.
punchline: The host awkwardly recalls embracing the supposed actress, and Dogbert dryly notes that his lack of a visible mouth spared them both from an even more embarrassing kiss.
summary: A dog sneaks onto a talk show by passing himself off as a movie star, and the host realizes too late that the affectionate greeting he gave was meant for a dog.

file: 1996/1996-04-19_dance_dogbert_employees_hired_more creative_poetry_souls_special blend_spiritually fulfilled_dog with hat_business.gif
title: Dogbert's Soul-Healing Dance Consultancy

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can make your employees more creative and spiritually fulfilled.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I use my special blend of poetry and dance to touch their souls.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. You're hired.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There once was a dog with a hat... who got paid to dance like that...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey! My soul just healed!

situation: Dogbert, wearing a hat, pitches the Boss on a consulting service that makes employees more creative and spiritually fulfilled through poetry and dance. The Boss hires him instantly. Dogbert then performs a self-serving poem and dance for the staff, and Wally claims his soul has been healed.
punchline: Dogbert's 'soul-touching' poem is really just a rhyme about a dog getting paid to dance, exposing the consulting gig as a scam, and Wally's instant 'healing' is a sarcastic or sycophantic reaction.
summary: A hat-wearing dog talks his way into a consulting job by promising spiritual enrichment, then delivers a poem about his own paycheck.

file: 1996/1996-10-17_consultant_attractive women_trade show booth_rejected idea_sexist_demeaning_increase traffic_dental floss_thong bikini dilberts_business.gif
title: Boss's Trade Show Booth Traffic Scheme

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Our consultant suggested putting attractive women in our booth at the trade show.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I rejected that idea. It is sexist and demeaning. I have a better idea to increase traffic to our booth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the dental floss for?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's your thong bikini. You'll stand in front of our competitor's booth.

situation: At a meeting, Alice reports that a consultant proposed placing attractive women in the company's trade show booth. The Boss says he rejected the idea as sexist and demeaning, then announces a better plan. Alice holds up dental floss and explains it is Dilbert's thong bikini, which he will wear in front of a competitor's booth.
punchline: The Boss rejects objectifying women as demeaning, but his 'better' idea is to objectify and humiliate Dilbert instead, a hollow, self-congratulating double standard.
summary: A boss proudly turns down a sexist marketing tactic only to replace it with an equally demeaning stunt aimed at one of his own male employees.

file: 1996/1996-07-05_pre meeting_preliminary pre meeting meeting_without planning_think funny_wally dilbert_the boss.gif
title: Premeeting Before the Premeeting Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's have a little premeeting to prepare for the meeting tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! Do you think it's safe to jump right into the premeeting without planning it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, let's get this preliminary premeeting meeting going.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You think you're funny, but you're not.

situation: The Boss proposes a premeeting to prepare for tomorrow's meeting, then jokes that it might be unsafe to start it without planning. Dilbert is sitting at his desk, and the group then gathers around a conference table where the Boss announces a preliminary premeeting meeting. Wally tells the Boss he thinks he's funny but isn't.
punchline: The Boss mocks meeting culture by escalating to a meeting about planning a meeting, and the staff are unamused because the absurdity is exactly how their meetings actually work.
summary: A manager's gag about holding meetings to plan meetings falls flat with his unimpressed employees.

file: 1996/1996-02-15_revised standard employment agreement_only company_pudding head_attitude_lawyes_rabies_psychology.gif
title: Employment Agreement With Attitude

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the revised standard employment agreement. Sign it or be fired.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "This agreement is between the company (hereafter referred to as 'the only company that would ever hire you') and you (hereafter called 'pudding head')."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It seems to have a bit of attitude.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our lawyers turned on us. I suspect rabies.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a revised standard employment agreement and tells him to sign it or be fired. Dilbert reads aloud from it and finds the contract openly insults him, calling the company 'the only company that would ever hire you' and him 'pudding head'. The Boss explains the hostile wording by suggesting the company's lawyers have contracted rabies.
punchline: The Boss treats an insulting, hostile employment contract as the product of rabid lawyers rather than as anything unfair, while the contract itself bluntly states how little leverage the employee has.
summary: A manager demands a signature on a new work contract that turns out to be full of insults, and blames the legal department's apparent madness.
keywords: only company that would hire you

file: 1996/1996-09-08_minor edits_product brochure_causes hallucinations_sterility_positive spin_greatest writing challenge_same old sights_great gift_conscince_three pager.gif
title: Spinning a Hallucinating, Sterilizing Product

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, we need a few minor edits on our product brochure.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Minor? Uh-oh...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've discovered that our product causes hallucinations and sterility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: See if you can put a positive spin on that.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: This will be my greatest writing challenge yet.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: "Are you tired of the same old sights? We've got you covered."

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: "... Makes a great gift for those people who - in your opinion - should not reproduce."

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Ooh... I feel a tiny pang of conscience.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That's one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So the brochure was only a three-panger?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Yeah, and I think I faked the third one.

situation: The Boss asks technical writer Tina to make minor edits to a product brochure, revealing the product causes hallucinations and sterility, and tells her to put a positive spin on it. Tina writes cheerful marketing copy that turns the side effects into selling points. She feels only a tiny pang of conscience, which Dilbert later learns was one of only three, and she admits she faked the third.
punchline: Tina's conscience barely registers while spinning dangerous side effects into sales pitches, and she even has to fake the third pang, showing how little ethical resistance marketing writers have.
summary: A writer cheerfully reframes a product's harmful side effects as perks and discovers she has almost no conscience about it.

file: 1996/1996-09-26_team building exercise_mile from shore_swim back_only hope_intelligent doplohin_plaught_tuna net.gif
title: Dolphin Offers Tuna Net Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The team-building exercise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... I'm a mile from shore and too exhausted to swim back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My only hope is that an intelligent dolphin will see my plight and rescue me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm in luck!

transcript.speaker: Dolphin
transcript.text: Two words: Tuna... net.

setting: Open water in the ocean, during a team-building exercise
situation: Dilbert is stranded in the ocean a mile from shore, too exhausted to swim back, and hopes an intelligent dolphin will rescue him. A dolphin does appear, but instead of helping him it just says 'Tuna... net.'
punchline: The dolphin is intelligent enough to speak, but it only offers a terse, unhelpful reminder of dolphins' tuna-net grievance instead of rescuing him, a jab at the myth of helpful dolphins.
summary: A drifting, worn-out swimmer finally gets his wished-for dolphin visit, but the animal has a grudge instead of a lifeline.

file: 1996/1996-01-09_new boss is posessed_evil force_one solution_drive stake_heart_be cruel_borrow pen_wimpy retractable.gif
title: Stake Through the Boss's Heart

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My new boss is possessed by an evil force. We need your advice, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There is only one solution. You must drive a stake through his heart.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no way we could be so cruel!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can I borrow your pen? All I have is this wimpy retractable.

situation: Dilbert and Alice consult Dogbert about their new boss, who they believe is possessed by an evil force. Dogbert advises driving a stake through the boss's heart. Dilbert objects that they could never be so cruel, while Alice asks to borrow a pen because hers is too wimpy for the job.
punchline: While Dilbert pretends to be morally opposed to killing the boss, Alice has already embraced the idea and only worries about having a sturdy enough pen to use as a stake.
summary: Faced with a deadly vampire-style solution to their awful new manager, one coworker recoils while the other just wants better equipment.

file: 1996/1996-10-01_audit_documented procedures_divided_two groups_unethical_unprodcutive_train department_lie to auditor_document_inane prcedures.gif
title: ISO Audit: Unethical or Unproductive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll be having an ISO 9000 audit soon. They'll check to see if we follow our own documented procedures for everything we do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've divided our preparation tasks into two groups: unethical and unproductive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll train our department to lie to the auditor. You can document our inane procedures.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No fair. You did unethical last time too!

situation: The Boss announces an upcoming ISO 9000 audit that will check whether the department follows its own documented procedures. He splits the preparation work into unethical and unproductive tasks, keeps the lying-to-the-auditor job for himself, and assigns Dilbert the tedious documentation work. Dilbert objects that the Boss got the unethical task last time as well.
punchline: The Boss treats lying to the auditor as the easy, desirable job and pushes the tedious paperwork onto Dilbert, showing that quality certification is about gaming the audit rather than improving anything.
summary: Facing a quality-standards inspection, a manager hands his employee the soul-crushing paperwork while reserving the deception for himself, as if choosing the better chore.

file: 1996/1996-08-16_dogbert_career counselor_enough people quit_best startegy_convince coworkers_video_exact moment_life force_leaves body.gif
title: Dogbert's Layoff Avoidance Strategy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Career counselor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The company won't lay you off if enough people quit first.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your best strategy is to convince your co-workers that their jobs are intolerable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We do this for all the young employees, Asok. I'll capture on video the exact moment that your life force leaves your body.

setting: Office, in a career counseling session at a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a career counselor, advises a balding man with glasses that the company will not lay him off if enough people quit first, so he should convince co-workers their jobs are intolerable. In the last panel the man holds a video camera and a flashlight aimed at Asok, announcing he will film the moment Asok's life force leaves his body.
punchline: The 'career counseling' amounts to sabotaging colleagues' morale and then gleefully filming a young employee being crushed by the soul-draining corporate grind.
summary: A canine career advisor coaches a worker to survive downsizing by driving his colleagues to resign, while a camera is readied to record a new hire's spirit dying.

file: 1996/1996-09-03_network administartor_my card_email_wag tail_pager numeber_tilde.gif
title: Network Administrator Can't Be Reached

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I got hired as the network administrator for your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my card. You can only reach me by e-mail or by pager.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When the network breaks, no e-mail. I'll just sit around and wag my tail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your pager number has a tilde... How do I dial a tilde?

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with Dogbert sitting on a chair
situation: Dogbert announces he has been hired as the network administrator for Dilbert's company and hands over his business card. He explains that he can only be reached by e-mail or pager, so when the network is down he will simply sit around doing nothing. Dilbert studies the card and discovers the pager number contains a tilde, which cannot be dialed.
punchline: The network administrator is unreachable by design: his only contact methods fail precisely when the network breaks, and his pager number contains a character that can't be dialed.
summary: A newly hired dog admin hands out a contact card that guarantees nobody can reach him when the network goes down.

file: 1996/1996-06-07_filbert's mother_all you can eat_mall_got a booth.gif
title: Dad Stuck at All-You-Can-Eat Buffet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Dilbert, I found your father. He's been at the "all you can eat" restaurant in the mall since 1989.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: He's so literal—he didn't want to leave until it was "all he could eat."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When's he coming home?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I'm thinking of joining him. He got a booth.

setting: Dilbert's mother's living room and Dilbert's desk, connected by a phone call
situation: Dilbert's mother phones him from her armchair to report that his father has been sitting in a mall's all-you-can-eat restaurant since 1989. She explains he took the slogan literally and refused to leave until he could eat no more. When Dilbert asks when he'll return, she says she may join him because he has a booth.
punchline: Dilbert's father has taken the buffet slogan so literally that he has been eating for years, and his wife is so unbothered by it that she is considering moving in with him for the comfortable booth.
summary: A mother casually reports that her husband has spent years at a mall buffet because he took its slogan at face value, and she thinks about joining him.

file: 1996/1996-08-25_accordingly_decrease details_greetings_increase lies_more funding_need more funding_variety super powers_senior vice president.gif
title: Coaching Staff to Lie to Executive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our senior vice president will be dropping in today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember to increase your lies accordingly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And decrease the details you provide.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I think you're being too informative, I'll signal by fidgeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just say everything is fine, but we need more funding.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here he comes.

transcript.speaker: Senior Vice President
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. How is everyone?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not saying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm fine, but I need more funding.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I have a wide variety of super powers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I feel a sudden, urgent need to unload my stock options.

transcript.speaker: Senior Vice President
transcript.text: Fidget fidget.

setting: Conference room and office during an executive visit
situation: The Boss briefs his team before the senior vice president arrives, instructing them to lie more, give fewer details, and ask for funding, and he will fidget if they say too much. When the executive asks how everyone is, the team members give absurd answers, including claiming super powers. The Boss then realizes the executive's fidgeting means he is dumping his stock options.
punchline: The Boss's carefully coached deception backfires when the senior vice president's own fidgeting signals that he suspects the company is in trouble and wants to sell his stock options.
summary: A manager rehearses his staff in feeding falsehoods and vagueness to a visiting executive, only for the executive's nervous tic to reveal he is bailing out of the company.

file: 1996/1996-01-13_shared laser printer_apollo space mission_wally invented cursor.gif
title: Wally Races to the Printer

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gotta hurry. One...two...three...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have twelve seconds to get to the shared laser printer.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Guess who saved the Apollo 13 space mission.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know that Wally invented the cursor?

setting: Office cubicles and the shared laser printer area
situation: Wally clicks print on his computer and then dashes toward the shared laser printer, counting down the seconds he has to reach it. When he arrives, Alice and Dilbert are standing at the printer reading his printout, which makes boastful claims about Wally's accomplishments, such as saving Apollo 13 and inventing the cursor. Wally peeks around the partition, watching them read.
punchline: Wally prints flattering fake claims about himself and races to the printer so he can plant them where coworkers will find them, but he is too late and they read his self-promotion.
summary: A coworker sprints to the communal printer to retrieve his own outlandish self-praise before anyone else sees it.

file: 1996/1996-01-10_stake through heart_demon mossed boss_raisin sized heart_blue betty pen.gif
title: Alice Needs Pens for Boss-Slaying
