transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice is ready to drive a stake through the heart of our demon-possessed boss.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whack whack whack

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's times like these when I'm glad my heart is the size of a raisin!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need all of your pens, including "Blue Betty."

setting: Office hallway outside a doorway or cubicle wall
situation: Dilbert warns a coworker that Alice is about to drive a stake through their demon-possessed boss's heart. Whacking sounds are heard from behind the wall, and then the Boss appears untouched, relieved that his tiny heart was missed. Alice emerges and demands everyone's pens, including a favorite named Blue Betty, since she has been using pens as stakes.
punchline: Alice's improvised wooden stakes were pens, and the Boss survives only because his heart is so small, implying he is heartless and she keeps missing it.
summary: A coworker's grim warning about Alice's vampire-style attack on their boss ends with the boss gloating about his own cold, shrunken heart while Alice raids the office for more pens.

file: 1996/1996-02-20_software development work_impoverished nation_elbonia_high quality code_no risk_red alert.elbonia_be computer tomorrow.gif
title: Elbonian Outsourcing: Humans as Computers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I moved our software development work to the impoverished nation of Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm brilliant. They write high-quality code for six cents a day! There's no risk!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Red alert!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Tomorrow, YOU be the computer.

setting: Dilbert's office, then a muddy village in Elbonia
situation: The Boss proudly tells Dilbert he has outsourced software development to Elbonia, boasting that the workers write high-quality code for six cents a day with no risk. Dilbert privately thinks 'red alert.' In Elbonia, one man hands another a box to wear on his head and tells him he will be the computer, revealing the country lacks actual computers.
punchline: The Boss's cheap outsourcing plan is far riskier than he thinks, because Elbonia is so impoverished that it has no computers and the developers will have to act as the computers themselves.
summary: A manager brags about shipping coding work to a poor country for pennies, unaware that the workers there don't even own computers.

file: 1996/1996-08-08_peer performance_reviews_limited budget_raises_slander coworkers_more money_weasel boy_hate empoyees.gif
title: Boss Encourages Slandering Coworkers for Raises

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time to do peer-performance reviews!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, there's a limited budget for raises. Your best strategy is to slander your co-workers so there's more money for you!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I plan to say very nice things about YOU.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice try, weasel-boy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) Managing is easy when you hate the employees.

situation: The Boss announces peer-performance reviews and openly advises his employees to slander each other, since the raise budget is limited and fewer raises for others means more for themselves. Wally tries to flatter Dilbert with promised praise, and Dilbert accuses him of scheming. The Boss's thought bubble reveals he manages by despising his staff.
punchline: The Boss deliberately sets up a review system that pits employees against each other, and privately admits he finds managing easy because he hates the employees.
summary: A manager turns performance reviews into a backstabbing contest over a small pool of raise money while quietly admitting he holds his staff in contempt.

file: 1996/1996-03-31_barry_epic mini series_hundreds of hours_quitters_retrospect_special bonus_staring at computer.gif
title: Bonus for Staring at Screensaver

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's my honor to present this special bonus check to Barry.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's you.

transcript.speaker: Barry
transcript.text: My name is Barry??

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is for working hundreds of hours of overtime.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: While you quitters were going home by 9 PM every night...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Barry remained at work staring at his computer for hours.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's important to recognize extra effort.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sadly, that's the end of the special bonus budget for the year.

transcript.speaker: Barry
transcript.text: Burp

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In retrospect, I shouldn't have told Barry that his screen saver is an epic mini-series.

situation: The Boss publicly presents a special bonus check to an employee named Barry, who doesn't even recognize his own name when Alice points him out. The Boss praises him for hundreds of hours of overtime while criticizing the other employees as quitters for going home at 9 PM. It turns out Barry was just staring at his computer, and the Boss admits he told Barry his screen saver was an epic mini-series.
punchline: The Boss rewards 'extra effort' that is really just an employee idly watching a screen saver, which the Boss himself mistook for gripping entertainment, showing how management confuses visible hours with real productivity.
summary: A manager lavishes a bonus on a worker whose long hours were spent gazing at a screen saver, while scolding everyone who left at a reasonable time.

file: 1996/1996-07-31_association_generous controbution_get elected_prison_cover tracks_wrecks chances_briber of month.gif
title: Bribing Dogbert Backfires Spectacularly

transcript.speaker: Lobbyist
transcript.text: I'm from the Association for Products That Are Bad for You. Here's a generous contribution to your campaign.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is so cool! I'll use your money to get elected, then I'll put your entire industry in prison to cover my tracks!

transcript.speaker: Lobbyist
transcript.text: This probably wrecks my chances of being named Briber of the Month.

setting: Dogbert's office, then the lobbyist's car
situation: A lobbyist from an association of harmful-product makers hands Dogbert a briefcase of campaign money. Dogbert cheerfully announces he will use the cash to win office and then imprison the lobbyist's whole industry to hide the evidence. The lobbyist drives away, reflecting on his lost chance at an award.
punchline: The lobbyist's bribe is turned against him, and his only concern is that the failure will hurt his standing in the bribery profession.
summary: A lobbyist's campaign payoff to Dogbert is promptly weaponized against the very industry that paid it.

file: 1996/1996-03-23_special chromosome_assignments_waste of time_sweet smell_men more perceptive.gif
title: Men Sense Pointless Assignments Instinctively

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't believe men have a special chromosome to tell them which assignments are a waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We do.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I will test the theory on young Asok the intern.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Mmm... the sweet smell of unnecessary work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe men are more perceptive than you'd think.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: She's aroused. I'll make my move.

situation: Alice walks past Dilbert and declares she doesn't believe men have a special instinct for spotting pointless assignments, and Dilbert quietly insists they do. She decides to test the idea by handing a piece of paper to Asok the intern. Asok sniffs the paper and comments on unnecessary work, but Alice's reaction makes him misread it as romantic interest.
punchline: Asok does detect the pointless assignment, which seems to prove the theory, but he then wrongly assumes Alice is aroused and plans to make a pass at her, showing men's perceptiveness is limited to that one thing.
summary: Alice sets out to disprove a stereotype about men sensing useless work, only to have her test subject spot the busywork and then completely misinterpret her intentions.

file: 1996/1996-11-07_liz_dating other men_internet_find hot babe_credit card number_inquisitive_technology.gif
title: Online Dating Scam Seems Charming

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Liz started dating other men. Two can play at that game.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will use the power of the Internet to find a hot babe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ah! Here's one.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: She wants your credit card number.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh! She's inquisitive. I like that.

setting: Dilbert's home at his computer desk
situation: After his girlfriend Liz starts seeing other men, Dilbert decides to retaliate by searching the Internet for a date. He finds a woman online, and Dogbert, looking over his shoulder, points out that she is asking for his credit card number. Dilbert misreads this obvious scam as a charming sign of curiosity.
punchline: Dilbert's romantic desperation makes him interpret a blatant credit card scam as the woman being flirtatiously inquisitive.
summary: A spurned Dilbert goes online hunting for a new romance and cheerfully mistakes a fraudster's request for his card details for genuine interest.

file: 1996/1996-02-13_hype_most excellent_pry myself away_warming device_windows 95_tormenting people.gif
title: Catbert Loves Warm Monitor Perch

transcript.text: I know I should be off tormenting people...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But I can't pry myself away from this most excellent butt-warming device.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's probably because of the hype, but I'm thinking this would be even better with "Windows 95."

setting: Catbert's perch on top of a computer monitor
situation: Catbert, the evil HR cat, sits on top of a computer monitor, musing that he ought to be out tormenting employees. He admits he can't leave the monitor because it keeps his rear end warm. In the last panel he drapes himself over it and wonders whether it would be even better with Windows 95.
punchline: Catbert values a computer only as a heated seat, yet even he is swayed by the Windows 95 hype and imagines the upgrade would make his warming device better.
summary: A cat lounging on a warm computer monitor is so content that he considers whether a famously hyped operating system upgrade would improve his cozy spot.

file: 1996/1996-04-12_dogcart versus catbert_dilbert death_bob the donosuar_fur wedgie_lost paperwork_ordering execustion.gif
title: Dogbert Sabotages Catbert's Death Sentence

transcript.text: Dogbert versus Catbert

transcript.text: I understand you've sentenced Dilbert to death.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Is that a problem?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My assistant, Bob the Dinosaur, will now demonstrate how to give a cat a "fur wedgie."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been pardoned. Somehow they lost the paperwork ordering my execution.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

situation: Dogbert confronts Catbert, the evil HR director, about having sentenced Dilbert to death. When Catbert shrugs it off, Dogbert has his dinosaur assistant Bob threaten to give the cat a painful fur wedgie. Dilbert then arrives, announcing he has been pardoned because the execution paperwork went missing.
punchline: Dogbert's threat of a fur wedgie got the execution order made to vanish, and his deadpan line about the paperwork falling into a crack hints that he engineered the loss himself.
summary: A menacing dinosaur-assisted warning makes a death warrant mysteriously disappear, saving a grateful engineer.

file: 1996/1996-10-16_attention grabbing_best result_booth babes_botth_magic tricks_raffkles_several options_special effcets_trade show.gif
title: Raffling Off the Booth Babes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: 1. Magic tricks 2. Special effects 3. Raffles 4. Booth babes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For the best result, combine all four: Create the illusion that you're raffling off the booth babes.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Booth babes?

setting: Conference room with an overhead projector
situation: Dogbert, acting as a marketing consultant, presents Tina with four ways to make her company's trade show booth attention-grabbing: magic tricks, special effects, raffles and booth babes. He then recommends combining all four by creating the illusion that the booth babes themselves are being raffled off. Tina reacts with alarm at the suggestion.
punchline: Dogbert's 'best result' combines every gimmick into a deeply tasteless scheme that treats the booth staff as raffle prizes, showing how marketing advice can be shamelessly sleazy.
summary: A consultant dog pitches a trade show strategy that merges every attention-getting trick into one objectionable stunt.

file: 1996/1996-06-23_mentor_automentor_job staidsfaction_massage_accomplishments_new job_resume stain_hopeless ness.gif
title: Automentor Software Dispenses Hopeless Career Advice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Automentor
transcript.text: Try giving yourself a massage in your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Automentor
transcript.text: That's not a problem at this company; nobody accomplishes anything.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Should I look for a new job?

transcript.speaker: Automentor
transcript.text: Too late. They don't call this place the "Résumé Stain" for nothing.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How do you handle all the hopelessness?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Office cubicles at the Dilbert company
situation: Dilbert tells Asok he has put all his career wisdom into a program called the Automentor. Asok asks it for advice on job satisfaction, getting his work noticed and finding a new job, and each answer is bleakly cynical about the company. When Asok asks Dilbert how he copes with the hopelessness, Dilbert says he passes it on to the new guy, which is Asok.
punchline: Dilbert's mentoring consists of dumping his own despair onto the newest employee, and the software's cynical advice is just his real wisdom.
summary: A veteran engineer's mentoring software gives a rookie gloomy answers about work, then the veteran reveals he offloads his misery onto newcomers.

file: 1996/1996-04-24_marketing plan_comments_obvious generalities_wishful thinking_business value_glamour career.gif
title: Marketing Plan Gets Brutally Reviewed

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: And that's the marketing plan. Any comments?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It appears to be a bunch of obvious generalities and wishful thinking with no apparent business value.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: Marketing didn't turn out to be the glamour career I expected.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I circled all the words you won't find in any dictionary.

situation: A marketing employee finishes presenting her marketing plan and asks for comments. Dilbert bluntly says it is vague and has no business value, while she privately thinks about how unglamorous marketing turned out to be. Wally then adds that he circled all the made-up words in the plan.
punchline: Marketing documents are so full of vague, invented jargon that Wally has to mark up every non-dictionary word, and even the presenter is disillusioned with her own career.
summary: A marketing presentation gets a blunt critique of its vagueness, and a coworker pointedly highlights its made-up buzzwords.

file: 1996/1996-11-01_alice crazy_can't complain_screen saver_wally clipping nails_made recording_alice_wally annoying sounds.gif
title: Wally's Annoying Cubicle Sounds Screen Saver

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, no... it's the maddening sound of Wally clipping his nails.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The sound makes me crazy, but I can't complain because it would sound silly.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... wait...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You made your own screen saver?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's called "Wally's 101 annoying cubicle sounds."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Slurp! Mmm...

situation: Alice sits in her cubicle, tormented by the sound of Wally clipping his nails, but she stifles her anger because complaining about it would seem petty. Her hair gets wild and she grits her teeth as she holds back. Dilbert then asks Wally about the sound, and Wally cheerfully explains it is his own screen saver of annoying cubicle noises.
punchline: The sounds driving Alice mad are actually just a recording on Wally's computer, so she has been suffering in silence over a deliberate screen saver of annoying noises.
summary: A coworker silently suffers through a neighbor's irritating noises, only to learn they are a computer program he built on purpose.

file: 1996/1996-06-14_company_compensate_healing begin_insane_working smarter_woefully understaffed_not working harder_business.gif
title: Working Smarter Cures Insanity, Then Doubt

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This company makes perfect sense, now that I'm insane.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For example, it might seem as though we're woefully understaffed, but I can compensate by working smarter not harder.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, if I'm capable of working smarter, then why do I work here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The healing has begun.

situation: Wally walks beside Dilbert, cheerfully explaining that the company makes sense to him now that he has gone insane, and that being understaffed is fine because he can work smarter rather than harder. Later, Wally stands in Dilbert's cubicle holding a cardboard box and old equipment, and he asks why he works there if he can work smarter. Dilbert thinks that the healing has begun.
punchline: Wally's brief insanity lets him accept corporate nonsense like 'work smarter not harder', but his sudden realisation that a smart person wouldn't work there signals he is regaining sanity.
summary: A colleague who finds the company logical only because he has lost his mind starts to recover when he questions why a smart worker would stay.

file: 1996/1996-03-27_department newsletter_experienced tech writer_intern_rat_respectively_skills_publisher taken.gif
title: Newsletter Team Grabs Editor Titles

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's get one thing straight before we start writing the department newsletter...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm an experienced technical writer. You are an intern and a rat, respectively. Therefore I will be the editor.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have no skills whatsoever. Therefore I'll be executive editor.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Is "publisher" taken?

situation: Alice sits at a conference table with Asok and Ratbert and announces that she will be the editor of the department newsletter because she is the only experienced technical writer. Asok, the intern, cheerfully claims the title of executive editor precisely because he has no skills. Ratbert then asks whether the title of publisher is still available.
punchline: Alice assigns roles based on merit, but the others cheerfully claim grander titles for themselves precisely because they have no qualifications, mocking how job titles are grabbed regardless of ability.
summary: A newsletter team splits up the leadership titles, with the skilled writer taking one role and the clueless helpers happily claiming fancier ones.

file: 1996/1996-06-12_new logo_sloppy_unimaginative_money to consultants_little return_too good_opinions.gif
title: Logo Reveals Company's Real Flaws

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your new logo might look like a simple coffee stain, but what does the image say about you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're sloppy and unimaginative?

transcript.speaker: Client Executive
transcript.text: We give lots of money to consultants and get little in return?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow. This is almost too good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh ooh! How about "Our opinions don't matter"?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, presents a new company logo that looks like a coffee stain and asks what the image says about the client. Dilbert and a big-haired executive eagerly list unflattering truths about their own company, such as being sloppy and wasting money on consultants. Dogbert is amazed at how well his pitch is working.
punchline: The consultant's meaningless logo becomes a mirror for the company's real problems, and the clients enthusiastically volunteer every criticism, even that their opinions don't matter.
summary: A consultant's coffee-stain logo prompts the clients to cheerfully diagnose their own organization's failings.

file: 1996/1996-02-19_3d colored pie chart_unexplained rise_expenses_binder_rising expenses_color copies cost_i see it_magic eye doofus.gif
title: Color Pie Charts Cause Rising Expenses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This 3-D colored pie chart shows an unexplained rise in expenses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You each get a binder of colored pie charts so you can help find the cause of our rising expenses.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How much do color copies cost?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I see it!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's not the "magic eye," doofus.

situation: The Boss uses an overhead projector to show a 3-D colored pie chart of an unexplained rise in expenses. He then hands out binders full of color pie charts so the staff can hunt for the cause. Wally asks what color copies cost, Dilbert stares at the pages hoping to spot a hidden image, and Alice scolds him.
punchline: The expensive color copies of pie charts handed out to find the cause of rising expenses are themselves a likely cause of rising expenses, and Dilbert mistakes the chart for a Magic Eye puzzle.
summary: A manager tries to track down rising costs by giving everyone expensive color-printed binders, which may be the very problem.

file: 1996/1996-05-13_being bought_long time rival_layoffs_engineers_divison_what we do_younger.gif
title: Spinning the Merger Layoff News

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company announced we're being bought by our long-time rival.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry about layoffs. They like engineers. In fact, they already have a division that does what we do!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Except they're younger and they aren't paid as much as we are...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Spin

setting: Office, where the engineers are gathered for an announcement
situation: The Boss announces to the engineers that the company is being bought by its long-time rival. He tries to reassure them that layoffs won't happen because the rival likes engineers and already has a division doing the same work. He then admits that division is younger and cheaper, and the engineers react in horror, with Dilbert spinning in place.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to reassure the engineers unravels into a confession that they are redundant and more expensive than their counterparts, so their jobs are clearly at risk.
summary: A manager tries to calm his staff about an acquisition, then accidentally reveals that cheaper, younger duplicates of them already exist at the buyer.

file: 1996/1996-09-07_network adminsitrator_routers_block employees_websites_program routers_useless activities_business plan.gif
title: Blocking Useless Activities, Including Business Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Network Administrator

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you program the routers to block employees from all fun web sites?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why stop there? I can program the routers to block ALL useless activities.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will that take?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Done.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've seen your business plan.

setting: Network administrator's office with a computer
situation: Dogbert, acting as network administrator, is asked by the Boss to configure the routers to block employees from fun web sites. Dogbert offers to block all useless activities instead, and when asked how long it will take, he instantly declares it done. He presses a key with a 'Poink' and explains that he has seen the boss's business plan.
punchline: Dogbert finishes instantly because he considers the boss's own business plan the only useless activity worth blocking, insulting its worthlessness.
summary: Asked to filter out amusing websites, Dogbert instantly finishes a much broader block and sneers that the boss's own plan was the only target.

file: 1996/1996-01-22_new compensation_bonuses paid_top ten percent_resigned bitter disgust_get better jobs.gif
title: Bonuses Only For Top Ten Percent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company announced a new compensation plan today. Bonuses will be paid only to the top ten percent of the employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In related news, 89% of the employees resigned in bitter disgust. The top ten percent also left, realizing they could get better jobs elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This could have an impact on those of you who remain.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We get the bonuses?

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: The Boss announces to a meeting that bonuses will go only to the top ten percent of employees. He then reports that nearly 90% of staff quit in disgust, including the top performers who found better jobs elsewhere. The few remaining employees, including Wally, ask whether that means they get the bonuses.
punchline: The remaining employees, the least capable ones, are hopeful the bonus plan now benefits them, while the plan has actually driven out everyone competent.
summary: A manager's elite-only bonus scheme empties the office, leaving only the staff who are pleased to have inherited the rewards.

file: 1996/1996-07-27_reason with idiots_waving paw.gif
title: Dogbert Dismisses Idiots With Bah

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: From now on, I will not try to reason with the idiots I encounter. I will dismiss them by waving my paw and saying "Bah."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just because someone thinks differently from you doesn't mean he's an idiot, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bah.

situation: Dogbert, sitting on the desk, announces a new policy of no longer reasoning with idiots and instead dismissing them with a wave of his paw and a "Bah." Dilbert points out that disagreeing with you does not make someone an idiot. Dogbert responds by waving his paw and saying "Bah" to Dilbert himself.
punchline: Dogbert applies his dismissive policy immediately to Dilbert's reasonable objection, proving he cannot tell disagreement from stupidity and treating Dilbert as one of the idiots.
summary: A smug dog vows to wave away anyone he thinks is foolish, then does exactly that to his friend's gentle correction.

file: 1996/1996-09-12_hopeless_losers_pencil_team building exercise_union rlules.gif
title: Sundial Teambuilding Exercise Breaks Union Rules

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Teambuilding exercise

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's hopeless! You're losers! We'll never make a sundial out of a pencil and an eaten donut!

transcript.speaker: Union Worker
transcript.text: Hee hee! All you had to do was stick the pencil in the donut.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We just broke all kinds of union rules.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But hey! Look at the shadow from the pencil!

setting: Conference room during a teambuilding exercise
situation: A team is asked to build a sundial from a pencil and a donut that has already been eaten, and Alice angrily declares the task hopeless. A union worker in a cap quietly points out that they only needed to stick the pencil in the donut. By doing so, the team has done the job of a union worker, and the worker collapses on the table in protest while Wally cheerfully notes the pencil casts a shadow.
punchline: The team solved the problem so simply that they violated union work rules, and the union worker collapsed, while Wally cheerfully admires the working sundial.
summary: A frustrated team fails at a silly craft task until a union worker reveals the obvious fix, which turns out to be forbidden labor that causes him to faint.

file: 1996/1996-03-10_assigned_boss summarizes_ceiling tiles_cnn report_engineer_lowly engineer_recommendation_technology decisons_technology descion_three bullet points_interactive holographs_engineering.gif
title: How Technology Decisions Really Get Made

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mysteries Revealed

transcript.speaker: Teacher
transcript.text: How do ceiling tiles get damaged?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It begins with a lowly engineer who makes a technology decision.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The engineer writes up his recommendation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ten pages.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The boss summarizes it for the executive director.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One-page summary.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The executive director summarizes it for the vice president.

transcript.speaker: Executive Director
transcript.text: Three bullet points...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The VP summarizes it for the president.

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: Nice necktie.

transcript.speaker: President
transcript.text: Thanks. Have some stock options.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The president sees a CNN report and makes a technology decision.

transcript.speaker: President
transcript.text: Interactive holographs are hot!

transcript.speaker: President
transcript.text: Get me some of that!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The engineer is assigned to justify the president's technology decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He took that well.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch

setting: Corporate offices at various levels of the management hierarchy, framed by a classroom-style 'Mysteries Revealed' intro
situation: A teacher poses a question about ceiling tiles, then the strip traces a technology recommendation as it is summarized at each management level, shrinking from ten pages to a single compliment about a necktie. The president then ignores it all and decides based on a CNN report, and the engineer is told to justify that decision.
punchline: The engineer's careful recommendation is reduced to nothing, the president picks technology based on a TV news hype story, and the engineer's frustration ends with his head hitting the ceiling tiles, which is how they get damaged.
summary: A carefully researched proposal gets summarized into oblivion up the chain of command before a top executive overrides it with whatever he saw on television.

file: 1996/1996-01-26_reduced service costs_technical support_unlisted phone number_customer email_freinds_don't have freinds.gif
title: Cutting Support Costs By Hiding Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've reduced your service costs by giving the technical-support group an unlisted phone number.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And a flaw in your product disables the customer's e-mail; they can't even write to you for help!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if they ask a friend to e-mail us?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: People who use our product don't have friends.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Really? I use it.

setting: Conference room during a consulting presentation with an overhead projector
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, presents to the Boss and his staff how he has cut service costs by giving technical support an unlisted phone number. He adds that a product flaw disables customers' e-mail, so they cannot even write for help. The Boss worries customers could ask a friend to e-mail, and a colleague insists the product's users have no friends, until Wally admits he uses it.
punchline: The product's users are so socially pathetic that they have no friends, and Wally unwittingly proves the point by cheerfully admitting he uses it.
summary: A consultant brags about saving money by making it impossible for customers to reach support, and the only loophole is dismissed with an insult that one employee accidentally confirms.

file: 1996/1996-03-01_facilitate this meeting_speak_begin saw display_may not speak_exercise_health.gif
title: Dogbert Facilitates With Absolute Power

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been asked to facilitate this meeting. I alone will determine who can speak.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like to begin with a raw display of my power. You may not speak.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, Wally... Did you ever hear of a thing called exercise?

situation: Dogbert, sitting at the conference table, announces he has been asked to facilitate the meeting and will alone decide who may speak. He opens by forbidding anyone to speak as a show of power. Wally, who cannot respond, is then needled by Dogbert about his weight and lack of exercise.
punchline: Having silenced everyone, Dogbert exploits his power to insult Wally with impunity, since Wally is not allowed to answer back.
summary: A dog put in charge of a meeting gags the attendees and then uses his authority to taunt a colleague who cannot reply.

file: 1996/1996-08-02_dominion_dolts_breathing air_dogbert.gif
title: Dogbert Declares Sovereignty Over Breathing Space

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My dominion over the planet is not widely recognized by the dolts who are breathing my air.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So I've declared total sovereignty over a small, ever-widening zone surrounding my body.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How big is the zone?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have just entered Dogbertland. Please show your passport and leave the oxygen alone!

setting: Dilbert's living room, on his green couch
situation: Dogbert, perched on the couch, complains that nobody acknowledges his rule over the planet. He announces a personal sovereign zone around his body, and when Dilbert asks how big it is, Dogbert uses a megaphone to inform him he has entered Dogbertland and demands his passport.
punchline: Dogbert's self-declared territory expands to include wherever others are standing, so Dilbert is already a trespasser, and Dogbert absurdly claims ownership of the air itself.
summary: A megalomaniacal dog annexes the space around himself and treats his friend as an illegal border crosser who is stealing his oxygen.

file: 1996/1996-01-18_bag of toys_dogbert_dogbert 2000_huge market_operating system_plastic important_software_software developers_silicon_engineering.gif
title: Dogbert Bribes Developers With Toys

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert meets with software developers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Note the huge market for software that runs on the "Dogbert 2000" operating system.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But who cares? The important thing is that I brought a bag of toys.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Some say the computer industry is built on silicon. I think foam and plastic are equally important.

setting: A meeting room where Dogbert pitches to software developers
situation: Dogbert gives a presentation to software developers, claiming there is a huge market for software running on his "Dogbert 2000" operating system. He then admits that the market doesn't matter and that what counts is the bag of toys he brought. The developers happily play with foam and plastic toys while Dogbert muses about what the industry is really built on.
punchline: Dogbert's sales pitch is hollow, but he wins over the developers by bribing them with toys, implying that programmers are easily swayed by trivial perks rather than real business merit.
summary: A scheming dog sells his imaginary operating system to programmers by handing out playthings instead of facts.

file: 1996/1996-09-06_netwrok administartor_take down network_keystroke_being doctor_goofy stuff_paws.gif
title: Network Admin Plays Doctor Gleefully

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: As network administrator I can take down the network with one keystroke.

transcript.speaker: Coworkers
transcript.text: AAGH!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworkers
transcript.text: WAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworkers
transcript.text: AEEE!!

transcript.speaker: Coworkers
transcript.text: EEEK!!

transcript.speaker: Coworkers
transcript.text: MY WORK!!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It's just like being a doctor but without getting gooky stuff on my paws.

setting: Office computer area with a desk and monitor
situation: Ratbert, working as the network administrator, thinks about how he can take down the whole network with one keystroke. He types happily while offscreen coworkers at their computers scream about losing their work. He then reflects that the job is like being a doctor, minus the messy bodily fluids.
punchline: The network administrator cheerfully enjoys the power of life and death over everyone's work while suffering none of the messy consequences a real doctor would face.
summary: A small, gleeful pet in charge of the computer network crashes everyone's files with a single key and compares his power to a surgeon's, minus the mess.

file: 1996/1996-07-08_supreme ruler_earth_go outside_runa round_mouth open_fresh air_exercise_hate flies_health.gif
title: Supreme Ruler's Fly-Catching Fitness Decree

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Someday when I become the supreme ruler of Earth...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll order everybody to go outside once a day and run around with their mouths open.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because you support fresh air and exercise?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because I hate flies.

setting: A park with a tree and a bench
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert are at a park, and Dogbert describes what he will do when he becomes supreme ruler of Earth: force everyone to run outside with their mouths open. Dilbert assumes this is a well-meaning health policy and asks if Dogbert supports fresh air and exercise.
punchline: Dogbert's decree isn't about public health at all; he simply wants people to eat flies because he hates them.
summary: A would-be world dictator reveals that his health-sounding mandate is really a plan to wipe out insects by having humans swallow them.

file: 1996/1996-09-23_problem_quietly sit_look mangerly_idiotic_leadership_iron man_team building_bunch leadership.gif
title: Iron Man Competition Passes for Leadership

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know how to fix any of the problems in this company. Maybe I'll just sit here quietly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, that wouldn't look managerly... I'll have to do something idiotic and hope it looks like leadership.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to have an "Iron Man" team-building competition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What a bunch of leadership...

situation: The Boss sits at his desk thinking that he has no idea how to fix the company's problems and considers doing nothing. He decides that would not look managerly, so he must do something idiotic and hope it looks like leadership. He then announces an "Iron Man" team-building competition to Dilbert, who responds sarcastically.
punchline: The Boss admits that his announcements are deliberately idiotic gestures meant only to look like leadership, and Dilbert's sarcastic reply shows he sees right through it.
summary: Clueless about real solutions, a manager invents a silly competition just to appear decisive while an employee mocks the result.

file: 1996/1996-09-29_accounting_airfare_business trip_saturday_reimburse_saturday hotel costs_business activity_understand_economic choices_waste money_ugly brain dead troll_free lunch money.gif
title: Saturday Stay Saves Money, Denied

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Groan.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Accounting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saved $500 in airfare by extending my business trip to Saturday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why won't you reimburse me for the Saturday hotel costs?

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: Saturday was not a business-related activity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hmm... Let me see if I understand this...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's NOT business-related to make sensible economic choices...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But it IS business-related to waste money like an ugly, brain-dead troll...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then he beat me up and took my lunch money.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you saying I can get free lunch money by beating you up?

setting: Accounting department, depicted as a cave, and later Dilbert's home or office
situation: Dilbert goes to the accounting department, portrayed as a troll's cave, and asks for reimbursement for a Saturday hotel stay that saved the company $500 in airfare. The troll refuses because Saturday wasn't business-related, so Dilbert insults him by summarizing the policy. In the last panel, Dilbert is bandaged and beaten up, and Dogbert sees a business opportunity.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic summary of the illogical expense policy gets him beaten up by the accounting troll, and Dogbert cheerfully misses the point, asking if he can profit from beating Dilbert up too.
summary: A cost-saving trip extension is rejected by a monstrous accountant, and Dilbert's honest mockery earns him a beating and an unhelpful business idea from Dogbert.

file: 1996/1996-01-01_opinions_self described feminists_non stereo typical_female characters_balance_antina_math_education.gif
title: Antina Balances Out Tina

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A while back I asked for opinions about this new character, "Tina the Brittle Tech Writer."

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: RRRR

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Results

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Most people, including nearly all self-described feminists, said keep her. But there were many requests to add "non-stereotypical" female characters for balance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In the interest of balance I give you "Antina."

transcript.speaker: Antina
transcript.text: Is anybody up for some math?

situation: Dogbert addresses the reader about feedback on the new character Tina, a snarling, brittle tech writer. He reports that most people, including self-described feminists, wanted to keep her, but many also asked for non-stereotypical female characters. He introduces Antina, a cheerful woman who eagerly asks if anyone wants to do some math.
punchline: The 'non-stereotypical' female character Dogbert provides is just another stereotype, a woman enthusiastically volunteering for math, mocking the idea that balance can be achieved by simply reversing a stereotype.
summary: Responding to reader feedback, Dogbert answers a request for unconventional women characters by unveiling a perky math-loving colleague.

file: 1996/1996-07-16_various problems_complied problems_requirements_thoughtful broken.gif
title: Fixing Girlfriend's Problems Like Software Bugs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In the year that we've dated, Liz, you've often mentioned various problems in your life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have compiled those problems into a list of requirements and developed a comprehensive set of solutions.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: How thoughtful. I didn't even know I was broken.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, no, not broken... just a bit buggy.

setting: Outdoors on a walk, then a close conversation
situation: Dilbert walks hand in hand with his girlfriend Liz and presents her with a written list he has made. He has turned the problems she mentioned over the past year into requirements and drawn up solutions, as if she were a software project. Liz is offended at the implication that she is broken.
punchline: Dilbert tries to reassure Liz by saying she is not broken, just buggy, which still treats her like faulty software and shows his engineering mindset ruins his romance.
summary: An engineer hands his girlfriend a requirements document for fixing her life and insists she is merely flawed rather than defective.

file: 1996/1996-04-23_co worker_current job_engineer_higher salary_throughly unqualified_unrealistic plans_wally resign_engineering.gif
title: Resign and Reapply for Raise

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I'm thinking I'll resign, then I'll reapply for my current job at a higher salary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a good plan except for the fact that you're thoroughly unqualified for your current job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I need to share my unrealistic plans with a friend who isn't an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm more of a co-worker than a friend, per se.

setting: Office break room with a coffee maker, then a cubicle area
situation: Wally pours coffee while telling Dilbert his plan to quit and then reapply for his own job at a higher salary. Dilbert points out that Wally is not even qualified for the job he currently holds. Wally says he wants to share his unrealistic plans with a non-engineer friend, and Dilbert replies that he is only a co-worker.
punchline: Wally's scheme ignores that he is unqualified for his job, and he then tries to shop it to a friend, only to be reminded by Dilbert that their relationship is merely professional.
summary: A lazy employee's plan to game his way into a bigger paycheck is shot down by a colleague who also declines to be considered a friend.

file: 1996/1996-07-01_friendship_quality assurance_find flaws_object intense_hatred_ridicule_fix flaws_respect_special bond_relationships.gif
title: Quality Assurance Means Being Hated

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, my company is hiring for our Quality Assurance group. You'd be perfect.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: What would I have to do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You would find flaws in our new product, thus making yourself an object of intense hatred and ridicule.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: But then you'd fix those flaws... and your respect for me would grow into a special bond of friendship, right?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, then we ship.

setting: Dilbert's home or a bare room, with Ratbert standing on a box
situation: Dilbert recruits Ratbert for his company's Quality Assurance group. He candidly explains that finding flaws will make Ratbert hated and ridiculed by the team. Ratbert hopefully suggests that fixing the flaws would earn him respect and friendship, but Dilbert reveals the flaws won't be fixed before release.
punchline: Quality assurance findings are ignored because the product ships regardless, so the tester gets all the hatred and none of the improvement or appreciation.
summary: A job pitch for a tester position turns bleak when the recruit learns that his bug reports will earn him scorn and will not even change what gets released.

file: 1996/1996-06-18_injury free days_very ironic_chart injuries_falls_putting up sign accident.gif
title: Injury-Free Sign Causes Injury

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: 10 injury free days

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BAM!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: AAAEEII!!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: R-r-roll

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: THUD

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is very ironic.

transcript.speaker: Man on floor
transcript.text: No, it was ironic when it happened eleven days ago.

setting: Office wall in a pink-walled office
situation: A maintenance man stands on a rolling office chair to hang a sign reading '10 injury free days' while Dilbert watches. The chair rolls out from under him and he crashes to the floor, injured. Dilbert comments on the irony, and the fallen man pedantically corrects him from the floor.
punchline: The man who just fell off the chair while hanging the injury-free sign pedantically insists the real irony was an earlier accident, which means the sign was already wrong, since it was only supposed to count ten days without an injury.
summary: A worker falls off a wheeled chair while posting a safety record sign, then argues about the proper definition of irony.

file: 1996/1996-10-13_meets expectations_review_two percent raise_eighty hour week_three patents_make millions_donated bone marrow_attendece problem_cheated on money_alice_take advantage_cheap_scammed.gif
title: Meets Expectations Despite Extraordinary Effort

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, your performance this year is "meets expectations." You get a two percent raise.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "Meets expectations"?! I worked eighty hours every week!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah... well, I expected that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I earned three patents this year! The company will make millions!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? Wow. I mean... I expected that too.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I donated bone marrow to our biggest customer!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Twice!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I noted that under "attendance problem."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I told you the bone marrow thing would haunt you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm starting to think the time I worked through lunch was for nothing.

setting: The Boss's office, then a lunch table in the break room
situation: The Boss gives Alice a 'meets expectations' rating and a two percent raise. Alice lists her extraordinary achievements (eighty-hour weeks, three patents, bone marrow donation to a customer), and the Boss dismisses each one as expected or even counts it against her. Afterward, Dilbert and Wally commiserate at lunch.
punchline: No matter how much an employee does, management treats it as baseline or penalizes it, so extraordinary sacrifice earns nothing.
summary: An overachieving engineer pleads her case for a better review, but her boss turns every sacrifice into an excuse to give her almost nothing.

file: 1996/1996-10-20_right on plan_project_bad idea_senior mangement_leadership_widespread mockery_lawyers_purging_gigantic failure_forget_mission statemnet_literal interpretation.gif
title: Planning to Fail Upward

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My project is right on plan.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It began last week as a bad idea from somebody in senior management.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thanks to my leadership, it is already an object of widespread mockery and derision.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As I speak, our lawyers are purging every last trace of value it might have had.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: With luck, the project will be a gigantic failure in a month.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: People will forget my failure and remember that I'm experienced. Promotions will follow.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In six months I'll be dating an executive secretary named Yvonne.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, have you ever read our mission statement?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yeah, but I don't subscribe to a literal interpretation.

setting: Conference room during a project status meeting
situation: Wally gives a project update at a meeting, cheerfully explaining that his project began as a bad idea from senior management and is on track to become a spectacular failure. He reveals his plan is for people to forget the failure and remember only his experience, leading to promotions and a new romance. The Boss then asks if he has read the company mission statement.
punchline: Wally deliberately engineers a failing project because he knows failure is quickly forgotten while 'experience' gets rewarded, and he dismisses the company mission statement as something not to be taken literally.
summary: A cynical employee proudly reports that his doomed project is exactly on schedule to fail, counting on the failure being forgotten while his supposed experience earns him a promotion.

file: 1996/1996-04-15_eighteen hour days_add person_effoerts_night shift manager_behind schedule_staus reprts_rendered in 3d.gif
title: Night Shift Manager Adds Pressure

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you've been working eighteen hours a day. I realized I must add a person to the effort.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I hired a night shift manager. After I go home at five o'clock he'll take over and ask why you're behind schedule.

transcript.speaker: Night Shift Manager
transcript.text: I like my status reports rendered in 3-D, but don't spend a lot of time on it.

situation: The Boss tells Alice, who is already working eighteen-hour days, that he has added a person to help. The new hire is a night shift manager whose only role is to take over after five o'clock and ask why she is behind schedule. He then adds a demand for elaborate 3-D status reports.
punchline: The 'help' management adds to an overworked employee is just another manager who interrogates her and creates extra reporting work, making her further behind.
summary: A boss responds to an exhausted employee's marathon hours by hiring someone whose sole job is to nag her about lateness and demand fancy reports.

file: 1996/1996-09-25_iron man team_team building_exercise_ten mile swim_parcticing_teamwork_doggie paddle_health.gif
title: Boss Skips Iron Man Swim

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The first leg of the "Iron Man" team-building exercise is a ten-mile swim, I think.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I won't be participating because my teamwork skills are already excellent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Two phrases you don't expect to hear in the same day are "Iron Man" and "doggie paddle."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey! No splashing!

setting: A beach, at the start of a company team-building event
situation: The Boss gathers Dilbert, Wally and Alice on the beach in swimsuits and announces that the first leg of an Iron Man team-building exercise is a ten-mile swim. He then excuses himself from taking part, claiming his teamwork skills are already excellent. Standing dry in his suit, he smugly thinks a joke about the contrast between Iron Man and doggie paddling while the employees are left to swim.
punchline: The Boss exempts himself from the grueling exercise with a self-congratulatory excuse, while mocking the very staff he is sending into the water, who he assumes can only manage a doggie paddle.
summary: A manager sends his staff off to swim ten miles in a triathlon-style team exercise while he stays dry and cracks jokes about their ability.

file: 1996/1996-08-28_flying around dearth_enough time_give parents contraception_travel back in time.gif
title: Time Travel Solution, Contraception Pamphlet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At first I thought you committed me to an impossible deadline. But I have a theoretical solution.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It involves flying around the earth so fast that I travel back to the past.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And then you'll have enough time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, then I'll give your parents this pamphlet on contraception.

situation: The Boss has committed Dilbert to an impossible deadline. Dilbert, at his computer showing a diagram, explains that he could fly around the earth fast enough to travel back in time. When the Boss hopefully assumes this will give Dilbert enough time, Dilbert says he'll instead use the trip to give the Boss's parents a pamphlet on contraception.
punchline: Dilbert's real purpose for time travel is to prevent the Boss from ever being born, an insult implying the world would be better off without him.
summary: Dilbert proposes a far-fetched time machine scheme, then reveals its true goal is to stop his boss's parents from conceiving him.

file: 1996/1996-07-11_quality initiative_decour_productive hours_lower morale_profitability_contest_qualicide.gif
title: Qualicide: Quality Initiative Kills Productivity

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm assigning each of you to a separate "quality" initiative.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is there any risk this will devour our productive hours, lower our morale and have no impact on our profitability?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And we'll have a contest to come up with a name for the overall initiative.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about "Qualicide"?

situation: The Boss announces he is assigning each employee to a separate quality initiative. Wally sarcastically asks whether the program might waste time, hurt morale and do nothing for profits. The Boss, oblivious, plans a naming contest, and Dilbert suggests a name that implies the initiative will kill quality.
punchline: The employees openly predict the quality program will be harmful and useless, and Dilbert's proposed name "Qualicide" mockingly labels it as something that kills quality, which the Boss fails to notice.
summary: Staff mock a management-mandated quality program by predicting its damage and proposing a name that literally means the death of quality.

file: 1996/1996-07-06_bugs program_diskette_fixed bugs_code_write program_updating resume_need it soon.gif
title: Garbage Man Out-Codes Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I couldn't help noticing the bugs in the program on this old diskette you threw away.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I fixed the bugs and tightened the code from twelve thousand lines to sixteen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took me three months to write that program.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I took the liberty of updating your resume. I'm guessing you'll need it soon.

setting: Outdoors on a street next to a garbage can
situation: A garbage man tells Dilbert he found an old diskette of Dilbert's program in the trash. He reveals he fixed its bugs and shrank the code from twelve thousand lines to sixteen. Dilbert is stunned, and the garbage man hands him an updated resume, implying Dilbert's job is now at risk.
punchline: A garbage man is a far better programmer than Dilbert, so the engineer's skills are obsolete and he will soon be out of work.
summary: A trash collector rescues a discarded diskette, dramatically improves the code, and hands the shocked engineer a resume as a warning.

file: 1996/1996-07-03_quality assurance_beta prodcut_few bugs_lethal boneheaded_vesing_lethal_vexing_bonehead_rent_stadium.gif
title: Bug Report Needs a Stadium

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My quality assurance review of your beta product turned up a few bugs, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I've classified the bugs by severity: 1) Lethal, 2) Boneheaded, 3) Vexing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All I see are lethal and vexing. Where's boneheaded?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to rent a stadium to hold the printout.

situation: Ratbert, acting as a quality assurance tester, tells Wally that his beta product has a few bugs. He has sorted them into lethal, boneheaded and vexing categories, with a long paper printout trailing behind him across the floor. Wally only sees two categories on the page he is holding.
punchline: The boneheaded bugs are so numerous that the printout listing them is too big for an office, implying Wally's product is riddled with stupid mistakes.
summary: A tiny tester delivers a bug report so enormous that the worst category of errors won't even fit in the building.

file: 1996/1996-06-19_idiot fell_twelve hours_chair safety training_do_not do.gif
title: Chair Safety Training After a Fall

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some idiot stood on a chair and fell off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now we all have to take twelve hours of chair safety training.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is that a "do" or a "not do"?

situation: The Boss tells Wally and Alice that someone stood on a chair and fell, so everyone must now complete twelve hours of chair safety training. In the final panel an employee is seen upside down in a chair near a flip chart, mid-fall, while a seated colleague asks whether that is a 'do' or a 'not do' for the training.
punchline: The training is so absurdly basic that a colleague wants it clarified whether falling off a chair is the right way or wrong way to do things, while the fall is happening in front of them.
summary: A manager announces mandatory chair safety training after a coworker's tumble, and a colleague mocks the absurdity by asking whether the demonstrated fall is correct procedure.

file: 1996/1996-10-05_both dead_doing nothing_hundred years_spread joy_whats funny_working hard_ratbert_dilbert.gif
title: Ratbert Finds Joy in Mortality

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You know what's funny?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll tell you.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You're working hard. I'm doing nothing. In a hundred years we'll both be dead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might not need to wait that long.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I think I'll spread some joy over this way.

situation: Dilbert sits typing at his computer while Ratbert, standing nearby, announces that it is funny that Dilbert works hard and Ratbert does nothing, since both will be dead in a hundred years. Dilbert replies that Ratbert might not have to wait that long, a dark threat, and Ratbert cheerfully decides to go cheer up someone else.
punchline: Dilbert's irritation at Ratbert's morbid, smug philosophizing leads him to hint he might kill him sooner, and Ratbert responds by blithely moving on to bother someone else.
summary: A slacking pet's cheerful reminder of everyone's eventual death earns a menacing retort from the overworked engineer he's pestering.

file: 1996/1996-06-02_phil_prince insufficient light_spreme ruler_hideous fates sins_high pay_eternal poverty_useful_appreciated_current job_telecommuting.gif
title: Devil Offers Dilbert Two Fates

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: My next victim.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I am Phil, the Prince of Insufficient Light and Supreme Ruler of Heck!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Phil.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You must choose one of these two hideous fates to pay for your sins.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You can choose eternal high pay, but all of your work will be burned in front of you at the end of each day...

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Or you can choose eternal poverty, but your work will be useful and appreciated.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! They're both better than my current job!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Wally, you might want to get in on this!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I watch TV when I'm supposed to be telecommuting.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I hate the nineties.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do me first!

situation: Phil, a red-suited devil with a giant spoon, appears in Dilbert's cubicle and offers him a choice of two hideous fates: high pay with all his work burned daily, or poverty with useful, appreciated work. Dilbert is delighted because both options beat his current job and calls Wally over to join in. Wally admits he watches TV while supposedly telecommuting, and Dilbert eagerly asks to go first.
punchline: The devil's supposedly terrible punishments sound better than Dilbert's real job, which is neither well paid nor meaningful.
summary: A demon threatens an engineer with two infernal career punishments, but the engineer finds either one an upgrade over his actual employment.

file: 1996/1996-02-01_leadership_air traffic control system_on time_under budget_feature creep_dangerous_wall clock.gif
title: Fake Air Traffic Control Under Budget

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks to my leadership, the new air traffic control system is designed on time and under budget.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I had to cut a few corners. This big radar-looking thing is a wall clock. And most of the buttons are glued on.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It looks like it might be um... dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Great... I finish early and what do I get: "Feature creep."

setting: Control room of a new air traffic control system
situation: Dogbert, acting as a project leader, proudly announces that the air traffic control system was finished on time and under budget. He then reveals that the radar is really a wall clock and most buttons are just glued on. The Boss hesitantly says it looks dangerous, and Dogbert complains that this is just feature creep.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses a legitimate safety concern as 'feature creep', showing how meeting schedule and budget targets by faking the product makes any criticism sound like scope expansion.
summary: A consultant boasts about delivering a safety-critical system early and cheaply, having used a clock and glued-on buttons in place of real equipment, then resents being asked for actual functionality.

file: 1996/1996-09-09_touchy feely institute_teamwork_exercise_trust_son blank checks_excellent quality_other people should have_health.gif
title: Trust Exercise With Blank Checks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've hired the "Dogbert Touchy-Feely Institute" to teach us about teamwork.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll start with an exercise about trust. I want each of you to sign blank checks and give them to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What will this teach us about trust?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It will teach you that trust is an excellent quality for other people to have.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces he has hired Dogbert's Touchy-Feely Institute to run a teamwork session. The first exercise is a trust test in which every employee must sign a blank check and hand it to him. When Dilbert asks what lesson this teaches, Dogbert answers that trust is a quality best possessed by other people.
punchline: The trust exercise is really a scam to collect signed blank checks, and Dogbert admits the lesson is that it pays to have gullible people who trust you.
summary: A consultant's teamwork workshop turns out to be a thinly veiled way to get employees to hand over access to their money.

file: 1996/1996-03-18_intern asok_sturdier than last_staple rmover_pass the intern.gif
title: Tossing the Intern Around

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, everybody. Meet our new intern, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hope this one's sturdier than the last one.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My staple remover is broken. Somebody toss that intern to me!

situation: The Boss introduces the new intern, Asok, to the team. Alice grabs him and hopes he is tougher than his predecessor. Wally, peering over a cubicle wall, asks for the intern to be thrown to him because his staple remover is broken.
punchline: The intern is treated as a disposable, physically abusable object, and Wally wants to use him as a replacement staple remover, implying the last intern was worn out by rough use.
summary: A newly introduced intern is promptly handled like a tool by his coworkers, who want him sturdier than his predecessor and useful for office chores.

file: 1996/1996-01-17_operating system_dominate market_dogbert 2000.gif
title: Dogbert Threatens Bill Gates-Like Executive

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you plan to remain in the computer business you'd better bundle the "Dogbert 2000" operating system with every unit you sell.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Otherwise, after I dominate the market you'll be last on my list to receive new products!

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: You remind me of somebody...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's the glasses, isn't it?

situation: Dogbert, sitting in a chair facing a desk, tells a bespectacled computer executive that he must bundle Dogbert's operating system with every unit sold. He warns that once Dogbert dominates the market, the executive will be last in line for new products. The executive says Dogbert reminds him of somebody, and Dogbert guesses it's the glasses.
punchline: Dogbert's monopolistic bundling threat mimics Microsoft's tactics, and the executive's resemblance remark is a nod to Bill Gates, whose famous glasses Dogbert wryly acknowledges.
summary: A scheming dog demands that a tech executive ship his software with every machine, and the executive notices a familiar resemblance to a famous software mogul.

file: 1996/1996-01-29_air traffic control_systems_blue hound bus lines_won bid.gif
title: Short Selling Air Traffic Control Winners

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We won the bid to rebuild our nation's air traffic control systems.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yippeee!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: To the phones!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't usually get that excited.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Buy a thousand shares of "Bluehound Bus Lines."

situation: The Boss announces that the company has won the contract to rebuild the nation's air traffic control systems. Alice, Dilbert and Wally cheer wildly, and Wally rushes to the phones. The Boss puzzles over their unusual enthusiasm while Wally is overheard ordering shares in a bus company.
punchline: The engineers are thrilled because they know their system will be so bad that people will stop flying, so Wally is investing in bus lines to profit from the coming air travel disaster.
summary: Staff celebrate landing a huge aviation contract, then hint they expect their own work to push travelers onto buses.

file: 1996/1996-07-14_making personal calls_stealing_fist of death_eighty cents_talk to family_bill for overtime_being competetive_office supplies.gif
title: Alice Bills Boss for Overtime

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to this phone bill, you've been making personal calls.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's like stealing from the company, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control... fist... of... death...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I spent eighty cents to tell my family I was working late.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Here's a dollar. The extra twenty cents is for the personal thought that I'm about to have on company time.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Mmm

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And here's my bill for $40,000 in unpaid overtime that the company stole from me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not stealing; that's being competitive.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think I'll be competitive with a few bushels of office supplies later today.

situation: The Boss accuses Alice of stealing from the company because of personal calls on the phone bill. Alice, barely containing her rage, pays him for the eighty-cent call and then hands him a bill for $40,000 in unpaid overtime. When he calls that competitive business rather than stealing, she says she will take a lot of office supplies.
punchline: The Boss's own excuse for the company underpaying her is turned around, so Alice can justify helping herself to office supplies as being competitive.
summary: A manager scolds an employee over a tiny phone charge, and she answers with a huge overtime invoice and a plan to raid the supply closet.

file: 1996/1996-01-19_software emoire_net wealth_twenty billion._popular opinion_sunset_license digital rights.gif
title: Dogbert Licenses the Sunset

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks to my software empire, my net wealth is twenty billion dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Contrary to popular opinion, it does seem to make me happy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Money can't buy a sunset, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, but I was able to license the digital rights.

setting: Outdoors on a path and a fallen log at sunset
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert take a walk outdoors. Dogbert boasts that his software empire has made him worth twenty billion dollars and says it makes him happy. When Dilbert points out that money can't buy a sunset, Dogbert replies that he did manage to license the digital rights to it.
punchline: Dogbert twists the old saying about money by showing that, while he can't buy a sunset itself, his wealth lets him own and profit from its digital reproduction.
summary: A wealthy software tycoon dog counters a platitude about money by pointing out he owns the intellectual property rights to a sunset.

file: 1996/1996-02-18_project time line_work portion_meet with people_competitive bids_predictable behavior_randomly reorganize_department_cut funding_final phase_death_bitter and broken_leaving building_medical.gif
title: Dilbert's Realistic Project Timeline Presentation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my project time line.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The "work" portion will take one week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll spend three weeks meeting with people whom you send to me because you don't feel like talking to them yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll spend eight weeks getting competitive bids from companies that I know I won't select.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... Six weeks to get the wisdom and approval of executives who are too busy to understand the issues.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: During that time you will randomly reorganize the department and cut my funding.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In the final phase I leap to my death, a bitter and broken shell of a man.

transcript.speaker: Chart
transcript.text: Eeee!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there some sort of manager thing I should be doing now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I time my leap right you'll just be leaving the building.

situation: Dilbert presents a project timeline to the Boss, showing that only one week is real work while the rest is consumed by pointless meetings, useless competitive bids, executive approvals, and a random reorganization with funding cuts. The final phase of the chart shows Dilbert leaping to his death from a building. The Boss asks if he should be doing something.
punchline: The Boss's only concern about Dilbert's planned suicide is whether there is a 'manager thing' he should do, and Dilbert notes he'll conveniently be leaving the building by then, showing the Boss's total indifference.
summary: A project plan reveals that nearly all the schedule goes to management-created obstacles and ends with the employee's despairing leap, which the oblivious boss barely registers.

file: 1996/1996-02-17_agreement_grant_sign_strategic omissions_waiver_proofread_company_forcing to sign_business.gif
title: Dogbert Advises Doctoring the Employment Agreement

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look at the agreement my company is forcing us to sign. They claim the rights to any idea an employee ever has.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No problem. Just retype it with a few strategic omissions and sign it. They can't proofread every one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that be dishonest?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could just show them some of your ideas and they'd grant a waiver.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert an employment agreement his company is forcing everyone to sign, which claims ownership of any idea an employee ever has. Dogbert suggests retyping it with strategic omissions and signing that version, since nobody can proofread every copy. When Dilbert objects that this would be dishonest, Dogbert offers an alternative: show the company some of his ideas and they'd grant a waiver.
punchline: Dogbert's 'honest' alternative is to reveal Dilbert's ideas to the company, which implies his ideas are so bad that the company would happily waive its claim on them.
summary: A dog advises his owner to quietly alter a company contract, then helpfully proposes an honest route that quietly insults the quality of the man's ideas.

file: 1996/1996-03-16_started own compnay_selling product_be rich_victory jog_employment agreement_patent rights.gif
title: Victory Jig Meets Patent Assignment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally and I started our own company. We're selling the product that you said nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Soon we will be rich.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We do our victory jig in your face.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ba-bum

transcript.speaker: Alice
