transcript.text: When he showed you your employment agreement - where you gave all patent rights to this company - what part of the jig were you doing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Turbo mooning.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sob

situation: Dilbert and Wally tell The Boss they have started their own company selling the product he said nobody wants, and they perform a victory jig in his face. Alice then points out that their employment agreement assigned all patent rights to the company they just left, and Dilbert sheepishly admits he was mooning the boss at the time.
punchline: Their gloating dance is exposed as foolish because they signed away the patent rights, making the product legally the old company's property, and Dilbert had even mooned the boss while being shown the agreement.
summary: Two employees celebrate launching a rival business, only to be reminded that they had already handed their patent rights to their former employer.

file: 1996/1996-02-10_dogbert_forget them_quietly supportuive_too many passwords_with draw money_phone messages.gif
title: Too Many Passwords, Unhelpful Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have too many passwords in my life. What if I forget them?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'd lose your job! You wouldn't be able to withdraw money or check phone messages! You'd be dead in a week!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would have been a good time to be quietly supportive, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh, yeah, that's a lot of fun.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert lying on the couch
situation: Dilbert lies on the couch and worries aloud about having too many passwords to remember. Dogbert responds by cataloguing every catastrophic consequence of forgetting them, which only makes Dilbert more anxious. Dilbert, now lying with his face hidden, tells Dogbert he should have just been supportive.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically admits he's enjoying Dilbert's misery, showing his earlier alarmist rant was not meant to be helpful at all.
summary: A worried man's pet turns his password anxiety into a doom spiral, then sarcastically owns up to enjoying it.

file: 1996/1996-01-30_dogbert consulting comapny_lead project_bright enough_bad attitudes_no apparent reason_introduce ourselves_chummy with locals.gif
title: Dogbert Consultant Snubs the Locals

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the "Dogbert Consulting Company" to lead the project because none of you is bright enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you all have bad attitudes for no apparent reason; that's no way to be a leader.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Shall we go around the table and introduce ourselves?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't get chummy with the locals.

situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting that he has hired Dogbert's consulting company to lead their project because none of them is bright enough. He also insults their attitudes. When a coworker suggests introductions around the table, Dogbert, sitting among them, refuses to get friendly with the staff.
punchline: The consultant brought in to lead the team openly looks down on the employees and refuses to even meet them, showing the arrogance of outside consultants and the boss's blind faith in them.
summary: A boss puts his staff down and hands the project to a consultant dog who cannot be bothered to know the people he will be leading.

file: 1996/1996-06-11_new company logo_brown ring_quality.gif
title: The Brown Ring of Quality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Dogbert Consulting Company will help us design a new company logo.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will you start?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I just finished. I call it the Brown Ring of Quality.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that Dogbert's consulting company will help design a new company logo. Dogbert sits at the table and drinks a cup of coffee. When the Boss asks when Dogbert will start, Dogbert says the design is already done: the brown ring left by his coffee cup.
punchline: Dogbert's 'logo' is just the coffee ring his cup left on the table, so he gets paid for doing no real work while giving it a pompous name.
summary: A consultant claims to have designed a corporate logo already, and it turns out to be nothing more than a stain left by his coffee mug.

file: 1996/1996-01-24_test new invention_dirty pictures_internet_youthful curioisty_technical brillainace_eyeballs_technology.gif
title: Kid Tests Internet Filter Invention

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Matt, your job is to test my new invention that blocks kids from seeing dirty pictures on the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: His youthful curiosity is no match for my technical brilliance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope that wasn't the sound of eyeballs getting really big.

setting: Office or lab with a computer
situation: Dilbert asks a boy named Matt to test his new invention, which is supposed to stop kids from viewing dirty pictures online. While Matt types at the computer, Dilbert boasts that his technical brilliance will defeat the boy's curiosity. A noise then makes Dilbert nervously realize Matt may have gotten past the filter and is staring wide-eyed at the screen.
punchline: Dilbert's overconfident claim of technical brilliance collapses when the sound of the kid's reaction suggests the filter doesn't work at all.
summary: An inventor confidently has a child try out his porn-blocking software, only to worry from the boy's reaction that it has failed.

file: 1996/1996-05-15_inert_leadership_morale boosting_next phase_pending merger_praised with fear_rigor mortis_unmotivated.gif
title: Paralyzed By Merger, Boss Suggests Potluck

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm paralyzed with fear because of the pending merger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks to your leadership I've gone from being unmotivated to being inert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'm advancing to the next phase. Hello, rigor mortis!! Take me, I'm ready!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) It might be time for a morale-boosting potluck lunch.

situation: Dilbert stands rigid with his arms stretched out, telling the Boss he is paralyzed with fear over the pending merger. He credits the Boss's leadership for taking him from unmotivated to inert, then cheerfully welcomes rigor mortis. The Boss, oblivious, privately thinks a morale-boosting potluck lunch might help.
punchline: Dilbert is so demoralized he is practically becoming a corpse, yet the clueless Boss's only idea is a potluck lunch.
summary: A frozen, fearful employee jokes that he is turning into a corpse while his manager offers only a cheap party as the fix.

file: 1996/1996-04-13_internal job postings_experience required_eric_potbellied_near sighted_red ford bronco.gif
title: Job Posting Written For Eric

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The internal job postings are out. Here's a job I'd love.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "Experience required: The candidate must be a guy named Eric, pot-bellied, nearsighted, must drive a red Ford Bronco."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They might have someone in mind already.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I squint... and leave my "control top" pantyhose at home...

situation: Alice tells Dilbert she has found an internal job posting she would love, then reads out its requirements, which describe one specific man named Eric down to his build, eyesight and car. Dilbert observes that management probably already has someone in mind, and Alice sarcastically wonders whether she could qualify anyway.
punchline: The job requirements are so absurdly tailored to one particular guy that the posting is a sham, and Alice sarcastically suggests she could only qualify by contorting herself into resembling him.
summary: A rigged internal job listing describes one particular man so precisely that a woman colleague can only joke about squinting her way into qualifying.

file: 1996/1996-05-30_alternatives_analysis_coworker not boss_information_urgent need_analysis of alternatives_science.gif
title: Coworker Learns He's Not the Boss

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need this information today. Plus a complete analysis of the alternatives.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Crinkle crinkle stuff

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That wasn't nice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In today's lesson, you learn that you're my co-worker, not my boss.

situation: A coworker stands over Dilbert's desk and demands information and a full analysis of alternatives by the end of the day. Dilbert ignores him, then in the middle panel appears to have grabbed the paper and crumpled it with a crinkling sound. When the coworker complains, Dilbert says he is teaching him that he is a peer, not Dilbert's boss.
punchline: Dilbert answers a coworker's bossy demand by crumpling up the paper and lecturing him that he has no authority over him.
summary: A peer who orders Dilbert around gets his paperwork crushed and a pointed reminder about office hierarchy.

file: 1996/1996-02-22_elbonia_check software_under contract_documentation_elbonian language_wiring easy_hope to read.gif
title: Elbonians Write But Cannot Read

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Somewhere in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been assigned to check the software you're writing for us under contract.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: The documentation is written in our own Elbonian language.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Is that a problem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's better than I'd hoped. I was afraid nobody here knew how to write.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Writing is easy. Someday we hope to read, too.

setting: Muddy hillside in Elbonia, an impoverished fictional country
situation: Dilbert travels to Elbonia to review software being developed for his company under an outsourcing contract. He learns the documentation is in the Elbonian language and says he is relieved they can write at all. The Elbonians cheerfully explain that they can write but hope to learn to read someday.
punchline: Dilbert's low expectations are exceeded, but the Elbonians reveal that writing without being able to read means the outsourced software and documentation are essentially unverifiable, so the contract is hopeless.
summary: An engineer visiting an overseas contractor is pleased to find they can write documentation, only to learn they still cannot read.

file: 1996/1996-05-06_wally compensation_equalibrium_project_lower quality_consistent_salary_first month_after raises_achieved equilibrium_money.gif
title: Wally's Compensation Equilibrium Project

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I kicked off the "Wally Compensation Equilibrium Project."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My goal is to lower the quality of my work until it is consistent with my salary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hate the first month after they see their raises.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd go on, but I just achieved equilibrium.

situation: At a meeting, Wally proudly announces a personal project to deliberately lower the quality of his work until it matches what he is paid. The Boss grumbles in a thought bubble about how employees slack off right after receiving raises. Wally cuts his presentation short because he has already reached his goal of doing as little as possible.
punchline: Wally frames his laziness as a formal project, and he completes it instantly because his work was already as poor as his pay justifies.
summary: Wally turns slacking off into an official initiative to make his effort match his paycheck, then finishes it on the spot.

file: 1996/1996-02-21_software development work_tiny nation_elbonia_integrating software_existing systems_tuberculosis vaccination.gif
title: Elbonia Outsourcing Gets Worse Still

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I heard that our software development work has been moved to the tiny nation of Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Things can't get worse than that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you're in charge of integrating the Elbonian's software with our existing systems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, NOW it can't get any worse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You might want to get a tuberculosis vaccination.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert that the company has moved its software development to the tiny nation of Elbonia, and Dilbert says things can't get worse. The Boss then puts Dilbert in charge of integrating the Elbonians' software with the company's systems, which means traveling there. When Dilbert says it surely can't get worse now, the Boss advises him to get a tuberculosis vaccination.
punchline: Just when Dilbert thinks things can't get worse, the Boss reveals the assignment will send him to a disease-ridden Elbonia, proving that things always can get worse.
summary: After learning that programming has been shipped off to a faraway backwater, a man's claim that nothing could be worse is undone when his boss assigns him to the project and recommends a disease shot.

file: 1996/1996-01-20_doing baby sitting_morton triplets_juggle three toddlers_ceiling fan.gif
title: Bob the Dinosaur Juggles Toddlers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I heard you were doing some baby-sitting, Bob.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Yeah! I did the Morton triplets last night.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It's not easy to juggle three screaming toddlers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you say "juggle"...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the Mortons with a question about their ceiling fan.

setting: A living room with a couch, in a home
situation: Dogbert asks Bob the dinosaur about his baby-sitting job, and Bob says he did the Morton triplets and that juggling three screaming toddlers is hard. Dogbert starts to question what he means by "juggle" just as Dilbert arrives, holding a clipboard, to say the Mortons are calling with a question about their ceiling fan.
punchline: Bob's talk of juggling the toddlers hints that he literally juggled them, and the Mortons' question about their ceiling fan implies the children ended up in or near it.
summary: A dinosaur babysitter brags about juggling three toddlers, and a parent's call about their ceiling fan suggests he meant it literally.

file: 1996/1996-08-23_all year_asok the intern_awards_built unit_design_minor change_weekend_working_half cost.gif
title: Intern Cuts Costs, Gets Catapulted

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Asok the intern

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I came in over the weekend and looked at the design you've been working with all year.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It turns out that you could have built the unit at half the cost with just one minor change.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is it true I can win awards for this sort of thing?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Fetch the internapult.

setting: Conference room during an engineering meeting
situation: Asok, the intern, tells the engineering team that he spent his weekend reviewing their year-long design and found a single change that would have halved the cost. Dilbert, Alice and a bald coworker listen as he proudly asks whether he can win awards for this. Alice, unimpressed and annoyed at being shown up, calls for the 'internapult' to launch him away.
punchline: Instead of being rewarded for saving money, the intern is threatened with being flung out by a catapult for making the veteran engineers look incompetent.
summary: A keen intern exposes a costly flaw in his colleagues' year of work and is met with a hostile plan to fling him away.

file: 1996/1996-06-10_advanced material_designing at work_good batch_pyrophoric mean.gif
title: Pyrophoric Jar Sparks Gender Jab

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: These are some of the advanced materials I'm designing at work. That jar holds a pyrophoric substance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flash

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yep, that's a good batch.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A person from a smarter gender might have said "What does 'pyrophoric' mean?"

setting: A lab or workroom table with sample jars and materials
situation: Alice shows Dilbert advanced materials she designs and warns that one jar holds a pyrophoric substance. Without asking what that means, Dilbert opens the jar, it bursts into a flash of flame, and he is left singed with smoking hair. Alice then jabs that someone from a smarter gender would have asked what the word meant first.
punchline: Dilbert rashly opens a jar of a self-igniting substance without knowing what 'pyrophoric' means, and Alice sarcastically implies men are the less intelligent gender for not asking first.
summary: A man who never asks what a technical warning word means gets a fiery lesson while his coworker snipes about gender and intelligence.

file: 1996/1996-09-10_team building exercise_build trust_trust_not biggest problem.gif
title: Trust Fall Without Anyone Catching

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Teambuilding exercise

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This exercise will build trust. The partner in front will fall. The partner behind will break the fall.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, maybe trust isn't your biggest problem here.

setting: Office meeting room during a teambuilding session
situation: Dogbert leads a teambuilding exercise in which one partner falls backward and the other must catch them. Dilbert stands behind a falling colleague and, instead of catching him, he is busy fidgeting with his tie. The colleague hits the ground, and Wally mutters curses while Dogbert observes that trust is not the real problem.
punchline: The team's real problem is that they are so indifferent or inept that no one will actually catch a falling coworker, making trust irrelevant.
summary: A trust-fall exercise goes badly when the catcher fails to catch, prompting the facilitator to point out the team has deeper issues than trust.

file: 1996/1996-07-09_product mock up_last week_don't make prodcut_competitors product.gif
title: Mock-Up Becomes Thousand-Unit Order

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Thanks for making that product mock-up last week. The customer liked it so much that he ordered a thousand!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was a mock-up! We don't make that product yet. It would take three years to make one.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Just give me a thousand mock-ups. The first one was terrific!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The mock-up was our competitor's product with duct tape over the logo.

situation: A salesman thanks Dilbert for a product mock-up and announces that the customer has ordered a thousand units. Dilbert explains that the product doesn't exist yet and would take three years to build. The salesman simply asks for a thousand more mock-ups, so Dilbert reveals the original was a competitor's product with the logo covered by duct tape.
punchline: The salesman sells a product that doesn't exist and expects engineering to keep faking it, while the supposed prototype was really a rival's product disguised with duct tape.
summary: A sales rep who sold a thousand units of a nonexistent gadget asks the engineer to simply fake the rest, even though the demo was a rival's product in disguise.

file: 1996/1996-07-26_dogcart institure_advanced thinking_ending pverty_televison_wretched lives_paid guests_straggler cops.gif
title: Ending Poverty With Talk Shows

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here in the "Dogbert Institute for Advanced Thinking," I have devised a plan for ending poverty.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My plan is to wait until there are so many talk shows on television that all the people with wretched lives can be paid guests.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about the poor people who don't want to be on talk shows?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll get the stragglers on "Cops."

setting: Dilbert's home office, at a desk with a computer
situation: Dogbert, seated at his computer, announces that his think tank has devised a plan to end poverty. His plan is to wait until talk shows multiply so much that every person with a miserable life can be hired as a paid guest. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks about those who refuse to appear, and Dogbert says they'll be caught on "Cops."
punchline: Dogbert's "solution" to poverty is to exploit people's misery as paid television entertainment, and anyone who refuses will simply be filmed being arrested on a reality crime show.
summary: Dogbert proposes eliminating poverty by turning every destitute person into a paid talk-show guest, with holdouts handled by a police reality program.

file: 1996/1996-01-11_over internet_credit card number_insecure.gif
title: Credit Card Handed to Waitress

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would never buy something over the Internet. I'd hate to have my credit card number floating around out there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are a lot of unscrupulous people on the net.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Bottom line, it just isn't common sense.

situation: Dilbert sits at a restaurant table with a date and lectures her about never giving his credit card number over the Internet because of unscrupulous people online. While he talks, he hands his credit card to the waitress without noticing. Later, still lecturing, he finishes his point as the waitress is off with his card.
punchline: Dilbert preaches caution about credit card security online while carelessly handing his card to a stranger in a restaurant, ignoring the same risk in the real world.
summary: A man warns his dinner companion about the dangers of sharing card details online while casually surrendering his card to a waitress.

file: 1996/1996-05-19_anti rust_bald_big field_butterfly turned opera singer_car dealer_data compression_dream analysts_extended warranty_new algorythm_running against wind_sealant_serious money.gif
title: Dogbert's Insulting Dream Analysis Service

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Dream Analysis

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I was in a big field full of tofu and carburetors.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It means you're a gullible moron.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's $25 please.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Then I was running, running, running against the wind

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That means you're ugly.

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: Then the butterfly turned into an opera singer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That means you're bald.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suddenly I saw a new algorythm for data compression.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It means you're boring.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I told the car dealer I wanted the anti-rust sealant, the extended warranty and the lease option.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do you think it means?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It means I'm going to make some serious money today.

situation: Dogbert runs a dream analysis business where a series of clients, including Dilbert and the Boss, describe their dreams. Dogbert gives each one a brief insult as the interpretation and charges for it. When the Boss describes a dream about buying every add-on from a car dealer, Dogbert says it means he will make serious money.
punchline: Dogbert's interpretations are just insults until the Boss's dream about being upsold at a car dealership shows Dogbert's real meaning: the gullible customer is the source of his profit.
summary: A dog charging for dream readings hands out cheap insults as diagnoses until a client who overpays for car extras reveals who the real mark is.

file: 1996/1996-05-27_panther_cup of coffee_phil_prince_golden boy_potato salad_spoon.gif
title: Phil, Devil of the Coffee Pot

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: He slips in like a panther to take the last cup of coffee and not make more.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I am Phil, the prince of insufficient light! I darn you to heck!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Phil?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You were always Mom's golden boy.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Somebody brought potato salad. Give me your spoon.

setting: Office break room with a coffee maker
situation: A pointy-haired man in a gray suit takes the last cup of coffee and leaves the empty pot, imagining himself as a stealthy panther. A devil-costumed Phil appears with a giant spoon, confronting him with silly mock-threats. Phil then makes a petty sibling-style jab and demands his spoon because someone brought potato salad.
punchline: The devil's supposed fearsome curse is comically mild, 'I darn you to heck', and his demands shrink to a spoon for potato salad, undercutting any menace.
summary: A man sneaking the last coffee is confronted by a cartoonish devil whose idea of damnation is mild cursing and cutlery requests.

file: 1996/1996-11-08_new sex symbols_online personals_tech prowness_moonlit walks_must like to dance_applicants.gif
title: Dilbert Writes Nerdy Online Personals Ad

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Men who understand technology are the new sex symbols. Your online personals ad should emphasize your technical prowess.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about "Looking for woman who likes moonlit walks so I'll have more time alone with my computer"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And "Must like to dance." That's so I won't get a flabby, uncoordinated applicant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't call them "applicants" on the first date.

situation: Dogbert coaches Dilbert on writing an online personals ad, advising him to highlight his technical skills. Dilbert, working on his laptop, proposes lines that reveal he cares more about his computer than about dating, and treats prospective dates like job candidates.
punchline: Dilbert's ad is really a hiring screen in disguise, and he treats dates as job 'applicants', showing he approaches romance like a corporate recruiter.
summary: A dog advises a lonely engineer on his dating profile, but the engineer writes it like a job posting that prizes computer time and fit candidates.

file: 1996/1996-06-13_artificial urgency_gibberish_god news_mission_objectives uncler_insane but happy.gif
title: Happily Insane Under Artificial Urgency

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our objectives are unclear and our mission statement is gibberish...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But thanks to an artificial sense of urgency, I'm working harder than ever!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the good news you said you have?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Apparently I'm insane. But I'm one of the happy kinds!

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting table, Wally reports that the team's objectives are unclear and its mission statement is nonsense. He then says an artificial sense of urgency has him working harder than ever. When the Boss asks for the good news he promised, Wally cheerfully announces that he has gone insane but is the happy kind.
punchline: Wally's only good news is that he has been driven insane by pointless management pressure, and he is contentedly delusional about it.
summary: A cheerful employee admits that manufactured deadlines and a meaningless mission have broken his mind, but insists he's content.

file: 1996/1996-02-23_software_under contract_methodology_village meetings_juggle_elbonians_slam out code_go roller skating_pig_animals_engineering.gif
title: Elbonian Programmers' Chaotic Development Methodology

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Before I accept the software you wrote under contract, tell me what development methodology you use.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Programmer
transcript.text: We hold village meetings to boast of our skills and curse the devil-spawned end-users.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Programmer
transcript.text: Sometimes we juggle.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Programmer
transcript.text: At the last minute we slam out some code and go roller skating.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would find this humorous if not for the pig on my back.

setting: Elbonia, a muddy village where Dilbert is visiting the contract programmers
situation: Dilbert, sitting with his laptop and a pig clinging to his back, asks the Elbonian programmers who wrote his contracted software what development methodology they follow. They describe boasting at village meetings, cursing end-users, juggling, and writing code at the last minute before going roller skating. Dilbert realizes the joke is on him since he is relying on this process.
punchline: The Elbonians' non-methodology of last-minute code slamming is alarming, and Dilbert can't enjoy the humor because he is stuck in Elbonia with a pig on his back and depends on their software.
summary: A visiting engineer quizzes his offshore coders about their process and discovers it consists of bragging, juggling, and frantic last-minute coding.

file: 1996/1996-08-29_idiotic promise_brain_amazing thing_untapped power_solution_enjoy walk.gif
title: Brain Filters Out Boring Story

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So the salesperson made an idiotic promise to our customer. Now it's MY job to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The brain is an amazing thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying that if I use the untapped power of my brain, there's a solution?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, I'm saying my amazing brain filtered out your boring story so I could enjoy my walk.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy path during a walk
situation: Dilbert walks with Dogbert while complaining that a salesperson made an idiotic promise to a customer and that he now has to fix it. Dogbert cryptically remarks that the brain is amazing, which Dilbert takes as a hint at a solution. Dogbert reveals he was just tuning Dilbert out.
punchline: Dogbert's comment about the amazing brain had nothing to do with solving Dilbert's problem; he simply ignored Dilbert's boring complaint to enjoy his walk.
summary: While Dilbert vents about a salesperson's reckless promise, his dog companion admits he mentally tuned the whole rant out.

file: 1996/1996-03-25_lprodcut complet_ships tomorrow_additional features_marketing department_customers_want hardware_times like this_psycho path.gif
title: Wishing He Were a Psychopath

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At long last our product is complete. It ships tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: That's terrific. I only have a few additional features to add and the marketing department will be happy.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Manager
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: I believe that our customers want hardware, not software.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's times like this I wish I were a psychopath.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're not?

situation: Wally announces the product is finished and ships tomorrow, but a marketing manager cheerfully says he has a few more features to add and then claims customers actually want hardware, not software. Frustrated, Wally says he wishes he were a psychopath, and Dilbert is surprised to learn he isn't one.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan 'You're not?' implies Wally already seems like a psychopath, while also underscoring how maddening the marketing department's late demands are.
summary: Just as a finished product is about to ship, a marketer demands last-minute changes, driving a worn-out engineer to wish for homicidal tendencies.

file: 1996/1996-04-22_catbert hr driector_new employees_always quit_reapply_old job_higher salary_catnip_rubbing body.gif
title: Quit, Reapply, Catnip Loophole

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, it might not seem fair that new employees are paid more than you...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But you could always quit and then reapply for your old job at a higher salary.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just might do that!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Would you mind rubbing this catnip all over your body first?

situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells Wally that new hires earn more than he does, then suggests he quit and reapply for his own job at a higher salary. Wally eagerly says he might do exactly that. Catbert then asks him to rub catnip all over his body first.
punchline: Catbert's seemingly helpful HR advice is really a pretext to indulge his own feline cravings by getting Wally covered in catnip.
summary: An HR cat pitches a salary workaround to a dazed employee, only to slip in a bizarre request that serves his own appetites.

file: 1996/1996-07-15_catbert_evil director_human resources_enjoying job_temporary_emplotyee manual_job satisfaction_stealing company_admisiion_fearing sheiks pain_business.gif
title: Job Satisfaction Equals Stealing, Says Catbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, the evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: According to my sources, you've been enjoying your job, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was temporary. I don't know what got into me...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Please refer to page one of the employee manual.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Job satisfaction is the same as stealing from the company."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll have to charge you for admission unless I start hearing some shrieks of pain.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, confronts Wally because he has been caught enjoying his job. Wally claims it was only temporary, and Catbert directs him to the employee manual, which Wally reads aloud and which declares job satisfaction to be theft. Catbert then says he'll charge Wally admission unless he hears shrieks of pain, as if Wally's suffering were entertainment.
punchline: The company treats employee happiness as a punishable offense, and Catbert expects Wally's misery to be a paid spectacle.
summary: Catbert disciplines Wally for the crime of liking his work, citing a manual that equates contentment with theft.

file: 1996/1996-05-24_had a cat once_two hours_beef of cat_selfish.gif
title: Petting Cats Doesn't Cheer Wally

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I had a cat once...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I petted that thing for two hours but I didn't feel any better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Petting is for the benefit of the cat, not your hand.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They're so selfish.

setting: Office break room, a lunch table next to a soda machine
situation: Alice, Wally and Dilbert sit around a table eating lunch. Alice mentions she once had a cat, and Wally complains that petting it for two hours did nothing for his mood. Dilbert points out that petting is meant to benefit the cat, and Alice concludes that cats are selfish.
punchline: Wally expected to get emotional benefit from petting a cat, and when told it's for the cat's benefit, the group dismisses cats as selfish for not serving his needs.
summary: A lunchtime chat about a former pet reveals a coworker's self-centered view of what animals owe their owners.

file: 1996/1996-02-14_such cubicle enviroment_regular emplyees_enjoy_sharing cubicle_co ops_new co op_lasted a day_fit in.gif
title: Co-op Cubicle Crammed With Interns

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As a co-op employee, you can't expect the same lush cubicle environment that the regular employees enjoy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be sharing this cubicle with our other co-ops.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard that the new co-op only lasted one day.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He didn't fit in.

setting: Office hallway and a tiny cubicle
situation: The Boss escorts a new co-op employee and warns him that he won't get the nice cubicle regular employees have. He then shows the cubicle, which is stuffed with a pile of co-op workers tangled on top of each other. Later, Dilbert and Alice discuss the new co-op who quit after one day.
punchline: The new co-op didn't 'fit in' literally, since the cubicle was physically packed with too many co-op workers.
summary: A manager shows a newcomer a cubicle jammed with human bodies, which explains why the last new hire left so quickly.

file: 1996/1996-04-17_do math_idiot_monday and fridays_shocking_sick days_idiot savant.gif
title: Sick Days Cluster Around Weekends

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Oh my! This is shocking!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: 40% of all sick days taken by your staff are Fridays and Mondays!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What kind of idiot do they think I am?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Not an idiot savant. They can do math.

situation: An employee reads a report and tells the Boss that 40% of all sick days taken by his staff fall on Fridays and Mondays. The Boss indignantly asks what kind of idiot his staff takes him for. The employee replies that he's not an idiot savant, because they can do math.
punchline: Fridays and Mondays are only 40% of the workweek, so the sick days are exactly what chance would predict, and the employee insults the Boss by saying his staff can do math while he can't.
summary: A worker presents the boss with a supposedly suspicious attendance statistic, only to point out that the boss is too innocent of arithmetic to realize it's perfectly ordinary.

file: 1996/1996-03-26_department newsletter_high profile assignment_technical writer_intern and rodent_spats page_raise based_topless model.gif
title: Raise Depends on Intern and Rodent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you three to write the department newsletter. It's an important, high-profile assignment.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I am an experienced technical writer. You have placed me on a project with an intern and a rodent.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My next raise will depend on their performance.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'll do the sports page!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll be the topless model on page two.

situation: The Boss assigns Alice, Asok and Ratbert to produce the department newsletter, calling it an important high-profile job. Alice, a veteran technical writer, complains that she has been teamed with an intern and a rodent, and that her raise will hinge on their work. Asok eagerly claims the sports page while Ratbert cheerfully volunteers to be the topless model.
punchline: Alice's raise depends on teammates who are hopelessly unqualified, as shown by Ratbert's absurd offer to be the newsletter's topless model.
summary: A skilled writer is dismayed to learn her pay raise rides on the efforts of a novice and a lab rat on a supposedly crucial newsletter.

file: 1996/1996-08-18_getting stupid_increasing geometrically_slow trickle_gushing_firehouse_teacup_crossroads in history_functionally stupid_leader_vision_fog_human incompetence.gif
title: Dogbert Campaigns for Supreme Ruler

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People are getting stupider every day, relatively speaking.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The complexity of the world is increasing geometrically.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But your ability to learn is at the same slow trickle it has always been.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Information is gushing toward your brain like a firehose aimed at a teacup.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're at a crossroads in history. Even the smartest among you has become "functionally stupid."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your only hope is to choose a leader whose vision can penetrate the thick fog of human incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dogbert for Supreme Ruler of Earth!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want my opinion?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What are the odds of that?

setting: Outdoor hillside path and rocky ridge
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert walk along a trail while Dogbert lectures about how the growing complexity of the world is outpacing humanity's ability to learn. He concludes that people need a visionary leader and proclaims himself the candidate for Supreme Ruler of Earth. Dilbert asks if Dogbert wants his opinion.
punchline: Dogbert has already decided to rule the Earth, so when Dilbert offers his opinion he dismissively implies it has no chance of mattering.
summary: Dogbert makes a grand case that humanity is drowning in information and needs a strong ruler, then brushes off Dilbert's attempt to weigh in on his self-nomination.

file: 1996/1996-03-29_write about newsletter_grand tradition_engineering_lowest priority_dont despise.gif
title: Wally Misreads Being Despised as Romance

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Wally, I'm hoping you'll agree to write about your project for the newsletter...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: And in the grand tradition of engineering, I expect you'll give this the lowest priority, thus making me despise you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So... Are you saying you don't despise me NOW?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We are NOT having a "moment" here!

situation: A coworker asks Wally to write an article about his project for the company newsletter. She predicts he will give it lowest priority and make her despise him, as engineers always do. Wally cheerfully takes this to mean she doesn't currently despise him and imagines a romantic spark, while she angrily shuts that down.
punchline: Wally twists her insult about engineers into a sign that she likes him, so being told he will be despised is heard as a flirtatious compliment.
summary: A newsletter editor's grumpy prediction that an engineer will blow her off gets mistaken by Wally for a hint of affection.

file: 1996/1996-09-28_naked and exhausted_fishing boat_grabbed line_held on_secondd time_threw back in.gif
title: Lucky for the Fishermen

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...There I was, naked and exhausted, miles from shore. Dolphins taunted me for hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suddenly a deep sea sport fishing boat happened by. I grabbed the line and held on for my life.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow! That's lucky.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what I thought... until the second time they threw me back in.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I meant lucky for them.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair and Dogbert beside him
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert a story about being stranded naked and exhausted in the ocean, taunted by dolphins. A sport fishing boat arrives and he clings to the line, only to be thrown back into the water twice as an undersized catch.
punchline: Dogbert's remark that it was lucky 'for them' implies the fishermen were the fortunate ones for hooking a rare, absurd catch, dismissing Dilbert's ordeal with deadpan indifference.
summary: A man recounts a bizarre ocean rescue that went wrong, and his canine companion callously reveals who he thought got the good deal.

file: 1996/1996-01-16_billionaire_charity work_contribution_fine arts_software company.gif
title: Dogbert's Billionaire Victory Dance

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After I become a billionaire from my software company I'll do a little dance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm so rich. It's me you hail. If I'm obnoxious kiss my tail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you plan to do any charity work?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let me put it this way—you just saw my contribution to the fine arts.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert, perched on the back of the couch, announces that he will dance once his software company makes him a billionaire. He then performs a song-and-dance number celebrating his wealth and obnoxiousness. Dilbert asks whether he plans any charity work, and Dogbert says the dance was his charitable contribution.
punchline: Dogbert considers his smug, self-congratulatory dance to be his gift to the arts, which shows he has no intention of ever giving anything away.
summary: A future tycoon dog performs a boastful dance and then insists the performance counts as his philanthropy.

file: 1996/1996-07-13_evil director_mandatory blood test_take drugs_stealing time_test_general health.gif
title: Blood Test Detects Time Theft

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, the Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, it's time for your mandatory blood test.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't take drugs.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm testing to see if you're stealing time from the company.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Time? How can you test for that?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We test your general health. If it's good, you're not working enough hours.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You thief.

situation: Catbert, the Evil Director of Human Resources, shows up at Wally's cubicle with a syringe for a mandatory blood test. Wally assumes it is a drug test, but Catbert says he is testing for stolen company time. He explains that good general health proves an employee is not working enough hours.
punchline: The company treats good health as proof of slacking, implying employees are expected to work themselves sick, and Catbert accuses the healthy of theft.
summary: A malevolent HR cat draws blood from an employee to prove that being healthy means he is cheating his employer of working hours.

file: 1996/1996-01-02_antina_non stereotypical woman_computer monitor_coffe machine_butch woman_shirt and tie.gif
title: Antina the Non-Stereotypical Woman

transcript.speaker: Antina
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Antina the non-stereotypical woman.

transcript.speaker: Antina
transcript.text: That computer monitor you're using is supposed to be 17 inches. But it's more like 16.5 inches.

transcript.speaker: Antina
transcript.text: I took the coffee machine apart just for fun—want to see?

situation: A new coworker named Antina, a woman in a shirt, tie and skirt, introduces herself to Dilbert as the non-stereotypical woman. She then shows off her technical know-how by pointing out that his monitor is smaller than advertised and offering to show him the coffee machine she dismantled for fun.
punchline: Antina is a parody of the "woman in tech" stereotype, written as an extreme caricature of a woman who loves hardware and tinkering, with a deliberately clumsy and over-literal self-introduction.
summary: A tie-wearing new coworker proudly announces she defies female stereotypes, then proves it with nitpicky hardware talk and a dismantled appliance.

file: 1996/1996-02-28_building databse_coffee mugs_poor processes_probelm_slogan on mugs_project team.gif
title: Database First, Then Coffee Mugs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You haven't heard what the problem is yet; how can you recommend building a database to solve it??

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We always build a database.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And we'll need coffee mugs for the project team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The problem is that we have poor processes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That could be the slogan on our mugs!

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: The Boss objects that the team is proposing a database before he has even explained the problem. Wally says they always build a database and Dilbert adds that the project team will need coffee mugs. When the Boss finally says the problem is poor processes, Wally suggests using that as the slogan on the mugs.
punchline: The team reflexively reaches for the same canned solution and merchandise regardless of the problem, treating the project's real issue as nothing more than a slogan for swag.
summary: A manager scolds his team for prescribing a database before hearing the problem, only for them to turn his answer into a mug slogan.

file: 1996/1996-05-11_blood suckers_coworkers_famous novelist_lowly tech writer_scathing email messages_write a book_write witty_dogcart career counselor.gif
title: Scathing Emails Toward a Book Deal

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Career Counselor

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm a lowly technical writer now, but my goal is to become a famous novelist.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: My plan is to write witty and scathing e-mail messages about co-workers until a publisher gives me an advance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They might expect you to write a book at some point.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Blood suckers!

situation: Tina, a technical writer, tells Dogbert, her career counselor, that she plans to become a famous novelist. Her plan is to write witty, scathing e-mails about her co-workers until a publisher offers her an advance. Dogbert points out that a publisher might eventually expect an actual book, and Tina reacts with indignation.
punchline: Tina wants the publisher's advance without the work of writing a book, and she angrily calls publishers blood suckers for expecting a finished product.
summary: A technical writer hopes that nasty office emails will somehow earn her a publishing advance, and is outraged to learn that a real book might be required.

file: 1996/1996-04-27_work avoidance device_leave meeting_scurry away_pager number_grasping concept.gif
title: Wally's Pager: Work-Avoidance Device Misunderstood

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got myself a little work-avoidance device.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I want to leave a meeting early, I just look down and say "Uh-oh" and scurry away.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's the pager number in case I need you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're not quite grasping the concept here, Alice.

setting: Office break area by the vending machine
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Alice at the vending machine that he got a pager as a device for dodging work. He explains he pretends to be paged so he can leave meetings early. Alice innocently asks for his pager number so she can reach him, missing the point entirely.
punchline: Alice asks for the pager number of a pager whose whole purpose is to be a fake excuse to avoid work, so being reachable defeats it.
summary: A slacker brags about a pager he uses as a fake excuse to escape meetings, and a coworker sincerely asks how to page him.

file: 1996/1996-08-30_very annoying_see therpaist_emotional problem_misinterprets speech.gif
title: Catbert Misinterprets Everything Dilbert Says

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I've become one of those people who misinterprets everything you say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Why? Are you saying that nothing should ever change? Maybe you shouldn't be so rigid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This could be very annoying.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should see a therapist for your emotional problem.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, with Catbert perched on top of the computer monitor
situation: Catbert announces that he has become a person who misinterprets everything others say. When Dilbert asks a simple 'Why?', Catbert twists it into an accusation that Dilbert is rigid and opposed to change. Dilbert's mild remark that this could get annoying is then answered with advice to see a therapist.
punchline: Catbert demonstrates his announced habit in real time, deliberately twisting innocent remarks into insults and ending by blaming Dilbert for having an emotional problem.
summary: A cat perched on a monitor proves he is a chronic misreader of words by turning every innocent reply into an accusation.

file: 1996/1996-06-03_highly fragmented_optimize heard drive_vague_one gig hard drive_pentium processor.gif
title: Mind-Scanning Security Guard Defragments Brain

transcript.speaker: Brainitor
transcript.text: Halt and submit to the mind scan of "Brainitor, the Guardian of Security."

transcript.speaker: Brainitor
transcript.text: The bag contains one computer... "Pentium" processor... one gig hard drive... highly fragmented...

transcript.speaker: Brainitor
transcript.text: Please wait while I optimize your hard disk...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is vaguely unsettling.

setting: Building security checkpoint with a desk
situation: A bald, big-headed security guard calling himself Brainitor stops Dilbert, who carries a bag, and announces a mind scan. He reads out the bag's contents like a computer inventory, then says he will optimize Dilbert's hard disk. Dilbert is left uneasy about what is being done to him.
punchline: The guard's mind scan treats Dilbert's brain like a computer hard drive, reporting it as highly fragmented and offering to defragment it, which Dilbert finds creepy.
summary: A psychic-style security guard scans a visitor's bag and then starts tidying up the visitor's mind as if it were a cluttered computer disk.

file: 1996/1996-04-20_dances_dancing dogs_go wild_healed_healthy_invoice_poems_primal screams_tech me_total well being.gif
title: Consultant Bills for Primal Screams

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have my poems and dances healed your soul yet, Alice? The company cares about your total well being.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Excuse me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We want more money, not more dancing dogs!!! M-O-N-E-Y!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So you're saying those primal screams are healthy? Can you teach me to do it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my invoice - go wild.

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's desk
situation: Dogbert, wearing a beehive-style hat, performs poems and dances for the staff as a wellness consultant and asks Alice if it has healed her soul. Alice screams over the cubicle wall that she wants money, not dancing dogs. The Boss hears the outburst, concludes the primal screams are healthy, and asks Dogbert to teach him, so Dogbert hands him an invoice.
punchline: Dogbert turns an employee's angry scream of frustration into a new billable service by selling the Boss lessons in primal screaming.
summary: A consultant's wellness program provokes an employee's furious outburst, which the clueless manager mistakes for a therapeutic success and pays to learn.

file: 1996/1996-04-14_electrical engineering_engineering proposal_engineers opinion_major_masters degree_naked statues_nickle_scratch and sniff_technology publications_thundering moron_art history.gif
title: Dogbert Insults the Boss's Edits

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert would like to speak with you about the changes you made to my engineering proposal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: While Dilbert was getting his masters degree in electrical engineering...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You were majoring in art history so you could look at pictures of naked statues.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dilbert often contributes articles to technology publications.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You, on the other hand, rub those same publications with a nickel, looking for hidden "scratch and sniff" panels.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In summary...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never question an engineer's opinion, you thundering moron!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nicely done, but I wouldn't have said "thundering."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What were you drinking when you wrote this piece of crud?!!

situation: Dilbert brings Dogbert to the Boss's office to complain about the Boss's changes to his engineering proposal. Dogbert lists Dilbert's technical credentials and then mocks the Boss's education and reading habits before delivering a final insult. In the last panel Dilbert gently critiques Dogbert's word choice while the Boss, stunned, angrily questions what Dogbert had been drinking.
punchline: Dogbert's rant is so over the top that Dilbert only critiques one word choice, while the Boss misreads the whole thing as a drunken proposal rewrite.
summary: Dogbert defends Dilbert's engineering work by humiliating the unqualified boss who edited it, then gets critiqued on style.

file: 1996/1996-07-22_job security_past_vanished_blunders of management_motivation_fluttered away.gif
title: Dilbert Admits He Has No Motivation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now that job security is a thing of the past, I've noticed that my company loyalty has vanished, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And when you made my bonus primarily dependent on the blunders of senior management, my motivation fluttered away like a lonely sparrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So your point is?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No point. I just didn't have any reason to be working.

situation: Dilbert stands before the Boss's desk and calmly explains that his company loyalty disappeared once job security did. He adds that tying his bonus to the mistakes of senior management destroyed his motivation. When the Boss asks what he is getting at, Dilbert admits he has no point and simply had no reason to work.
punchline: Dilbert makes no demand or complaint; he just points out, with deadpan honesty, that management has removed every incentive for him to do his job.
summary: An employee politely lists the ways his employer has eliminated every reason for him to care about his work, then declares he wasn't even making a request.

file: 1996/1996-07-18_recognition program_assign names_levels performance_highest level_precious gem_sparkle.gif
title: Talc Isn't a Precious Gem

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new "Recognition Program" assigns the names of precious gems to your levels of performance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The highest level is diamond. You get a new ring at each level.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you sure talc is a precious gem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I saw it sparkle.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces a new employee recognition program that rewards performance levels named after precious gems, with a ring given at each level. Wally questions whether talc counts as a precious gem, and Dilbert halfheartedly defends it, suggesting he may have seen it sparkle.
punchline: Talc is one of the softest, cheapest minerals, so its inclusion implies that the lowest performance level is a worthless gem, and Dilbert's weak defense underscores how silly and insulting the tiered recognition scheme is.
summary: A manager unveils a gem-themed rating system with rings as rewards, and the staff wryly notice that one of its levels is named after a common, worthless mineral.

file: 1996/1996-08-11_voice mail message_department_quality thought_websters dictionary_african mammel_aardvark_shared printer_spewing resume.gif
title: Aardvark Thought Triggers Resume Exodus

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This voice-mail message is for the whole department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every morning from now on you'll get my "quality thought of the day."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today's thought is... um...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see... according to Webster's dictionary...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aardvark is a burrowing African mammal that eats ants.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if we were more like that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I mean like the aardvark, not the ants...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's weird. Every time I leave my quality thought of the day, the shared printer starts spewing résumés.

setting: Office cubicles and the boss's office
situation: The Boss leaves a voice-mail for the whole department announcing a daily 'quality thought,' but he has to improvise one and reads the dictionary definition of aardvark. He suggests the staff be more like the aardvark, not the ants it eats. Afterward he notices the shared printer keeps spewing résumés whenever he leaves a message.
punchline: By implying employees should be the predator rather than the ants, the Boss insults his staff, who respond by printing résumés to find new jobs, which he fails to connect to his own message.
summary: A manager's improvised motivational voice-mail comparing his team to ant-eating wildlife sends everyone hunting for other jobs, and he never works out why.

file: 1996/1996-04-18_40 % sick days_fridays_mondays_good one_kidding.gif
title: Sick Days Cluster Around Weekends

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It has come to my attention that 40% of your sick days are on Fridays and Mondays. This is unacceptable.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!!! That's a good one!!!

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Please tell me he was kidding.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Welcome to hell, kid.

situation: The Boss, reading from a paper at a conference table, complains that 40% of the staff's sick days fall on Fridays and Mondays. A newly hired employee laughs loudly, assuming it's a joke, while Dilbert and Wally sit stone-faced. The newcomer then realizes the boss is serious and asks if he was kidding, and Wally welcomes him to hell.
punchline: The naive new hire mistakes the boss's absurdly humorless accusation for a joke, and the jaded veteran Wally tells him that the workplace is actually this miserable.
summary: A rookie guffaws at what he thinks is a joke about suspicious sick-day patterns, only to learn from a weary coworker that management is deadly serious.

file: 1996/1996-04-11_vending machine_stole money_sentenced to death_director human resources_desensitized_tragic news_execution is scheduled.gif
title: Desensitized Dilbert Faces Execution Tomorrow

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today was a bad day. First the vending machine stole my money...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and by the end of the day I had been sentenced to death by the Director of Human Resources...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've become totally desensitized to tragic news!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The execution is scheduled for tomorrow. I should call in sick.

situation: Dilbert comes home with his briefcase and tells Dogbert, who is reading a newspaper on the couch, about his terrible day. He lists a vending machine stealing his money and being sentenced to death by the Director of Human Resources as if they were comparable misfortunes. Dogbert hums along, unbothered, as Dilbert concludes he should call in sick for the execution.
punchline: Dilbert is so numbed by constant workplace misery that a death sentence barely registers, and his only concern is how to handle the absence from work.
summary: A worn-down engineer recounts his day, treating a death sentence from HR as just another annoyance to schedule around.

file: 1996/1996-06-24_new objectoves_achievable_objectives approved_measurable.gif
title: Measurable Objectives Involve Organ Removal

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Here's a draft of my new objectives. I tried to make them achievable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "No matter how stupid my co-workers are, I will not punch a hole in anyone's torso, rip out a vital organ and keep it in my cubicle as a warning to others."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope she gets those objectives approved.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes! It's measurable!

setting: Boss's office and the hallway outside it
situation: Alice hands her boss a draft of her new performance objectives, saying she tried to make them achievable. The boss reads aloud a violent goal about not ripping out a coworker's organ. Outside the office, Wally and Dilbert watch her leave, and she cheers that the objective is measurable.
punchline: Alice's objective is a promise not to commit gruesome violence against stupid coworkers, which she gleefully celebrates as measurable, implying she is on the verge of doing it and mocking the management jargon requirement that goals be measurable.
summary: An employee submits a gory but technically quantifiable goal for her annual review and celebrates that it meets the criteria.

file: 1996/1996-10-28_catbert_evil hr director_like about work_making popcorn_microwave_pretend tow ork_body language_popcorn priviledges.gif
title: Catbert Threatens Wally's Popcorn Privileges

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hey, Wally, is there anything you still like about working here?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Um... I like making popcorn in the microwave and eating it while I pretend to work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your body language tells me that something evil is going to happen to my popcorn privileges.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I love my job.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, asks Wally whether anything about working at the company still appeals to him. Wally honestly admits he likes microwaving popcorn and eating it while pretending to work. Catbert reads this as a weakness to exploit and decides to take away Wally's popcorn privileges, while secretly thinking how much he loves his job.
punchline: Catbert gets sadistic joy from discovering the one small pleasure Wally has left at work and immediately plans to destroy it.
summary: An H.R. cat probes a lazy employee for his last workplace joy, then gleefully plots to ruin it.

file: 1996/1996-10-23_catbert evil hr director_random acts_catness_ink suit_appproaching_purring_shedding_curl and style.gif
title: Catbert Purrs at Woman in Pink

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I feel like committing random acts of catness.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Woman in pink suit approaching... Activate purring and shedding.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purr purr purr

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, Alice, how long does it take to curl and style a suit like that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you dry-clean it or just give it a perm?

setting: Office hallway, then a conference room
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, wanders the hallway feeling like acting like a cat. He spots a woman in a pink suit approaching and switches on purring and shedding to charm her. In a meeting, Dilbert and Wally mock Alice's frizzy pink suit, which appears to be as fuzzy as her hair, as if it were covered in cat fur.
punchline: Catbert's purring and shedding on the pink suit leaves Alice's outfit looking permed and fuzzy, and her coworkers mockingly ask how she styles and dry-cleans it.
summary: After an H.R. cat rubs against a woman's pink suit and sheds all over it, her coworkers tease her about the suit's curly fuzz.

file: 1996/1996-09-17_cause problems_dogcart consulting_one full year_smarter_ten million doallrs_work guraenteed_year 2000_y2k.gif
title: Y2K Consultant Sells Worthless Guarantee

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When the year 2000 comes, your computers will think it's the year "00" and cause major problems.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Consulting Company can fix the problem for only ten million dollars. Our work is guaranteed for one full year, starting today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But why would I care? The year "00" is before I'm born.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Amazing... you'd actually have to be smarter to do something stupid.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, warns the Boss about the Y2K bug and offers to fix it for ten million dollars with a one-year guarantee starting today. The Boss, reading the proposal, responds that the year 00 is before he was born, so he doesn't see why he should care. Dogbert marvels at his stupidity.
punchline: The Boss's reasoning is so absurdly wrongheaded that Dogbert remarks it would take more intelligence than he has to manage something that stupid.
summary: A consultant pitches an expensive millennium-bug fix to a manager whose baffling logic leaves even the pitchman astonished.

file: 1996/1996-04-25_experiment 1_exposing rat marketing plan_no adverse response_introduction_background_far more exposure_humans_tolerate.gif
title: Rat Tested on Marketing Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Experiment #1: I am exposing a rat to my company's marketing plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He seems to have no adverse response to the introduction and background.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is already far more exposure than humans could tolerate.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Sales projections... Brain tumor... Get Tylenol...

situation: Dilbert conducts a lab-style experiment, exposing Ratbert to his company's marketing plan while taking notes. Ratbert is fine while reading the introduction, but as he gets further into the document he starts muttering about a brain tumor and needing Tylenol. Dilbert notes that this is already more exposure than a human could endure.
punchline: The company's marketing plan is so painfully tedious and bad that reading it gives a rat a headache and makes him fear he has a brain tumor.
summary: A man tests whether a lab rat can survive reading his employer's marketing document, and the rodent quickly begins showing signs of distress.

file: 1996/1996-07-20_update objectives_need targets_hard work_support management_picture.gif
title: Boss Delegates Writing Alice's Objectives

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time for me to update your objectives, Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need targets that can only be achieved by amazingly hard work plus the constant support of management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm busy, so you'll have to write them yourself.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's wrong with this picture?

situation: The Boss tells Alice it is time to update her performance objectives and says the targets should require hard work and constant management support. He then announces he is too busy and tells Alice to write the objectives herself. Alice points out the contradiction.
punchline: The Boss demands targets that depend on constant management support, yet he is too busy to provide any, even for writing the objectives, which exposes his hypocrisy.
summary: A manager insists goals must rely on his constant backing, then hands the goal-writing job back to the employee because he has no time.

file: 1996/1996-08-21_new data encryption_phb_pointy haired boss_converts email_manager babble_carry pepper spray_supermodel.gif
title: Encryption Program Called P.H.B.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a new data encryption program called P.H.B. which stands for Pointy-Haired Boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It converts e-mail into manager babble. Nobody can intercept and decode my private messages without the key.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Who would want to read your messages?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Somebody might want to read my messages. It could happen!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And maybe you should carry pepper spray in case supermodels try to kiss you.

situation: Dilbert proudly explains that he has invented an encryption program that turns his e-mail into incomprehensible manager babble so nobody can read his private messages. Dogbert, sitting nearby, asks who would ever want to read his messages. Dilbert insists someone might, and Dogbert sarcastically suggests he also carry pepper spray against supermodels trying to kiss him.
punchline: Dogbert mocks Dilbert's self-importance by implying that his messages are as unlikely to be of interest to anyone as supermodels are to pursue him romantically.
summary: After inventing a scrambler that makes his e-mails sound like management nonsense, Dilbert is sarcastically told by Dogbert that nobody cares enough to snoop on him.

file: 1996/1996-09-19_year 2000 problkems_computer problems_head spun_dint explode_left money_table.gif
title: Dogbert's Year 2000 Invoice Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my invoice for fixing your "Year 2000" computer problems.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: AAAEE!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So his head spun, but it didn't explode?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah. I guess I left some money on the table.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's living room
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, hands the Boss an invoice for fixing the company's Year 2000 computer problems, and the Boss reacts with a scream and is sent flying out the door. Afterward Dogbert tells Dilbert that the Boss's head spun but did not explode, which he takes to mean he could have charged more.
punchline: Dogbert measures the success of his price gouging by how violently the client reacts, so since the Boss's head didn't explode, he concludes he undercharged.
summary: A canine consultant judges how much he overbilled by whether his client's skull detonates at the sight of the bill.

file: 1996/1996-09-16_pager vibrate_not wearing_classic case_phantom pager_technology workers_relocate it.gif
title: Phantom Pager Syndrome Therapy Session

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On weekends I'll feel my pager vibrate... But when I go to check it, I realize I'm not wearing it.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: It's a classic case of phantom-pager syndrome. It's common among technology workers.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: There's no treatment for it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want to treat it. I want to relocate it.

situation: Dilbert lies on a couch and tells his therapist that on weekends he feels his pager vibrate even though he isn't wearing it. The therapist diagnoses phantom-pager syndrome, common among tech workers, and says there is no treatment. Dilbert replies that he doesn't want treatment, he wants to relocate the pager.
punchline: Dilbert is not interested in curing the phantom vibration; he wants to relocate the pager, implying he'd like to shove it somewhere painful.
summary: A tech worker in therapy learns that his imaginary pager buzzing is a recognized condition and responds with a crude suggestion for where the pager should go.

file: 1996/1996-10-08_strategic alliance_approve projects_small company_seat of pants_flexible_not wearing pants.gif
title: Small Company Flies Without Pants

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Strategic Alliance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These are the procedures my company uses to approve projects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess a small company such as yours is used to flying by the seat of the pants.

transcript.speaker: Small Company Owner
transcript.text: Not necessarily.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean you're flexible?

transcript.speaker: Small Company Owner
transcript.text: I mean I'm not wearing pants.

setting: Small company's office during a strategic alliance meeting
situation: Dilbert visits a small company's owner to discuss a strategic alliance and hands over a thick binder of his company's project approval procedures. He remarks that a small company probably operates by the seat of its pants. The owner denies it, and when Dilbert guesses he means he's flexible, the owner reveals he literally isn't wearing pants.
punchline: The owner takes the idiom 'flying by the seat of the pants' literally, admitting he is sitting at his desk without pants on.
summary: A big company's rep mocks a small firm's improvised approach, only to have its owner turn the idiom into a literal confession of pantslessness.

file: 1996/1996-08-19_hit glass ceiling_play the game_promote you_dresses like boss_suit_pointy haired.gif
title: Dressing Like the Boss for Promotion

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've hit the glass ceiling. I'll never be promoted again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because you're not willing to "play the game." You have to look and act like the person who can promote you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooo-la la!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This had better work.

setting: Office conference room, then a hallway or office
situation: Alice complains at a table that she has hit the glass ceiling and will never be promoted again. A male coworker advises her to look and act like the person who can promote her. In the last panel she has styled her hair into the Boss's pointy shape and wears a suit, while a coworker reacts approvingly and she hopes it works.
punchline: Alice takes the advice literally and imitates the Pointy-Haired Boss's hairstyle and clothes, mocking the idea that promotions go to people who mimic their superiors rather than to the competent.
summary: After being told that advancement means resembling whoever hands out promotions, a frustrated employee turns up styled as a copy of her boss.

file: 1996/1996-06-25_sit do mothing_implement_bold quality initiative_talented_energetic coworkers.gif
