title: Dilbert Mocks Quality Initiative Fantasy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could sit here doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or I could implement a bold quality initiative with the help of my talented and energetic coworkers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I crack me up.

situation: Dilbert sits alone in his cubicle and thinks about doing nothing. He then imagines the alternative of launching a bold quality initiative with talented, energetic coworkers, and laughs to himself at how absurd that idea is.
punchline: Dilbert finds the idea of an energetic, talented team pulling off a quality initiative so unrealistic that it is only a joke, so doing nothing is the real plan.
summary: A lone cubicle worker weighs idleness against an inspiring team project and decides the second option is simply funny.

file: 1996/1996-09-24_iron man event_improve teamwork_stairs_potatoe_good hspae_wrenched muscle.gif
title: Dilbert Flexes, Dogbert's Potato Insult

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss is making the engineers compete in an "Iron Man" event. It's supposed to improve teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm glad I take the stairs sometimes instead of using the elevator. I'm in pretty good shape.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, you are, to the extent potato is a pretty good shape.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just wrenched a muscle.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert comes home carrying his briefcase and tells Dogbert that his boss is forcing the engineers into an "Iron Man" competition to build teamwork. He sits on the couch and smugly flexes his arm, claiming he is in good shape because he sometimes takes the stairs. Dogbert retorts that a potato counts as being in good shape too, and Dilbert immediately strains a muscle.
punchline: Dilbert's boast about his fitness is demolished by Dogbert's insult that his shape is merely potato-like, and he promptly injures himself while flexing.
summary: A self-satisfied engineer brags about his fitness before an enforced athletic contest, only to be mocked by his dog and hurt himself mid-flex.

file: 1996/1996-08-22_lowly intern_obvious solution_clear buffers_initialize link_code patch_memory leak_salary_twice as much_money.gif
title: Intern Fixes Wally's Computer Problem

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I am only a lowly intern, but I see an obvious solution to your problem.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Just click here... Clear your buffers and initialize the link... Now use this code patch for the memory leak.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: This is funny if you consider that your salary is twice as much as mine.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm laughing on the inside.

situation: A young intern notices a colleague struggling with a computer problem and walks him through the fix, pointing out where to click and which code patch to apply. Once the problem is solved, the intern remarks that it's ironic since the colleague earns twice his salary. The seated coworker, now embarrassed, says he is laughing on the inside.
punchline: The better-paid employee had to be rescued by a lowly intern, and his deadpan claim to be laughing on the inside reveals his embarrassment.
summary: A junior helper effortlessly repairs a senior colleague's software trouble, then wryly notes the pay gap between them.

file: 1996/1996-03-09_dazzling demo_dark angel demos_demo_sham_doomed_file server_worst is over.gif
title: Dark Angel of Demos Sabotages Presentation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We planned a dazzling demo for you, but as you can see we're being visited by the Dark Angel of Demos.

transcript.speaker: Dark Angel of Demos
transcript.text: The demo is a sham. Their project is doomed. Cut their funding before your name is associated with it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The worst is over.

transcript.speaker: Dark Angel of Demos
transcript.text: Look at some of the pictures the "boys" store on the file server ..

setting: Office, in front of a computer during a demo
situation: Dilbert apologizes to two visitors, a man with glasses and the Boss, because the planned demo is being ruined by the Dark Angel of Demos, a small red devil figure on the computer screen. The devil tells the visitor the demo is a sham and urges him to cut the project's funding. Just when Dilbert thinks the worst is over, the devil reveals embarrassing pictures stored on the file server by the team.
punchline: Dilbert thinks the demo has hit rock bottom, but the demon sabotages them even further by exposing the questionable pictures the engineers keep on the file server.
summary: A malicious demon in the computer torpedoes a product demonstration, then twists the knife by exposing the team's embarrassing hidden files.

file: 1996/1996-07-24_empowered_own deciosns_independantly_three months_empowerment_project canceled.gif
title: Empowerment Was Really Neglect

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I admit I was skeptical when you said I would be empowered to make my own decisions...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But I give you credit. You've let me work independently for three months...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's that look on your face?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please tell me that it was empowerment I was experiencing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I ever mention that your project was canceled?

situation: Alice thanks her boss for the empowerment she believes she has enjoyed, having been left to work independently for three months. Noticing his odd expression, she asks him to confirm it was really empowerment. He casually reveals that her project was canceled long ago and he never told her.
punchline: What Alice thought was management trust and empowerment was actually the boss neglecting to tell her that her project had been canceled.
summary: A grateful employee praises her manager's hands-off style, only to learn he simply forgot to inform her that her work had been scrapped months earlier.

file: 1996/1996-02-25_aging_embarrased_our dept secreatry_our mail room_pay simple invoice_protect reputation_six months_work at company.gif
title: Invoice Takes Six Months to Pay

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm embarrassed to work at my company, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can't even pay a simple invoice in less than six months.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "First it comes to our mail room for aging."

transcript.speaker: Mail Room Worker
transcript.text: Do we like Dilbert?

transcript.speaker: Mail Room Coworker
transcript.text: Bad haircut. Penalty box.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Months later it gets to our department secretary."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's urgent.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: I'll start ignoring it immediately.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Eventually my boss gets it. He uses it to demonstrate his inability to grasp the concept of time."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's get some more bids.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was the past. This is the present.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "If it makes it to the accounts payable group, it will be eaten by trolls."

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: No, thanks. I'm full.

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: Just a taste.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How would you protect your reputation if you were associated with something so pathetic?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd tell everybody that the doofy guy is my butler.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hypothetically.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch for the therapy-style conversation, with cutaways to the mail room, a secretary's desk, the boss's office and the accounts payable trolls
situation: Dilbert complains to Dogbert that his company takes over six months to pay a simple invoice, and narrates the invoice's journey. It is aged and penalized in the mail room, ignored by a secretary, misused by the boss to demand more bids, and finally eaten by trolls in accounts payable. Dilbert then asks Dogbert how he would protect his reputation if tied to something so pathetic.
punchline: Dogbert answers by saying he would disown Dilbert and claim he is his butler, rather than offer any comfort about the company's absurd payment process.
summary: A single bill drifts through a chain of absurd corporate dysfunction before reaching payment, and the dog consoling the complaining employee only offers to deny knowing him.

file: 1996/1996-02-09_move project_due date_reach objective_perfromance.gif
title: Boss Keeps Moving Wally's Deadline

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I've decided to move your project due date up a month.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Every time it looks like I'll reach an objective, you move it! What does this prove about my performance?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It proves I'm better at setting objectives than you are at achieving them.

situation: The Boss sits behind his desk and tells Wally he is moving his project's due date up by a month. Wally complains that every time he is close to hitting an objective, it gets moved, and asks what that says about his performance. The Boss smugly twists it into evidence that he is the better objective-setter.
punchline: The Boss turns his own habit of moving the goalposts into a compliment to himself, blaming Wally's performance rather than his own unfair management.
summary: A manager who keeps shifting a deadline earlier claims the constant changes show his own skill at planning, not any flaw in the process.

file: 1996/1996-08-05_hunk_burning love_cubicle_working_sending steamy email_send to all_thank you.gif
title: Steamy Email Sent To Everyone

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Tom, you delicious hunk of burning love: If you were in my cubicle now I'd...

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: It looks as if I'm working. Nobody can tell that I'm sending steamy e-mail to my new boyfriend.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tina, two things: Watch out for the "send to all" address, and thank you very much.

situation: Tina types a steamy love message to her new boyfriend Tom at her computer, smugly thinking that nobody can tell she isn't working. Dilbert then walks up and tells her she should watch out for the "send to all" address, and thanks her, revealing that her private message went out to the whole company.
punchline: Tina accidentally sent her racy email to everyone in the company, which Dilbert politely lets her know while thanking her for the unexpected entertainment.
summary: A coworker believes her flirtatious email to a new boyfriend is secret until a colleague reveals that everyone received it.

file: 1996/1996-10-18_trade show_free stuff_cheap pens_eye contact_hit buffet.gif
title: Trade Show Freebie Hunting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the trade show

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What kind of free stuff do you have?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Cheap pens? That's original. Okay, fill 'er up. But I'm afraid I can't give you any eye contact.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's enough industry research for today. It's time to hit the buffet.

setting: A busy trade show floor with vendor booths
situation: Wally arrives at a vendor's booth at a trade show and demands to know what free items are on offer. Learning it's only cheap pens, he sarcastically has the vendor fill his bag while refusing to make eye contact. He then declares his 'industry research' done and heads off to the buffet.
punchline: Wally treats the trade show as nothing more than a chance to collect freebies and food, calling it 'industry research' while giving the vendor zero genuine interest.
summary: A freeloading employee stuffs his bag with giveaways at a convention booth and ends his supposed research with a trip to the free food.

file: 1996/1996-03-03_new candidte_interview_reveal ugly truth_dedicated_employee empowerment_jennifer_special pharse_job interview_snarky woman_jettison dignity.gif
title: Candidate Sees Through Empowerment Buzzword

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to interview the new candidate for engineering. Don't reveal any ugly truths.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At this company we're dedicated to the principle of employee empowerment, Jennifer.

transcript.speaker: Jennifer
transcript.text: The "principle of employee empowerment"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Jennifer
transcript.text: Why would you have a special phrase for something like that?

transcript.speaker: Jennifer
transcript.text: If you could really make decisions on your own it would never occur to you to invent a phrase for it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My shields are down... a hull breach is imminent...

transcript.speaker: Jennifer
transcript.text: Just don't tell me you have "quality teams."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Run for it, Jennifer!!! It's too late for me but you can save yourself!!! Run!!!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Whoa! Hull breach. Any survivors?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One. I had to jettison my dignity but she made it to the escape pod.

setting: Office interview room, with a Star Trek-style dramatic imagining of the interview
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to interview a job candidate without revealing any ugly truths. Dilbert recites the company's commitment to employee empowerment, but the candidate, Jennifer, sharply points out that a company that needs a special phrase for it clearly doesn't practice it. Dilbert panics and warns her to flee, then afterward reports that he sacrificed his dignity so she could escape.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to hide the company's ugly truths collapses when the candidate sees through the buzzwords, so he treats the interview like a doomed spaceship and helps her flee the company.
summary: A sharp job applicant dismantles the company's management jargon, leaving the interviewer to stage a dramatic starship-style rescue of her from the firm.

file: 1996/1996-03-12_product idea_quit_start business_run new company_cucbilces_immoral_people already in hell.gif
title: Moonlighting From Cubicles Already In Hell

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If this company won't use our product idea let's quit and start our own business!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why quit? We can run our new company from our cubicles and get paid too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that be immoral?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's only an issue for people who aren't already in hell.

situation: Dilbert proposes quitting to start a business based on a product idea his company rejected. Wally suggests they instead run the new company from their cubicles while still collecting their salaries. When Dilbert asks if that's immoral, Wally says morality only matters for people not already in hell.
punchline: Wally justifies stealing company time for a side business by implying that working at this company is already hell, so ethics no longer apply.
summary: Rather than leaving to launch a startup, a lazy coworker proposes building it on the employer's dime and shrugs off the ethics by calling his job damnation.

file: 1996/1996-05-25_two percent annual_disppoint_compensated_drastic_low expectations_good sign_thinking.gif
title: Two Percent Raise Breaks Her Mind

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: A two percent annual raise?!! Wowee!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Ha ha! You tried to disappoint me but I compensated by drastically lowering my expectations!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, it might be a good sign, but I'm thinking not.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Weeee!!

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, reacts to a meager two percent annual raise with manic glee, claiming she has compensated for the disappointment by drastically lowering her expectations. In the final panel she spins wildly in her office chair while Dilbert and Wally look on, doubtful that her cheerfulness is a healthy sign.
punchline: Carol's delighted reaction to a tiny raise is so extreme that it suggests she has cracked under the stress rather than genuinely coping.
summary: A cheerful employee meets a stingy pay increase with unhinged enthusiasm, leaving her coworkers to suspect she has lost her grip.

file: 1996/1996-04-21_ken from sales_nobody buys_current prodcut_new version_entire product line_biggest comepetitor_brisk sales_commissions galore_justice_idiots punished.gif
title: Sales Guy Kills Current Product

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Yo, Dil-Man!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh, it's Ken from Sales.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: I told our biggest customers how great our next product will be. Now nobody will buy our current product.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: When will the new version be available?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In a year or two.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Hmm... I seem to have single-handedly destroyed an entire product line.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Luckily our biggest competitor is hiring sales people. And I'm betting they'll have brisk sales this year!

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Commissions galore!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If there's justice in this world, the idiots will be punished...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Before they get promoted.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Um... we need the new version by Tuesday.

situation: Ken, a salesman, tells Dilbert he has pre-announced the next product to the company's biggest customers, so no one will buy the current product anymore. He admits he has destroyed a product line, then plans to jump to a competitor to earn commissions. Dilbert wishes for justice, but Ken then demands the new version by Tuesday.
punchline: The salesman wrecks the product line with premature promises and escapes the consequences by switching companies, while still demanding that engineering deliver the impossible new version immediately.
summary: A salesman's premature hype ruins current sales, yet he cheerfully heads for a competitor and still expects the engineer to deliver overnight.

file: 1996/1996-05-31_need input_end of day_drop request here_perpeytaul ignorance_touch stuff.gif
title: Wally's Pile of Perpetual Ignorage

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, I need your input on this by the end of the day.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Please drop your request here, in "Wally's pile of perpetual ignorage."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can't I just give it to you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't like to touch that stuff with my hands.

situation: A coworker asks Wally for his input on a document by the end of the day. Wally gestures to a huge pile of papers on his desk and tells the coworker to drop the request there. When the coworker asks to hand it over directly, Wally explains that he avoids touching the pile with his hands.
punchline: Wally's pile of ignored requests is so untouchable that even he won't handle it, which shows that anything placed there will never be dealt with.
summary: Wally directs a colleague to dump a request onto his towering heap of neglected paperwork, which he refuses to touch himself.

file: 1996/1996-01-28_fear of action_festering cynicism_lame company_loyalty_micromanged_need help_only one on earth_physical abnormalities_six years experince_downsizing.gif
title: Writing Job Requirements To Survive Downsizing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your help, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company is downsizing. They told us to write our own job requirements then reapply for our jobs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why do you want to keep working for such a lame company?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Loyalty!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha! Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. You must write your job requirements so you are the only one on Earth who fits.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The candidate must have six years experience sitting in a big box being micromanaged by a nitwit.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The candidate must have a festering cynicism and an acquired fear of action.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That narrows it to ten thousand employees.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll have to focus on your physical abnormalities.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and his home
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for help because his company is downsizing and making employees write their own job requirements and reapply. Dogbert mocks his loyalty, then helps draft requirements so narrowly tailored that only Dilbert fits. Even Dilbert's cynical, passive traits still match ten thousand employees, so Dogbert resorts to his physical abnormalities.
punchline: Even job requirements built from Dilbert's own bleak workplace traits are so common that Dogbert has to resort to mocking his physical abnormalities to make him unique.
summary: To help his friend survive layoffs, a scheming dog drafts a tailor-made job description, but the traits describe thousands of equally beaten-down coworkers.

file: 1996/1996-05-12_new vp_cost containment_first priority_reduce expenses_office supplies_supply cabinet locked_butter efficient secreatray_naive question_dispirited hollow shells_product shoddy_get supplies_like honesty.gif
title: Intern Questions Supply Cabinet Lockdown

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you all to meet our new vice president in charge of cost containment.

transcript.speaker: New VP
transcript.text: My first priority is to reduce our spiraling expenses for office supplies.

transcript.speaker: New VP
transcript.text: From now on, your supply cabinet will be locked.

transcript.speaker: New VP
transcript.text: The only key will be under the control of your bitter and inefficient secretary.

transcript.speaker: New VP
transcript.text: Questions?

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I am only an intern so please excuse this naive question...

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I've noticed that the employees are all dispirited hollow shells, management is random and our products are shoddy.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: How are you going to solve that by making it hard to get supplies?

transcript.speaker: New VP
transcript.text: I thought you said they like honesty.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ask how much he's paid. It shows you care.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The new VP of cost containment announces that the office supply cabinet will be locked, with the only key held by a bitter, inefficient secretary. An intern, apologizing for being naive, points out that the company's real problems are demoralized employees, random management and shoddy products. The VP is irritated and the boss's reply is to ask how much the intern gets paid.
punchline: The company's real problems are morale, management and quality, yet the cost-cutter fixates on locking up pens and paper, and the one person who honestly says so gets shut down with a jab about his pay.
summary: A penny-pinching executive clamps down on stationery while an earnest intern politely points out the much bigger rot he's ignoring.

file: 1996/1996-09-15_catbert_cubicle plan_densification project_dignity_evil director_human resources_lower morale_patented head cubicle_recycled_business.gif
title: The Patented Head Cubicle

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mr. Catbert, our evil director of human resources, will describe our new cubicle plan.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Last year we reduced the size of cubicles in the densification project.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We didn't save much money, but we did lower morale.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This year we'll build on that success...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: With the patented "head cubicle."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hold still, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And the head cubicle can be recycled after you're downsized!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We really need to draw the line at some point.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: While we still have our dignity.

setting: Conference room during a management presentation
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, presents the company's new cubicle plan to the staff. After last year's shrinking of cubicles only lowered morale, he unveils a "head cubicle", a cardboard box placed over each employee's head, and demonstrates it on Wally. The employees, now wearing boxes, remark that they need to draw the line somewhere.
punchline: Cubicles have been shrunk so far that the next step is a box over the head, and the employees only now think it's time to protest, long after losing their dignity.
summary: Catbert follows up on a failed cubicle-shrinking scheme by fitting employees with cardboard boxes over their heads that can be recycled once they're laid off.

file: 1996/1996-02-03_first email_message_how to use email_forgot watch_change jobs.gif
title: Boss's First Email: What Time Is It

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Wally! The Boss sent his first e-mail message!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you said he wasn't bright enough to figure out how to use e-mail!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What's his message?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "I forgot my watch. Does anybody know what time it is?"

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Time to change jobs.

situation: Dilbert excitedly tells Wally that the Boss has sent his first e-mail, pointing out that Wally was wrong to doubt him. Wally asks what the message says, and Dilbert reads out that the Boss merely asked everyone what time it is because he forgot his watch. Wally concludes it is time to change jobs.
punchline: The Boss finally masters e-mail only to use it for a trivial question he could have answered by glancing at a clock, confirming how clueless he is and making Wally want to quit.
summary: A supposedly clueless manager manages his debut e-mail, but it turns out to be a request for the current time that leaves his employees despairing.

file: 1996/1996-06-30_d chop_television_feel safer_screens_violent shows_news_sports_dramas_sexual innuendo_comedy commercials_weather reports_tornado rips_entertainment.gif
title: The D-Chip Filters Everything Fun

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call my invention the D-chip television filter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I feel safer already.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It screens out any show with violence.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There goes the news, sports and dramas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It also gets rid of shows that feature dishonesty or sexual innuendos.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Goodbye comedy and commercials.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's hook it up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All we're getting is weather reports.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A huge tornado ripped through a BEEP ssss sssssssss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It works! The evil can't get to us now, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Unhook that #!*% thing or I'll rip off your leg and beat you to death with it.

setting: Dilbert's home workbench and living room
situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert his invention, a television filter that blocks violence, dishonesty and sexual innuendo. Dogbert realizes it will eliminate nearly all programming, and once it is hooked up they get only weather reports, which the filter even bleeps when a tornado is described. Dilbert is pleased it works, while Dogbert angrily demands he remove it.
punchline: A filter strict enough to block everything objectionable leaves only weather reports, and Dogbert responds with a violent threat that the filter would itself have blocked.
summary: A homemade content filter strips television down to nothing but weather updates, driving a once-supportive Dogbert to threaten its inventor.

file: 1996/1996-10-15_trade hsow_dogbert_design_deluxe booth_more revenue.gif
title: Dogbert Sells Deluxe Trade Booth

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you plan to have a booth at the trade show, you need the "Dogbert Trade-Show Consulting Company" to design it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend the deluxe booth. It's guaranteed to generate the most revenue.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: How would the deluxe booth generate more revenue for my company?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh, suddenly this is about your company?

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Dogbert, acting as a trade-show consultant, tells a woman she must hire his firm to design her booth and recommends the most expensive deluxe option as a revenue generator. When she asks how the deluxe booth would benefit her own company's revenue, Dogbert reveals he only cares about his own income.
punchline: Dogbert's "guaranteed revenue" claim was about his own company's earnings, not the client's, exposing the consultant's self-serving upselling.
summary: A scheming dog consultant pushes a pricey exhibit package, then admits the promised payoff was only ever his own.

file: 1996/1996-03-17_ethical question_low quality product_timely fashion_lie about prodcut_bugs are fixed_assistant_dogbert smacks rat bert.gif
title: Dogbert's Ethics Lesson Hits Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have an ethical question, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm here to help.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it better to give customers a low quality product in a timely fashion...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or is it better to lie about product availability until the bugs are fixed?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will need my assistant, Ratbert, to address your ethical question.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Snap

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's say Ratbert is a trusting and innocent customer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Suppose somebody abuses his trust like this...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Smack

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How does this relate to my situation?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: To be honest, I wasn't listening to you.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on and around the green couch
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for advice on whether to ship a buggy product on time or lie about availability until it is fixed. Dogbert summons Ratbert to play a trusting customer and smacks him to demonstrate abused trust. Dilbert asks how this applies to his dilemma, and Dogbert admits he never listened to the question.
punchline: Dogbert's elaborate ethics demonstration was built on a question he never actually heard, so it has nothing to do with Dilbert's problem.
summary: An ethics consultant puts on a violent demonstration for a client's dilemma, then confesses he was ignoring the client the whole time.

file: 1996/1996-07-04_angels dance in head_fault_huge number_jeopardizing_prototype_quality assurance_schedule_tree falls forest.gif
title: Quality Assurance Blamed For Finding Flaws

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In the short time you've worked in quality assurance, you've found a huge number of flaws in our prototype.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: That's my job!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're jeopardizing our schedule. The entire project will fail and it's all your fault.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Why is it my fault?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If a tree falls in the forest... and we've already sold the tree... does it have quality?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How many angels can dance on your head?

setting: Office, beside a desk with a computer
situation: The Boss complains to Ratbert, a new quality assurance tester, that he has found too many flaws in the prototype. He blames Ratbert for endangering the schedule and the project. When the Boss offers a pseudo-philosophical riddle about a tree that's already been sold, Ratbert answers with a nonsense riddle of his own.
punchline: The Boss's pretentious tree-in-the-forest riddle is just as meaningless as Ratbert's angels-on-a-head retort, mocking the idea of shipping products that were sold before they were finished.
summary: A manager punishes his new tester for uncovering defects, then dresses up his excuse as a philosophical riddle that gets a nonsensical one in return.

file: 1996/1996-11-04_dogcart consulting_add credibility_selfish_idiotic opinions_current budget_tingle_i feel_credibility.gif
title: Consultant Sells Credibility to Boss

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Consulting Company will add credibility to your own selfish and idiotic opinions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, your current budget should be... um...

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Doubled.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Doubled. It should be doubled.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, what's that tingle I feel all over my body?!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Credibility. If you want another hit, it'll cost you.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a turban and posing as a consultant, offers the Boss his services to lend credibility to the Boss's own self-serving opinions. Prompted by a whispered cue, he declares the Boss's budget should be doubled, and the Boss feels a pleasurable tingle. Dogbert explains the sensation is credibility and charges for another dose.
punchline: Dogbert treats validation of a manager's self-interested opinions like an addictive drug, selling the Boss another 'hit' of credibility at a price.
summary: A turbaned Dogbert tells his boss exactly what he wants to hear about his budget, then sells the resulting pleasure like a drug dealer.

file: 1996/1996-05-07_cafeteria_catbert_human resources_labeling entrees_life threatening_red lump_health care_evil director_business.gif
title: Cafeteria Style Benefits Taken Literally

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, the evil director of human resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're moving to "cafeteria style" benefits.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Under this system, if you need health care, you wander through the cafeteria asking "Does anybody know what this red lump is?"

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What if it's a life-threatening problem?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That reminds me, the cafeteria won't be labeling the entrees anymore.

setting: Conference room during an HR benefits presentation
situation: Catbert, the evil director of human resources, announces a switch to 'cafeteria style' benefits and explains it as wandering a cafeteria asking strangers about medical problems. Alice asks what happens with a life-threatening condition. Catbert ignores the concern and announces that the cafeteria's food will no longer be labeled either.
punchline: Catbert's cruel, deadpan non-answer to a life-or-death question shows HR cares nothing for employees' health, and he even adds a further insult about the unlabeled food.
summary: An evil HR cat redefines a benefits overhaul as a lunchroom free-for-all where sick workers must crowdsource medical advice, then shrugs off the danger.

file: 1996/1996-10-10_coprotae cultures_strategic allance_issues_beta code_internet_empowerment_press release_technology.gif
title: Corporate Culture Clash Over Empowerment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Issue one: Our two companies have very different corporate cultures.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Strategic alliance issues

transcript.speaker: Partner Programmer
transcript.text: While you were droning I slammed out some beta code and put it on the Internet for comments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company prefers to have that kind of decision made by uninformed executives. We call it "empowerment."

transcript.speaker: Partner Programmer
transcript.text: I'll mention that in the press release.

setting: A conference room during a presentation with an overhead projector, in an alliance meeting between two companies
situation: Dilbert is giving a presentation on strategic alliance issues, starting with the differences in corporate culture. The programmer from the partner company, who has been working on a laptop, announces he has already coded a beta and published it online for comments. Dilbert explains that his own company leaves such decisions to uninformed executives and calls that empowerment.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically presents his company's habit of letting clueless executives make decisions as 'empowerment', and the partner's programmer cheerfully agrees to put that spin in the press release.
summary: A slide-show about merging company cultures is interrupted when the partner's coder admits he simply acted on his own, prompting a bitter explanation of how Dilbert's firm handles such choices.

file: 1996/1996-05-22_unsightly stacks_papers_violation_clean desk_policy_ergonomics_situation.gif
title: Clean Desk Policy Versus Wally's Paper Pile

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, these unsightly stacks of papers are a violation of my "clean desk" policy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...And don't even get me started about the ergonomics of this situation.

situation: The Boss scolds Alice for the stacks of paper on her desk, saying they violate his clean desk policy. In the next panel Wally sits at his computer while a huge stack of papers is visible over a cubicle wall. The Boss then stands at Wally's cubicle, where a pair of legs sticks out of a big pile of papers, and complains about the ergonomics.
punchline: The Boss fixates on trivial desk-tidiness and ergonomics rules while ignoring that someone is apparently buried head-first in a paper pile, so his concern for 'ergonomics' is absurdly misplaced.
summary: A manager obsessed with tidy desks lectures about paperwork piles and workplace posture while a person lies buried upside-down in a heap of documents.

file: 1996/1996-08-10_economic success_stock price_fire batch_incompetence_lying customers.gif
title: Firing Employees Boosts Stock Price

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You employees are the key to our economic success.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anytime we need a little stock-price boost, we just fire another batch of you. It's like printing money!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In fact, "incompetence" has become our most profitable product.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Wow. It beat out "lying to customers."

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss addresses the employees at a conference table, praising them as the key to success before admitting that layoffs are used to pump up the stock price. He then declares incompetence the company's most profitable product, and Carol marvels that it surpassed lying to customers.
punchline: The company openly admits it profits from mass firings and incompetence, and Carol's deadpan reaction reveals that lying to customers was already a profitable product.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits that regular layoffs inflate the share price and that incompetence outsells even deception.

file: 1996/1996-08-14_layoff list_wally_claimed chair_few minutes ago_hard on survivors.gif
title: Layoff Survivors Fight Over Chair

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hear you're on the layoff list, Wally. Has anyone claimed your chair, yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I claimed it a few minutes ago.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Liar!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ow!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pow!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I guess it's true what they say about layoffs being hard on the survivors.

situation: A coworker asks Wally, who is rumored to be on the layoff list, whether anyone has taken his chair yet. The coworker admits he claimed it minutes ago, which enrages the other man, who punches him and knocks him to the floor. Wally, sitting in the chair, calmly remarks on how layoffs are hard on the survivors.
punchline: Wally sarcastically twists the saying that layoffs are hard on the survivors into a literal description of the survivor getting punched for his callousness.
summary: A man gleefully admits he has already grabbed a soon-to-be-laid-off colleague's chair and gets beaten up for it, prompting a dry quip about survivors.

file: 1996/1996-09-30_catbert_evil_hr dircetor_hire programmer_project team_first seek candidates_nine qualified_sock puppet_policies_designed_sole purpose_saditic tendencies.gif
title: Catbert's Sock Puppet Hiring Policy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I need to hire a programmer for my project team.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our policy is to first seek candidates from within the company. If none is qualified, you must use a sock puppet.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: How many of your policies are designed for the sole purpose of satisfying your sadistic tendencies?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All of them. Some are just more obvious.

situation: A woman with big hair asks Catbert, the evil H.R. director, for permission to hire a programmer. Catbert recites a policy requiring internal candidates first, and a sock puppet if none qualify. She asks how many of his policies exist just to satisfy his cruelty, and he admits all of them.
punchline: Catbert cheerfully admits that every H.R. policy is designed to indulge his sadism, with the sock puppet rule just being the most blatant example.
summary: An H.R. cat imposes an absurd hiring rule and then freely confesses that all his rules exist to torment employees.

file: 1996/1996-03-28_dying from boredowm_inetrview_department newsletter_background_project is good_engineer_moms fallopian tubes_engineering.gif
title: Engineer's Background Starts at Conception

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: At the risk of dying from boredom, I must interview you for the department newsletter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me give you some background before I talk about my project...

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: "The project is good," quipped the engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So there I am in my mom's fallopian tube...

situation: A reporter reluctantly arrives to interview Dilbert for the department newsletter, openly admitting she expects to be bored. Dilbert offers some background before discussing his project, and the reporter imagines the tidy quote she will write. Dilbert then begins his story at the moment of his own conception.
punchline: Dilbert's idea of 'some background' goes back to before he was born, confirming the reporter's fear that an engineer will bore her to death while she dreams of writing a short, positive quote.
summary: An unenthusiastic newsletter writer interviews an engineer whose project background begins in his mother's womb.

file: 1996/1996-09-02_network administartor_dogbert_good opportunity_annoy idiots_start tomorrow_pager number.gif
title: Dogbert Interviews as Network Administrator

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do you want a job as our network administrator, Mister Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't like people. This is a good opportunity to annoy idiots such as yourself for my own entertainment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow. You're perfect. Can you start tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure, as far as you know. I'll give you my pager number.

setting: The Boss's office, during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews Dogbert for a network administrator position and asks why he wants the job. Dogbert openly admits he dislikes people and wants to torment idiots like the Boss for fun. The Boss is delighted by this answer and hires him on the spot, while Dogbert hands over a pager number.
punchline: Dogbert's frank admission of hostility is exactly what the Boss considers ideal for a network administrator, and the pager number hints that Dogbert will be unreachable or the Boss will be the one annoyed, with 'as far as you know' implying he may not actually show up.
summary: A cheerfully hostile applicant confesses his contempt for coworkers and is hired immediately for his attitude.

file: 1996/1996-04-06_vice president_marketing_losing scruples_valuable lesson_fun to say scruples_business.gif
title: Fun To Say "Scruples"

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I quit my job as vice president of marketing...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I was losing my scruples... becoming unscrupulous. Yes, I learned a valuable lesson about scruples.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that lesson would be?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It's fun to say "scruples."

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, at his desk with computer
situation: Ratbert tells Dilbert, who is working at his computer, that he quit his job as vice president of marketing because he was losing his scruples. He says he learned a valuable lesson about scruples, and when Dilbert asks what it was, Ratbert gives a trivial answer.
punchline: After building up a serious moral lesson about quitting a corporate job over ethics, Ratbert's only takeaway is that the word "scruples" is fun to say.
summary: A small rodent who walked away from a lofty marketing post over ethical concerns reveals his big insight is just that the word itself is enjoyable to pronounce.

file: 1996/1996-02-24_become mimes_blame the mimes_debug_elbonia_four million dollars_one million dollars_quality assurance_software_programmers_engineering.gif
title: Blame the Mimes Who Won't Talk

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You saved one million dollars by having programmers in Elbonia write software for us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But we wasted four million dollars trying to debug the software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And the entire staff of our quality assurance group quit to become mimes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's blame the mimes; they won't talk.

situation: Dilbert presents a bar chart to The Boss showing that outsourcing software development to Elbonia saved one million dollars but cost four million in debugging. He adds that the whole quality assurance group quit to become mimes. The Boss responds by proposing to pin the blame on the mimes.
punchline: The Boss picks the scapegoat who cannot defend themselves, since mimes are silent and can't object to being blamed.
summary: A presentation on a failed offshoring effort ends with management choosing the speechless ex-employees as the perfect fall guys.

file: 1996/1996-02-27_biggest problem_databases_dwell on negative_network_probelm_tracking database.gif
title: Consultant Recommends Database, Ignores Problem

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just got our consultant's report. He's identified our biggest problem.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I recommend that we build a tracking database.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can put it on the network.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you like to hear what the problem is first?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hate to dwell on the negative.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We like databases.

situation: The Boss announces that a consultant's report has identified the company's biggest problem. Before he can say what it is, Wally and Dilbert jump in with enthusiasm for building a tracking database on the network. When the Boss offers to explain the problem first, they brush it off because they simply like databases.
punchline: The engineers are so eager to build a database that they refuse to even hear what problem it is supposed to solve.
summary: Two engineers gleefully plan a new database without any interest in learning what problem their boss wants solved.

file: 1996/1996-02-26_shirts_has either stain_or missing button_engineers_not concerned with fashion_stain with tie_marinara.gif
title: Engineers and Their Stained Shirts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate my shirts. Each one has either a stain or a missing button.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They say engineers are not concerned with fashion, but that's not fair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which stain goes with this tie?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Definitely the marinara.

situation: Dilbert stands at his closet complaining that every shirt he owns has a stain or a missing button. He claims the stereotype of engineers ignoring fashion is unfair, then holds up a stack of shirts and asks Dogbert which stain matches his tie. Dogbert, lounging on the couch, deadpans a suggestion.
punchline: Dilbert insists he cares about fashion, but his only criterion for coordinating an outfit is choosing among stained shirts, which proves the stereotype true.
summary: A man with a closet full of ruined shirts protests the idea that engineers ignore style, then asks his dog to help match a blemish to his necktie.

file: 1996/1996-05-14_after merger_reduce staff_redundant_employees_evaluated_buying company_bald guy_steal office furniture_business.gif
title: Merger Redundancy: We Already Have Wally

transcript.speaker: Man from the buying company
transcript.text: After the merger, we'll reduce staff in areas that are redundant.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope the employees of this company will be evaluated fairly compared to those in the buying company.

transcript.speaker: Man from the buying company
transcript.text: We already have a bald guy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does yours steal office furniture, too?

setting: Conference room during a merger meeting
situation: An executive from the acquiring company announces that redundant staff will be cut after the merger. Wally, sitting at the table, hopes his company's employees will be judged fairly against the buyer's. The executive replies that they already have a bald guy, treating Wally as a duplicate, and Dilbert asks if the other bald guy steals office furniture too.
punchline: Wally is deemed redundant simply because the buying company already has a bald employee, and Dilbert implies that Wally's real distinguishing trait is stealing office furniture.
summary: A visiting executive's talk of merger layoffs turns absurd when he judges Wally replaceable purely on his baldness, prompting a jab about Wally's furniture habit.

file: 1996/1996-04-02_ivy league degree_vice president_rerganized_training ratbert_teching_grooming for position_powerful position.gif
title: Coaching Ratbert to Be Vice President

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wish I had an Ivy League degree so I could be promoted to vice president.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You don't need one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's impossible to be a vice president without one.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll bet $100 I can turn a rat into a vice president.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That was good, but try saying it as though your soul just abandoned your body.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: "We've reorganized to focus on our core competency."

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and a bare room with a mirror
situation: Dilbert laments that he lacks an Ivy League degree and so cannot become a vice president. Dogbert bets $100 he can turn a rat into a vice president, then coaches Ratbert in front of a mirror to deliver corporate jargon in a soulless, dead-eyed tone.
punchline: Becoming a vice president apparently requires no qualifications beyond reciting empty buzzwords like "reorganized to focus on our core competency" in a hollow, soul-dead manner.
summary: Dogbert trains a rat to pass as a vice president by drilling him on lifeless management-speak instead of any real credentials.

file: 1996/1996-04-16_specially trained_wasted resources_project_behind schedule_manager_done playing around.gif
title: Waste-Detecting Dog Plays Around

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: This dog is specially trained to detect wasted resources.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: He'll help me find out why your project is behind schedule even after adding me as manager.

transcript.speaker: Dog
transcript.text: Sniff sniff

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: We'll begin as soon as he's done playing around.

situation: A consultant introduces a dog he claims is trained to sniff out wasted resources, saying it will help find why a project is late even after he was added as its manager. The dog sniffs around, then is shown playing with a toy arrow and chewing on a stick instead of working, and the consultant cheerfully says they will start once the dog is finished playing.
punchline: The wasted resource the dog should be detecting is obviously the consultant and his useless dog, who are themselves goofing off while the project stays late.
summary: A manager brings in a sniffer dog to hunt for wasted resources, then waits patiently while the dog wastes time playing.

file: 1996/1996-05-16_access_due dilogence_information_maniacal laughter_merger_phase_proprietary.gif
title: Merger Due Diligence Gets Exploited

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: In the "due diligence" phase of our merger you will give us access to all of your proprietary information.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wouldn't that let you know how to crush us competitively? Couldn't you cancel the merger and take our customers without paying a cent?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Must... contain maniacal... laugh...

setting: Office meeting area with a couch and a desk
situation: Two executives from a company proposing a merger sit on a couch and tell the Boss that during due diligence he must hand over all his company's proprietary information. The Boss, uncharacteristically sharp, points out they could simply cancel the merger and steal his customers. The executives silently fight back maniacal laughter, since that is exactly their plan.
punchline: The Boss accidentally spots the scheme, and the visiting executives' suppressed evil laughter confirms the merger is a pretext for stealing his customers.
summary: A pair of visiting suitors ask for all the secrets of the company they claim to be merging with, and the target's boss innocently describes their hidden plan while they struggle not to cackle.

file: 1996/1996-04-30_another banner week_accomplishements_streamlined_business process_valuing diversity_mandatory training vidoes_lost free will.gif
title: Training Videos Cost Wally His Free Will

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm pleased to report another banner week of accomplishments!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I streamlined my business processes while honing my participatory style and my proactive attitude, all while valuing diversity!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You watched the mandatory training videos?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I lost my free will!

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: At a meeting, Wally proudly reports a week of accomplishments using a stream of corporate buzzwords. The Boss sees through the jargon and asks if he simply watched the mandatory training videos. Wally cheerfully agrees and adds that the videos cost him his free will.
punchline: Wally's impressive-sounding buzzword report is just parroted training-video language, and he admits the videos brainwashed him into it.
summary: A employee's report full of corporate jargon turns out to be nothing more than the vocabulary absorbed from compulsory training videos that drained his independence.

file: 1996/1996-03-06_demo_ne wpordcut_vp next week_delay_ship date_lower morale_create unending demand_unproductive demos_doing valuable work_quality_banner.gif
title: Boss Requests Demo, Wants Quality Banner

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Could you do a demo of the new product for our VP next week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... that would delay the ship date, lower morale and create an unending demand for more unproductive demos...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Logically, since your objective is to show that we're doing valuable work...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And we'll need a banner that says "Quality."

situation: The Boss leans into Dilbert's cubicle and asks him to demo the new product for the VP next week. Dilbert objects that a demo would delay shipping, hurt morale and spawn endless further demos. The Boss ignores the objection, twists the logic to claim the demo's purpose is to look productive, and adds a request for a 'Quality' banner.
punchline: The Boss dismisses Dilbert's sound objections and doubles down, treating the appearance of valuable work, complete with a 'Quality' banner, as more important than actually shipping a quality product.
summary: A manager brushes aside an engineer's well-reasoned warning about a demo and instead demands a slogan banner to impress a superior.

file: 1996/1996-09-22_use speakerphone_voice mail_speaker phone_inconsiderate_too stupid_annoying_bob dinsoaur_wedgie_service elevator_look on face_way they yell_philiosphers.gif
title: Speakerphone Voicemail and the Wedgie Dinosaur

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's time to use my speakerphone to do voice mail.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't remember if I use the speakerphone because I'm inconsiderate or because I'm too stupid to know how annoying it is.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll leave that question to the philosophers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hi. Thanks for the information. Talk to you later!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did I tell you about my cyst?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, send Bob the Dinosaur quickly!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: E-mail sent

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: I'm here to deliver a wedgie.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Use the service elevator.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sign in

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: Yank!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Aaeee!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the best part-- the look on their faces or the way they yell?

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: I'll leave that question to the philosophers.

setting: Office cubicles and a front reception desk
situation: A coworker loudly uses his speakerphone for voice mail and rambles on about his cyst, annoying everyone nearby. Dilbert emails Dogbert to send Bob the Dinosaur, a dinosaur who delivers wedgies, and Bob yanks the offender's underwear. Dilbert then asks Bob what he enjoys most about the job.
punchline: The obnoxious speakerphone user is punished by a professional wedgie-delivering dinosaur, who echoes the coworker's own line about leaving the question to the philosophers.
summary: A cubicle dweller who broadcasts his private calls to the whole office gets an unwelcome visit from a green dinosaur who specializes in underwear-based justice.

file: 1996/1996-10-21_cartoonits_goat herder_good points_newbie identity_technology_technology bigot.gif
title: Technology Haves and Elitist Bigots

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: On the surface, you seem to make some good points about technology...

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: But your e-mail address reveals your newbie identity. You're probably a goat herder or a cartoonist.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How does it feel to be an elitist technology bigot?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I prefer to think of myself as a technology "have."

setting: Dilbert's home, at his computer and then on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer clicking away while a voice from the screen dismisses his online posts because his e-mail address marks him as a newbie, guessing he is a goat herder or a cartoonist. In the last panel Dilbert sits on the couch with Dogbert, who asks how it feels to be an elitist technology bigot. Dilbert answers with a spin on the 'haves'.
punchline: Dilbert recasts his snobbery toward less tech-savvy people as being a technology 'have', as if technological status were simply a matter of class.
summary: After an early-internet snob brushes off his online arguments because of his e-mail address, Dilbert dresses up his own tech elitism with a euphemism.

file: 1996/1996-01-08_performance review_engineering work_shoved down stairs_killed boss_forces of darkeness_posses body.gif
title: Performance Review With Demonic Possession

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your engineering work was excellent, Alice. But there was the little incident where you...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shoved me down a flight of stairs and killed me, thus inviting the forces of darkness to possess my body!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Back!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd it go?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I swear, this job is all politics.

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review, then the hallway outside
situation: During Alice's performance review, The Boss starts to praise her engineering work but then brings up the 'little incident' of her shoving him down the stairs and killing him. He is now demonically possessed, with horns, tail and forked tongue, and Alice holds up a cross to ward him off. Afterward Dilbert asks how it went and Alice complains about office politics.
punchline: Alice treats a review with a literally demon-possessed boss as ordinary 'office politics', mocking how people blame politics for any workplace dysfunction.
summary: A boss turned into a demon after being pushed down the stairs conducts a review while the employee fends him off with a cross, then grumbles about workplace politics.

file: 1996/1996-07-25_re; ese new prodcut_many defects_economic impact_projected icome_assumptions.gif
title: Hoping Nobody Notices the Defects

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like we'll release our new product on time, despite its many defects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've minimized the economic impact of the defects via an advanced business process called "hoping nobody notices."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And we've doubled our projected income by modifying our assumptions!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: A lot of this job is mental.

setting: Conference room during a project status meeting
situation: Dilbert reports to colleagues at a meeting table that the defective product will ship on schedule. He explains the defects' impact has been handled by simply hoping nobody notices, and that projected income was doubled just by changing the assumptions. A bald coworker in glasses remarks that much of the job is mental.
punchline: The company's 'advanced' strategies are really just wishful thinking and fudged numbers, and the coworker's remark that the job is 'mental' doubles as a hint that it's all made up (and a bit crazy).
summary: A team presents shipping a flawed product on time by ignoring the problems and inflating revenue forecasts through rosier assumptions.

file: 1996/1996-07-02_quality assurance_heres resume_words spelled wrong_not even bothered_hired_base salry.gif
title: Ratbert Applies for Quality Assurance

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'd be perfect for the job in Quality Assurance. Here's my resume.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you bothered by the fact that half of your words are spelled wrong?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Nope! I'm not even bothered by your anal-retentive behavior.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired. Your bonus will equal negative 100% of your base salary. Okay?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I don't see any problem with that.

situation: Ratbert hands the Boss his resume while applying for a job in Quality Assurance. The Boss notes that half the words are misspelled, and Ratbert cheerfully says it doesn't bother him. The Boss hires him on the spot with a bonus structure that would cost him his entire salary, and Ratbert sees no problem.
punchline: Ratbert's total obliviousness to errors makes him a perfect fit for Quality Assurance, and he is equally oblivious to a bonus plan that would leave him owing money.
summary: A cheerfully clueless rodent with a typo-ridden resume lands a quality job and happily accepts a pay deal that costs him everything.

file: 1996/1996-06-04_time_sequence_discreet eventsmlime ofperception_infinite possibilities_magazine_moments_have togather_less often_life.gif
title: Time Is Like a Magazine

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you see "time" as a sequence of discrete events or simply a line of perception through infinite possibilities?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see "time" as more of a magazine.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You know these moments we have together -- we really must have them less often.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ask me about "life."

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert reclining like a patient
situation: Dogbert lies back like a patient on a couch and poses a deep philosophical question about the nature of time. Dilbert, sitting in an armchair reading a tech magazine, gives a flippant answer that he sees time as a magazine. Dogbert, unimpressed, says they should spend less time together and sarcastically invites Dilbert to ask about "life."
punchline: Dilbert's glib non-answer to a profound question frustrates Dogbert, who sarcastically suggests they have these talks less often and invites Dilbert to ask about life, implying the next question will get a similarly deadpan dismissal.
summary: A philosophical chat about time derails when Dilbert gives a smart-aleck answer and Dogbert, annoyed, wants fewer of these conversations.

file: 1996/1996-08-13_layoffs_mobility pool_run around_finding job_internal job_ax falls_layoffs dignified_nonexistent job.gif
title: Mobility Pool Is Just Layoffs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't do "layoffs" at this company. But you HAVE been selected to participate in our mobility pool!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As the name implies, you get to scurry around trying to find a nonexistent internal job before the ax falls.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How's this different from a layoff?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With layoffs you get to keep your dignity.

setting: Boss's office with a conference table
situation: The Boss tells Wally he has been selected for the company's 'mobility pool' rather than being laid off. He explains that Wally must scramble to find an internal job that doesn't exist before being cut. When Wally asks how this differs from a layoff, the Boss says layoffs at least let you keep your dignity.
punchline: The euphemistic 'mobility pool' is a layoff in disguise that is actually worse, since employees must humiliate themselves hunting for jobs that don't exist.
summary: A manager rebrands firing as a pool where staff frantically chase imaginary openings, admitting it strips away the dignity a plain layoff would preserve.

file: 1996/1996-08-20_small fonts_save disk space_semi colons_colons_was fun_new ideas_next staff meeting.gif
title: Asok's Pointless Ideas at Staff Meeting

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My idea is that everyone should be required to use small fonts. That way we'll save disk space.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And I've noticed that many people use entire colons in situations where a semicolon would do just fine.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You're right. That was fun.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The real fun is when he describes his new ideas at the next staff meeting.

situation: Asok, the eager intern, pitches his ideas to The Boss and Dilbert: forcing everyone to use small fonts to save disk space, and replacing colons with semicolons because they supposedly take up less room. Pleased with himself, Asok comments on how fun the exchange was, and Dilbert dryly notes that the real fun will come when Asok presents these ideas at the staff meeting.
punchline: Asok's cost-saving ideas are absurdly trivial and technically nonsensical, and Dilbert sarcastically suggests that the real entertainment will be watching him pitch them to the whole staff.
summary: An enthusiastic intern proposes ridiculous space-saving measures involving tiny text and punctuation swaps, while a coworker sardonically looks forward to his upcoming presentation.

file: 1996/1996-06-17_100% complete_50% done_action item_estimate.gif
title: Action Item Is Half Done

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The status of my action item is 50% done.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Specifically, I finished the item part but not the action.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have an estimate for when the action will be done?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, and that estimate is 100% complete!

setting: Conference room during a status meeting
situation: At a meeting table, Wally reports his action item is 50% done, then explains he only finished the 'item' part and not the 'action' part. When the Boss asks for an estimate of when the action will be done, Wally cheerfully claims his estimate is fully complete, without giving any actual date.
punchline: Wally exploits literal wording to report progress on meaningless fragments of a task and dodges the real question by declaring his estimate 100% complete without providing a date.
summary: A lazy employee uses wordplay to make a task sound half finished and sidesteps a deadline question with more wordplay.

file: 1996/1996-08-07_cat likes petting_catbert_company resources_evil_hr director_pet cat_soft furry belly_ugly incident.gif
title: Catbert Trades Silence for Belly Rubs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil HR Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It has come to my attention that you used company resources to send e-mail to your boyfriend

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm willing to overlook this ugly incident in exchange for five minutes of quality petting on my soft, furry belly.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This seems so wrong.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try using both hands.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, confronts a female employee with evidence that she used company e-mail to write to her boyfriend. Instead of punishing her, he offers to ignore the violation if she gives him five minutes of belly petting. She reluctantly pets him and he tells her to use both hands.
punchline: The evil HR director's blackmail is not for money or power but for a petting session, and he keeps pushing his luck by demanding even more attention while she is trapped.
summary: A scheming feline human-resources chief blackmails a worker over personal e-mail, demanding a belly rub as the price of his silence.

file: 1996/1996-11-06_date other men_break up_need a spare_not break up_other dates.gif
title: Dating Other Men, Needing a Spare

transcript.speaker: Girlfriend
transcript.text: I've decided to date other men.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nooo!!! Don't break up with me!

transcript.speaker: Girlfriend
transcript.text: I'm not. I just want to date other men at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am not happy right now.

transcript.speaker: Girlfriend
transcript.text: That's exactly why I need a spare.

setting: Outdoors, on a grassy path where Dilbert and his girlfriend are walking
situation: Dilbert's girlfriend announces she has decided to date other men, and Dilbert panics, assuming she is breaking up with him. She explains she wants to date the others at the same time as him. When Dilbert says he is unhappy about it, she introduces another man and says that is exactly why she needs a spare.
punchline: Dilbert's unhappiness at being one of several boyfriends is treated as proof that she needs a backup boyfriend, so his complaint justifies the very arrangement he is objecting to.
summary: A woman tells her boyfriend she plans to see other men while staying with him, then answers his protest by presenting her replacement boyfriend.

file: 1996/1996-01-06_manager ted_planned better_pushed down stairs_soul left body_evil entity_performance reviews.gif
title: Pushed Down Stairs, Now Evil Manager

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you like being a manager, Ted?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Yesterday my staff pushed me down ten flights of stairs. My soul left my body and now I'm a lifeless evil entity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just in time to do performance reviews!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I couldn't have planned it better.

situation: The Boss pokes his head into Ted's office and asks how he likes being a manager. Ted, sitting with a bandaged head, explains that his staff pushed him down ten flights of stairs and that his soul has left his body, leaving him a lifeless evil entity. The Boss cheerfully notes the timing is perfect for performance reviews.
punchline: Being murdered by his staff and turned into an evil entity makes Ted ideally suited to deliver ruthless performance reviews, and the Boss sees only the convenience.
summary: A new manager reveals his team killed him and turned him into a soulless fiend, which his boss treats as ideal preparation for evaluating employees.

file: 1996/1996-10-26_manager_actual work_decisons_prodcue_carbon dioxide.gif
title: Manager Produces Only Carbon Dioxide

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm a manager, so I don't do actual work...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And all the decisions are made above me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carole, tell me again what I produce.

transcript.speaker: Carole
transcript.text: Carbon dioxide. Our plants would need that if they weren't plastic.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and his secretary's cubicle
situation: The Boss sits in his chair musing that as a manager he does no actual work and that all decisions are made above him. He then asks his secretary Carole to remind him what he produces. She replies that he produces carbon dioxide.
punchline: Carole sarcastically points out that the Boss's only output is the carbon dioxide he exhales, implying he contributes nothing of value to the company.
summary: Realizing he does no real work and makes no decisions, a manager asks his assistant what he actually contributes and gets a cutting answer about his breathing.

file: 1996/1996-10-24_battle_cubicle warriors_fighting_grandchildren ask_overwhelming boredom_hobo.gif
title: Cubicle Warrior Lies to Grandchildren

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The cubicle warrior prepares for battle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fighting, fighting against the overwhelming boredom!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When my grandchildren ask me what I did for a living, I'm going to lie.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I usually tell people you're a hobo.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then his home living room
situation: Dilbert sits in his cubicle, imagining himself as a heroic warrior fighting a battle against overwhelming boredom. At home, he says he will lie to his future grandchildren about what he did for a living. Dogbert, lounging on the couch, replies that he already tells people Dilbert is a hobo.
punchline: Dilbert is so ashamed of his dull office job that he plans to lie about it, and Dogbert deadpans that he already hides the truth by claiming Dilbert is a hobo.
summary: A bored office worker daydreams of heroic combat against tedium, then admits he is too embarrassed to tell his descendants about his career, while his dog cheerfully reveals a worse cover story.

file: 1996/1996-01-03_grow a beard_ted_not smart enough_grows horn.gif
title: Ted's Beard Wins Boss's Approval

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I've decided to mask my boyish looks by growing a beard.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't think Ted was smart enough to know how to grow a beard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hee hee.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two weeks later

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: How do you like my beard?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My search for a new manager is over.

setting: Office break area, with coffee cups in hand
situation: Ted announces he will grow a beard to look less boyish, and Wally mocks him as too dim to manage it while Dilbert snickers. Two weeks later Ted shows off his beard to the Boss, who thinks to himself that his search for a new manager is over.
punchline: The Boss judges managerial ability purely by appearance, so a beard alone qualifies Ted for promotion, with no regard for competence.
summary: A man hoping to look more mature grows facial hair and ends up impressing the boss enough to be seen as management material.

file: 1996/1996-10-11_strategic alliance_doomed_inefficient managemnet_create competing compnay_must find_new company_strategic allainace.gif
title: Doomed Alliance, Then Another Alliance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
