transcript.text: The status of our strategic alliance is "doomed."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our ponderous and inefficient management style caused their best people to quit and create a competing company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must find a way to destroy that new company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll see if they're interested in a strategic alliance.

situation: Dilbert presents a slide marked "DOOMED" showing the status of the company's strategic alliance with a partner. He explains that the company's slow, inefficient management drove the partner's best people to quit and form a rival firm. The Boss wants to destroy the new competitor, and Dilbert offers to propose a strategic alliance with it instead.
punchline: Dilbert's solution to destroying the competitor is to propose another strategic alliance, which implies the company will repeat the same doomed pattern and wreck this partnership too.
summary: After a failed partnership spawns a rival firm, the boss demands its destruction and his employee cheerfully suggests partnering with them, which is how the last one died.

file: 1996/1996-01-12_camping girl_entire morning_woe is carl_escape tunnel.gif
title: Dilbert Escapes Carl's Whining Visit

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: It's time for a visit from "Camping Carl."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There goes my entire morning.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: I'd like to begin with a monologue entitled "Woe is Carl."

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: I'm working every minute!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They all laughed when I built the escape tunnel.

situation: A coworker named Carl, who habitually camps out in other people's cubicles, arrives at Dilbert's desk and announces he will begin with a monologue about his own troubles. Dilbert privately dreads losing his whole morning. While Carl complains at an empty cubicle that he works every minute, Dilbert has slipped away through a hole in the floor.
punchline: Dilbert had prepared for Carl's long-winded visits by building an escape tunnel, and Carl keeps complaining without noticing that his audience is gone.
summary: A self-pitying coworker settles in to unload his troubles on Dilbert, who has already vanished down a tunnel he dug for exactly this occasion.

file: 1996/1996-03-02_fascilitator_breakthrough_moment of silence_honor_despite_surrounded by dolts.gif
title: Facilitator Honors Her Own Brilliance

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think you'll agree that this meeting went smoothly with me as facilitator.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The breakthrough was when I realized I was the only one here with anything valuable to say.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's have a moment of silence to honor me for my brilliant work despite being surrounded by dolts.

situation: Dogbert, seated low at the conference table, acts as meeting facilitator and wraps up the session. He praises how smoothly it went, credits himself for realizing he was the only one with anything valuable to say, then asks everyone to observe a moment of silence to honor himself. The colleagues around the table sit by in silence.
punchline: The facilitator takes all the credit and insults the attendees, demanding that they honor his genius while calling them dolts.
summary: A self-congratulating meeting facilitator declares his own brilliance and asks the room to silently celebrate him.

file: 1996/1996-07-23_ignorant rat_ignorance_bliss.gif
title: Ratbert Forgets Ignorance Is Bliss

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I may be an ignorant rat, but that's okay because ignorance is... um... um...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bliss... Ignorance is bliss.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Oh, great. Now it's gone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, at his computer desk
situation: Ratbert sits on the back of Dilbert's chair and tries to console himself about being ignorant by reciting the proverb, but can't remember the last word. Dilbert, typing at his computer, helpfully supplies the missing word. Ratbert then complains that supplying the answer has ruined his state of ignorant happiness.
punchline: By helpfully filling in the word 'bliss,' Dilbert cured Ratbert's ignorance and thereby destroyed the very bliss the proverb promised.
summary: A rat trying to recall a comforting proverb about being ignorant gets corrected by a helpful coworker and loses his happy cluelessness.

file: 1996/1996-09-01_two day workshop_mission_vision_useless jargon_illiterate execustives_mind numbing_job security_ethical behavior_better idea_high marks_class evalutaion.gif
title: Workshop Leader Bribed to Leave

transcript.speaker: Workshop Leader
transcript.text: In this two day workshop, you will learn to embrace our company's mission and vision.

transcript.speaker: Workshop Leader
transcript.text: At first glance it will appear to be a bunch of useless jargon created by functionally illiterate executives.

transcript.speaker: Workshop Leader
transcript.text: But after we do some mind-numbing group exercises...

transcript.speaker: Workshop Leader
transcript.text: ...you'll forget that you're underpaid and you have no job security.

transcript.speaker: Workshop Leader
transcript.text: We'll begin by writing down all the things that "ethical behavior" means to you.

transcript.speaker: Woman Attendee
transcript.text: I've got a better idea: If you let us leave now, we'll give you high marks on the class evaluation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good job. You touched me.

transcript.speaker: Workshop Leader
transcript.text: You wish.

situation: A workshop leader candidly admits that the company's mission and vision training is useless jargon designed to make employees forget their poor pay and lack of security. When he starts an exercise on ethical behavior, an attendee offers him high evaluation scores if he lets them leave early. He accepts, and the final panel shows the easy exchange of the paperwork.
punchline: The leader's own ethics workshop ends with him accepting a bribe of good evaluations, showing the exercise on ethical behavior is as hollow as the jargon he mocked.
summary: A trainer who openly mocks his own corporate seminar ends up trading an early dismissal for glowing reviews, undermining the ethics lesson he was about to teach.

file: 1996/1996-05-03_hit market window_ride market research_technical testing_overhead_like a bird_hit window.gif
title: Hitting the Market Window Like a Bird

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll have to eliminate a few steps in order to hit the market window.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think we can get rid of market research and technical testing. They're basically "overhead."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gone! Now we'll hit the window!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Like a bird.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss says steps must be cut so the product can hit its market window. He decides to eliminate market research and technical testing, dismissing them as overhead. Dilbert sarcastically predicts the result by comparing the launch to a bird flying into a window.
punchline: Dilbert points out that hitting a window without research or testing means crashing into it, like a bird colliding with glass.
summary: A manager axes the safeguards in a project plan to meet a deadline, and an employee wryly foresees a messy collision.

file: 1996/1996-05-26_business language_competetive_salary increase goodbye_core business_lost_empowered_unimportant deciosns_reengineering_essential_people person_canibal_hire trained people_market driven_balme cutsomers_value employee input_hour_important.gif
title: Business Language Explained: Corporate Buzzword Translations

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Business language explained

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "We have to be more competitive."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nice barrel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This old thing?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meaning: Say goodbye to salary increases.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "We must focus on our core business."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hello.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meaning: We can't find our butts with both hands.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "You are empowered."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I proclaim this to be "green ink day."

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meaning: You're the monarch of unimportant decisions.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "We're reengineering your function."

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meaning: Adios, Tonto, and the horse you rode in on.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Training is essential."

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: You were a cannibal?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'm a people person.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meaning: We're trying to hire some trained people.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "We're market driven."

transcript.speaker: Market Researcher
transcript.text: What's your favorite odor?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Research

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meaning: We blame customers for our lack of innovation.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "We value employee input."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for listening.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meaning: We think humor is important.

setting: Various office scenes, including a cubicle, an interview room, and a boss's desk
situation: The strip presents a series of common corporate buzzwords, each illustrated with a visual gag and followed by a cynical translation of what management really means. Examples include employees in barrels after pay cuts, a boss who cannot find his own rear end, and a cannibal applying for a job.
punchline: Each cheerful corporate buzzword is translated into its blunt, cynical real meaning, exposing how management jargon masks incompetence, cost-cutting and disregard for employees.
summary: A cartoon glossary decodes eight management catchphrases into the unflattering truths they conceal.

file: 1996/1996-03-19_ask the intern_assignments_gain experince_mouse pad inventory_status.gif
title: Intern Gets Status Report Assignment

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Asok the intern

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As an intern, your assignments won't be as glamorous as mine, but you'll gain experience.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need a status report on the mouse pad inventory.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See? My assignment has the word "status" built right in.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Danger! Alert!

situation: Dilbert tells intern Asok that his assignments will be less glamorous than Dilbert's own. The Boss then pops around the cubicle wall and asks Dilbert for a status report on the mouse pad inventory. Dilbert points out to Asok that his own assignment is just as mundane.
punchline: Dilbert brags that his assignments are glamorous, but his is a trivial status report on mouse pads, and he tries to spin it as impressive because it has the word "status" in it.
summary: A boastful Dilbert lectures the intern about glamorous work right before the boss hands him a dull inventory report.

file: 1996/1996-08-06_career day_co workers_email_every person_red faced monkey_torrid love letter_professionalism.gif
title: Tina, Red-Faced Monkey of Love

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I accidentally sent my torrid love letter to every person on our e-mail system.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Should I hide forever or can I count on the professionalism of my co-workers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll complete our "Career Day" tour with an exhibit that I call "Tina, the red-faced monkey of love."

transcript.speaker: Child
transcript.text: It's hiding.

setting: Office cubicles during a Career Day tour
situation: Tina, mortified, hides behind her cubicle wall after accidentally e-mailing a torrid love letter to everyone in the company. She wonders whether her co-workers will be professional about it. The Boss then leads a group of visiting children on a Career Day tour and presents Tina as an exhibit.
punchline: Tina's hope that her co-workers will behave professionally is destroyed when the Boss turns her embarrassment into a zoo-style display for schoolchildren.
summary: An employee cringing over a company-wide e-mail blunder gets treated like a captive animal by her boss during a visit from schoolkids.

file: 1996/1996-03-21_executive review board_popcorn for soul_prepare presentation_smell_meeting canceled.gif
title: Smelling Unnecessary Work Before Canceled Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want everyone to prepare a presentation for the Executive Review Board. Urgent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's that smell? Yes!!! ...It's the scent of unnecessary work for a meeting that will be canceled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sniff sniff

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you smell the unnecessary work? We can ignore it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's like popcorn for the soul.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Urgent

situation: The Boss leans around a cubicle wall and announces an urgent presentation for the Executive Review Board. Dilbert sniffs the air and gleefully identifies the smell of unnecessary work for a meeting that will never happen. Wally and Dilbert agree they can ignore it, while Alice mutters 'urgent' in the background.
punchline: Employees have learned that 'urgent' presentations for executive meetings usually get canceled, so the announcement is something to savor and ignore rather than a call to action.
summary: A manager's panicked request for a rush presentation is greeted with cheerful cynicism by staff who know the meeting will evaporate.

file: 1996/1996-04-03_corporate vice presdient_win bet_action plan_spend money_vice president_annoying rodent.gif
title: Ratbert Poses as Vice President

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remember everything I taught you, Ratbert. If you can pass yourself off as a corporate vice president, I'll win my bet.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yo, headcount! If you have any issues, put together an action plan. Our people are the best. Don't spend money.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you think he's really a vice president?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'm not ready to rule out "annoying rodent" yet.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Quality.

situation: Dogbert coaches Ratbert to impersonate a corporate vice president as part of a bet. Ratbert strolls up to an employee and spouts empty management buzzwords about headcount, action plans and not spending money. Two coworkers watching wonder if he's genuine, and one admits he could still be just an annoying rodent.
punchline: Ratbert's vague management clichés are convincing enough that coworkers can't tell a real vice president from a rodent, which says everything about how empty executive speak really is.
summary: A rodent mimicking executive jargon is so believable that employees can't decide whether he's a real vice president or just a pest.

file: 1996/1996-05-29_phil_ruler of heck_patented exerspoon_seven million_exercises_innovative spoon shape.gif
title: Phil's Exerspoon Infomercial

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: This is Phil, Ruler of Heck, with a special offer for my patented "Exerspoon."

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You can do over seven million exercises with the "Exerspoon!" It even trims problem areas!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And thanks to the innovative spoon shape, storage is a breeze!

transcript.speaker: Sleeping person
transcript.text: Mmm...

setting: Living room with a TV, then a bedroom
situation: Dogbert sits in an armchair watching an infomercial in which Phil, dressed as a devil, pitches a giant spoon-shaped exercise device. The ad claims millions of exercises and easy storage thanks to the spoon shape. In the final panel, a couple sleeps spooned together in bed, showing the 'storage' the ad refers to.
punchline: The 'storage is a breeze' claim is a pun: two people sleeping in a spooning position are the spoon-shaped storage, a gag about the product's shape.
summary: A devilish infomercial host hawks a ridiculous spoon-shaped fitness gadget whose storage perk turns out to be a cuddling couple in bed.

file: 1996/1996-08-26_catbert_high morale_hr director_love feedback_morale is low_more frequent reviews_employees underpaid.gif
title: Catbert Prescribes Reviews Instead of Raises

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert the HR Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Morale is low because the employees are underpaid.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You can compensate by having more frequent performance reviews. They love feedback.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The hardest part is keeping a straight face.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me again why I'd want morale to be high?

situation: Catbert, acting as HR Director, tells the Boss that low morale stems from underpaid employees. Instead of recommending raises, he suggests more frequent performance reviews, claiming employees love feedback. In his thoughts he admits he is struggling not to laugh, while the Boss asks why he should even want high morale.
punchline: Catbert offers a cheap, absurd substitute for fair pay and privately finds his own advice hilarious, while the Boss shows he doesn't care about morale at all.
summary: An HR director suggests that extra evaluations can stand in for higher salaries, and his boss wonders whether happy staff are even worth the bother.

file: 1996/1996-08-03_change master_adaptive environment_increase workload_job security_flexibility_bad morale.gif
title: Change Masters Blamed for Bad Morale

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we are to succeed, you must become change masters in an ever-changing, change-adaptive environment.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me get this straight... Every change seems to increase our workload while decreasing our job security and real earnings after inflation...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And the problem is our lack of flexibility?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not entirely. There's also your bad morale.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his employees at a meeting that they must become change masters to succeed. Wally summarizes that each change adds work while reducing job security and real pay, and asks if the real problem is the employees' lack of flexibility. The Boss agrees and adds their bad morale to the list of faults.
punchline: Management blames employees' inflexibility and low morale for problems that are plainly caused by the changes management itself imposes.
summary: A manager demands adaptability from his staff, then faults their attitude when they point out that every reorganization leaves them worse off.

file: 1996/1996-10-31_next award_exceptional work_worked evenings_incompetence_full plate.gif
title: Award for Fixing Her Own Mistakes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This next award goes to Kim for her exceptional work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Kim worked evenings and weekends to fix the problems that were caused by her own incompetence.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And it looks like Kim has a full plate for the coming year, too.

transcript.speaker: Kim
transcript.text: Which side faces the wall?

situation: The Boss presents an award to an employee named Kim, praising her exceptional work. He then explains that she earned it by working evenings and weekends to repair problems she caused herself through incompetence. He adds that she will be similarly busy next year, and Kim, holding her award plaque, asks which side faces the wall.
punchline: Kim recognizes that the award is really an insult, so she asks which side of the plaque to hang facing the wall to hide it.
summary: A manager hands out a recognition plaque while openly spelling out that it rewards the overtime needed to clean up her own blunders.

file: 1996/1996-10-22_heres card_email_address_eighty characters_meaningless_reply function.gif
title: Embarrassing Email Address on a Business Card

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Thanks for the meeting. Here's my card.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You call that an e-mail address? It's eighty characters long and mostly meaningless.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: People with embarrassing e-mail systems...

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: I tell people, "The reply function doesn't work. You have to type in my address."

transcript.speaker: Man in audience (thought)
transcript.text: Loser.

situation: After a meeting, a businessman hands Dilbert his card. Dilbert complains that the e-mail address printed on it is absurdly long and mostly gibberish. A final panel shows the same man in a group, claiming the reply function is broken to excuse his address, while a colleague silently thinks he is a loser.
punchline: The man blames the reply function for not working rather than admit his unwieldy email address is the problem, and everyone privately judges him for it.
summary: A man with a sprawling, cryptic email address makes excuses about broken software while others quietly mock him.

file: 1996/1996-05-28_manager_chose path_phil_ruler of heck_punisher_minor sins_procter and gamble_home exercise spoons.gif
title: Phil, Ruler of Heck, Sells Out

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Mom wanted me to be a manager like you. But I chose my own path.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I became Phil, the ruler of heck, the punisher of minor sins!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you make money?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Corporate sponsorship. "Procter and Gamble" pays me to stay away from them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should sell a line of home-exercise spoons.

situation: Phil, dressed in his red devil costume, tells the Boss, who is his brother, that he rejected their mother's wish for him to become a manager and instead became the ruler of heck. When the Boss asks how he earns money, Phil explains that a corporation pays him to stay away from it. The Boss responds with a merchandising idea: home-exercise spoons.
punchline: Even the self-proclaimed ruler of heck ends up with corporate sponsorship and a tacky merchandising scheme, so he is no more independent than the manager he refused to become.
summary: A man who rejected a management career for a life as a devilish tyrant admits a big company funds him, and his manager brother proposes selling novelty spoons.

file: 1996/1996-09-21_battery back up_product_no electricity.gif
title: Battery Backup for Non-Electric Product

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got an idea. Let's add a battery backup to our product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One... two... three...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got an idea. Why don't we add a battery backup to our product?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because our product doesn't use electricity.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss proposes adding a battery backup to the company's product. Dilbert silently counts to three, apparently to calm himself, then the Boss repeats the idea as a question. Dilbert finally answers that the product doesn't use electricity.
punchline: The Boss's feature idea is absurd because the product uses no electricity, showing how clueless management makes uninformed product decisions.
summary: A manager pitches a power-failure feature for a product that has no power source, and an exasperated engineer counts to three before pointing it out.

file: 1996/1996-01-23_collective sex drive_internet_itelligence_new technology_smut_time in hell_technology.gif
title: Dilbert Versus Teenage Internet Smut

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm inventing a new technology to prevent kids from seeing smut on the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, you're pitting your intelligence against the collective sex drive of all the teenagers who own computers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What is your point?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you know that if you put a little hat on a snowball it can last a long time in hell?

setting: Dilbert's desk at home or in the office, in front of a computer
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is inventing technology to keep kids from viewing smut online. Dogbert points out that he is competing against the combined sex drive of every teenager with a computer. When Dilbert asks what his point is, Dogbert answers with a non-sequitur about a snowball with a hat surviving in hell.
punchline: Dogbert's snowball-in-hell remark sarcastically implies that Dilbert's effort has virtually no chance of succeeding, since the hat on the snowball only delays the inevitable.
summary: Dogbert mocks a filtering project by suggesting that brainpower stands no chance against teenage determination, likening it to a snowball in the underworld.

file: 1996/1996-09-27_shore safely_try to distarct_accomplice_cruel joke_trunks_humming fish_jaws theme song.gif
title: Dolphins Steal Dilbert's Swim Trunks

transcript.speaker: Dolphin
transcript.text: Some dolphins in my situation would help you get to shore safely.

transcript.speaker: Dolphin
transcript.text: Others might try to distract you while an accomplice played a cruel joke.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Come back here with my trunks!!!

transcript.speaker: Dolphin
transcript.text: Let's ask the humming fish to do the "Jaws" theme song.

situation: Dilbert is treading water in the sea while a dolphin calmly explains that some dolphins would help him reach shore, but others would distract him while an accomplice played a cruel joke. In the last panel Dilbert shouts for someone to return his trunks, and the dolphin suggests that a humming fish play the Jaws theme to scare him further.
punchline: The dolphin's hypothetical 'others might' speech was a thinly veiled confession that it and its accomplice stole Dilbert's swim trunks, and it keeps tormenting him by proposing the Jaws shark music.
summary: A smug sea creature coyly describes mean-spirited pranks that turn out to be exactly what is happening to a stranded swimmer who has lost his shorts.

file: 1996/1996-01-21_most diabolical work_director_human resources_play_hundreds employees_evil mister_strap a broom_buttocks_marketing_more meetings_five minutes_business.gif
title: Catbert's Broom-Strapping Janitorial Memo

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hee hee! This is my most diabolical work yet as Director of Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Thanks to e-mail I can play with hundreds of employees at once!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... A message from the evil Mister Catbert.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "In order to reduce our janitorial expenses..."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's a phrase you don't want to see.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Every engineer will be required to strap a broom to his or her..."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "...buttocks."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: On the positive side, Marketing invites us to a lot more meetings now.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Five minutes; we're still eating cookies.

situation: Catbert, as Director of Human Resources, gleefully sends an e-mail to hundreds of employees. The memo, read aloud in pieces by Dilbert, Alice, Wally and the Boss, announces that engineers must strap a broom to their buttocks to save on janitorial costs. Wally is then seen sweeping the floor as he walks, noting that Marketing now invites them to more meetings.
punchline: To cut cleaning costs, management has engineers sweep the floor with brooms strapped to their behinds, and the only upside is being invited to more meetings.
summary: An evil HR cat emails a cost-cutting edict turning engineers into walking brooms, and the staff cope with sarcasm.

file: 1996/1996-04-28_authentic slave owners_career expectations_casual day_company logo_elfin_new record forprofits_petite_slave labor_small_t hsirts.gif
title: Record Profits Earn Slave-Labor T-Shirts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great news! The company set a new record for profits!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That means T-shirts for everyone!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can choose from sizes "small," "petite" or "elfin."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Shouldn't these have the company name or logo on them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, that's an idea for next year!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's 1% cotton, 99% "miscellaneous" and all hand-made by authentic slave laborers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's great! With slave labor you don't have the problem that the shirts made on Fridays aren't as good!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you ever worry that our career expectations have gotten too low?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't go there, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Casual Day," here I come!

setting: Office, where the boss hands out company gifts
situation: The Boss announces record profits and rewards employees with T-shirts that are tiny, unbranded and made from mostly mystery material by slave laborers. Alice and Dilbert mock the shirts' quality, until Alice realizes how low their expectations have fallen. Wally cheerfully puts on his shirt, excited for Casual Day.
punchline: Employees are so conditioned to meager rewards that they are grateful for a cheap, slave-made T-shirt after record profits, and Wally proves the point by being happy about it.
summary: After record earnings, the company's only reward is a bargain-bin shirt, and the staff's willingness to accept it exposes how little they expect.

file: 1996/1996-03-30_boring_idiotic coworkers_main accomplishment_newsletter_no raise_performance review_two percent raise_uninteresting_value of team work.gif
title: Newsletter Costs Alice Her Raise

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your main accomplishment was the department newsletter which was both uninteresting and unimportant. You get no raise.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The newsletter was your idea, and it's boring because most of the articles are contributed by my idiotic coworkers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't seem to understand the value of teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I understand its value; it just cost me a two-percent raise.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Alice during her performance review that her main accomplishment, the department newsletter, was boring and unimportant, so she gets no raise. Alice points out that the newsletter was his idea and is dull because her coworkers write the articles. The Boss then accuses her of not valuing teamwork.
punchline: Alice sarcastically agrees she understands the value of teamwork, since blaming her for her coworkers' poor contributions just cost her a two-percent raise.
summary: A manager denies a raise over a dull newsletter that was his own idea, then scolds the employee for lacking team spirit when she blames her colleagues.

file: 1996/1996-03-04_executive summary_approval page_executives_understand_know less_aaa road service_uphill.gif
title: Executives Know Less Than Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Add an executive summary to the approval page.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep it simple. Our executives don't understand as much about technology as I do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could they know less than you do? You haven't figured out how to make your car go uphill.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wrong; I got AAA road service.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to add an executive summary to an approval page and to keep it simple because the executives understand less about technology than he does. Dilbert replies that this is hard to believe, since the Boss can't even make his car go uphill. The Boss proudly claims he solved that problem by getting AAA road service.
punchline: The Boss thinks calling a roadside assistance service counts as technical competence, which shows he understands technology barely better than the executives he is belittling.
summary: A manager brags about his superior tech knowledge, but his only proof is that he pays for a tow service to handle his car trouble.

file: 1996/1996-04-10_catbert hr director_went nuts_vending machine_offer counseling_more economical_death penalty_possible_microwave oven.gif
title: Catbert Executes Vending Machine Rager

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert the H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This report says you went nuts at a vending machine because it took your money.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company used to offer counseling in these cases. But we found it was more economical to apply the death penalty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?! How is that possible?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm not sure yet. You're too big for the microwave oven...

situation: Catbert, the H.R. Director, confronts Dilbert about a report that he lost his temper at a vending machine that swallowed his money. Catbert explains that the company dropped counseling in favor of the cheaper option of the death penalty. When Dilbert protests, Catbert admits he is still working out the logistics, noting Dilbert is too big for the microwave oven.
punchline: The H.R. director casually treats execution as a cost-saving measure and is only troubled by the practical problem of how to carry it out, mocking corporate cost-cutting and heartless H.R. policy.
summary: An evil H.R. cat informs an employee that the firm replaced counseling for angry outbursts with cheap capital punishment, though the method is still undecided.

file: 1996/1996-03-13_fair enogh_no signs_running side business_yellow pages_employees_business.gif
title: Side Businesses Hidden In Cubicles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It has come to my attention that some employees are running side businesses from their cubicles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really??

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to see any signs of that in my department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What about "Yellow Pages" ads?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has heard that employees are running side businesses from their cubicles and says he doesn't want to see any signs of it. Dilbert agrees, but in the last panel the cubicles are covered in business signs for a software outlet, a sale, palm reading and a shoe store, with Wally hanging a Walbert Inc. sign. The Boss, oblivious, only asks about Yellow Pages ads.
punchline: The Boss's order is so loosely worded and the rule so unenforced that the office is plastered with obvious business signs, yet he only worries about a technicality like Yellow Pages ads.
summary: A manager forbids visible evidence of cubicle side businesses, then fails to notice the whole floor covered in shop signs.

file: 1996/1996-01-05_beard_close my eyes_crazy beard_new boss_pet emplyee_spin chair.gif
title: Boss Picks Pet Employee by Spinning

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As your new boss I have yet to select my "pet" employee. I shall do this by closing my eyes and pointing the beard on my forehead.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To make it fair, I'll close my eyes while one of you spins my chair!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice... um... technically this isn't "spinning."

situation: A new boss announces he will choose a favorite employee by closing his eyes and pointing at someone, with a chair spin to make it seem fair. Alice takes charge of the chair and, in the last panel, pushes him toward the stairs door instead of spinning him. Dilbert points out that this isn't really spinning.
punchline: Alice rigs the supposedly random selection by steering the blindfolded boss's chair toward the stairs, which looks like she's sending him out of the room or toward harm rather than fairly spinning him.
summary: A new manager's silly lottery for choosing a favorite is hijacked when an employee wheels his chair away instead of spinning it.

file: 1996/1996-02-29_facilitate meetings_fix product developemnt_preplanning meetings_project name_death spiral.gif
title: Naming the Project Death Spiral

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dogbert, I need you to facilitate some meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What kind of meetings?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're creating a process to fix our product development process. But first we're having some preplanning meetings...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...to decide on a project name.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about "Death Spiral"?

situation: The Boss asks Dogbert, who works as a consultant, to facilitate meetings. He explains that the company is building a process to fix its product development process, but first it needs preplanning meetings just to choose a project name. Dogbert suggests the name 'Death Spiral'.
punchline: Dogbert's suggested name 'Death Spiral' sarcastically implies that a process-about-a-process, delayed by meetings about meetings, is doomed to collapse.
summary: A manager hires a consultant to run meetings that precede the meetings that will fix a broken process, and the consultant offers a grimly fitting project name.

file: 1996/1996-05-04_budget estimates_year_bungling_indecison_no capital several months_reckless_ear end_orgy of aquisition_capital.gif
title: Budget Plan: Reckless Year-End Spending

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: Here are my budget estimates for the year.

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: Thanks to management bungling and indecision, I plan to use no capital for several months followed by a reckless year-end orgy of acquisition.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that what you were looking for?

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: Tell me again what "capital" is.

situation: A bald, bespectacled employee hands his boss his budget estimates for the year. He cheerfully explains that, because of management's own bungling and indecision, he will spend nothing for months and then go on a reckless year-end buying spree. The boss, holding the paper, asks whether that's what the employee was looking for, then reveals he doesn't even know what capital is.
punchline: The employee openly blames management for the wasteful use-it-or-lose-it spending pattern, and the boss, oblivious to the insult, shows he doesn't understand basic budgeting terms.
summary: A worker presents a budget that bluntly pins a feast-or-famine spending plan on his superiors, who clearly don't grasp the financial vocabulary involved.
themes: use it or lose it spending

file: 1996/1996-03-05_50 page proposal_one pargraph_executive summary_impossible_give us 3 million_cool tech_resumes_festering boil_feel obligated_customers.gif
title: Dogbert's Brutally Honest Executive Summary

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to turn this fifty-page proposal into a one-paragraph executive summary for our CEO. It's impossible.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Simple.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about "Give us three million dollars so we can buy cool technology, pump up our résumés and escape this festering boil you call a company"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel obligated to say something about our customers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about "I'm glad I'm not one of them."

situation: Dilbert complains that he must condense a fifty-page proposal into a one-paragraph executive summary for the CEO. Dogbert offers a blunt summary admitting the project is really about getting money for cool technology and resume-building so the staff can leave the company. When Dilbert wants to mention customers, Dogbert suggests a line expressing relief at not being one.
punchline: Dogbert's honest summary reveals that the proposal's true motives are self-serving, and that even the company's own employees would hate to be its customers.
summary: A canine consultant distills a lengthy proposal into a candid confession of selfish motives and contempt for the customer base.

file: 1996/1996-10-14_big trade show_strategic incompetence.gif
title: Strategic Incompetence Wins Alice the Booth

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'm putting you in charge of developing our booth for the big trade show.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I picked you because the males in the department have disqualified themselves through a process of strategic incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What is strategic incompetence?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had that written down someplace, but I lost it.

situation: The Boss assigns Alice to organize the company's booth at a big trade show. He explains he chose her because the men in the department have made themselves ineligible through 'strategic incompetence.' When Alice asks what that means, Dilbert, humming at his desk, demonstrates it by claiming he lost his notes on it.
punchline: Dilbert unwittingly (or deliberately) demonstrates strategic incompetence by feigning forgetfulness to dodge the unwanted trade show work, while the Boss unknowingly admits the men are shirking.
summary: A manager dumps a dreaded project on the only woman in the department because her male coworkers have deliberately acted useless to avoid it.

file: 1996/1996-06-01_not paid big bucks_presentation_use walkie talkie_walk the talk_carol_look at paycheck.gif
title: Walk the Talk with Walkie-Talkies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When Dilbert comes by, tell him to add "walk the talk" to his presentation.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He wants you to use a "walkie-talkie" to do the presentation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Did he say why?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Hey, look at my paycheck! I just realized I don't get paid the big bucks!

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to relay an instruction that Dilbert add "walk the talk" to his presentation. Carol garbles it into an order to use a walkie-talkie for the presentation. When Dilbert asks why, she deflects by showing her paycheck and noting she isn't paid enough to understand or explain management's requests.
punchline: Carol mangles the buzzword into a literal walkie-talkie instruction and, unable to justify it, points out she isn't paid enough to make sense of the Boss's nonsense.
summary: A secretary turns a management cliché into an absurd literal order and shrugs off the confusion by citing her low salary.

file: 1996/1996-06-09_dogbert_gullible_spend money_gullible freinds_touch tone phone.gif
title: Dogbert's Gullible Friends Hotline Infomercial

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where's Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you gullible? Do you spend money on stupid stuff?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Call the "Dogbert Gullible Friends Hotline" for help. Only four dollars per minute.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Hello, Dogbert. I bought an exercise machine and I'm still lazy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Please hold.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Call now, and I'll replace your old television with a new one that looks just like it, while you sleep!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you don't have a touch tone phone, stay on the line...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Until you get one.

situation: Dilbert realizes Dogbert is missing and then sees him on TV running an infomercial for a "Gullible Friends Hotline" that charges four dollars a minute. A gullible caller phones in and is put on hold, while Dogbert keeps pitching increasingly shady offers to the viewing audience.
punchline: Dogbert's hotline for gullible people is itself a scam that exploits the gullible, charging per-minute fees while keeping callers on hold and absurdly promising to swap their TV while they sleep.
summary: Dogbert fleeces television viewers with a paid hotline pitched at people who waste money on foolish purchases.

file: 1996/1996-03-07_cut corners_demo ready_under table_opretned_3d interface_useless demos_little fuzzy_electric shaver.gif
title: Wally Fakes the 3-D Interface

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We had to cut some corners to get the demo ready this soon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally is under the table. He'll pretend to be the 3-D interface that we could build if we weren't doing useless demos.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's a little fuzzy. Can you adjust it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try the electric shaver.

setting: Office demo room with a computer on a draped table
situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a product demo and admits corners were cut. He explains that Wally is hiding under the table, pretending to be the 3-D interface that could have been built if time weren't wasted on demos. When the Boss says the image is a little fuzzy, Dilbert suggests he use an electric shaver on it.
punchline: The 'fuzzy' 3-D interface is just Wally's face behind the monitor, so the fix for the blurry image is to shave him.
summary: A fake interface demo is exposed as a coworker hiding behind a monitor, and the picture-quality complaint gets a literal grooming solution.

file: 1996/1996-06-27_gather requirements_designing child care_sewing garments_windowless room_illegal aliens_discounts.gif
title: Child Care Requirements Become Sweatshop

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Alice, I need to gather some requirements before designing the company child care facility.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if your children spend the day sewing garments in a windowless room full of illegal aliens?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I mind.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll put you down as a maybe.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Would I get discounts on those garments?

setting: Office meeting room, at a conference table
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant designing the company child care facility, interviews Alice about her requirements. He casually asks whether she'd mind her children working in a sweatshop sewing garments in a windowless room full of illegal aliens. After she objects, he marks her as a maybe, and she asks if she would get discounts on the garments.
punchline: Alice's initial objection to a child-labor sweatshop evaporates the moment a discount is mentioned, showing how easily principles bend for a perk.
summary: A requirements interview for a workplace daycare turns into a sweatshop proposal that one parent is willing to entertain for a price break.

file: 1996/1996-05-17_class action law suit_due diligence_good employees_merger_projects are doomed_secrets_worth something.gif
title: Merger Due Diligence Brutal Honesty

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Due diligence" before the merger.

transcript.speaker: Man from other company
transcript.text: You must reveal your secrets so my company knows what it's buying.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: All of our projects are doomed. Most of the good employees left. Our customers are starting a class action suit...

transcript.speaker: Man from other company
transcript.text: At least the building is worth something.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: If you feel a tickle, that's asbestos.

situation: During due diligence before a merger, a representative of the buying company demands that Carol reveal her company's secrets. She candidly lists the doomed projects, departed talent and looming class action suit. The buyer hopes the building at least has value, and she warns him that any tickle in his throat is asbestos.
punchline: Even the one supposedly valuable asset, the building, is a hazard, since the buyer is breathing asbestos right now, so the acquisition target is worthless or worse.
summary: A candid seller tells a prospective buyer everything wrong with her company, right down to the toxic building they are sitting in.

file: 1996/1996-10-07_technology allaince_small silicon startup_corporate culture_different_pierced brain_mister conservative.gif
title: Dilbert Meets Quirky Startup Partner

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll head our technology alliance with a small Silicon Valley start-up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Their corporate culture is a bit different from ours. Try to be flexible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never seen a pierced brain before.

transcript.speaker: Startup Employee
transcript.text: I think I'll call you "Mister Conservative."

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's meeting with the startup employee
situation: The Boss puts Dilbert in charge of a technology alliance with a small Silicon Valley start-up and warns him that their corporate culture is different, so he should be flexible. Dilbert then meets his startup counterpart, a laid-back person with a halo-like ring floating over their head and feet up on the table, who promptly nicknames him "Mister Conservative."
punchline: Dilbert, the nerdy engineer who thinks of himself as normal, is cast as the stuffy conservative by a startup employee so unconventional that Dilbert is reduced to marveling at their pierced brain.
summary: Sent to partner with an eccentric Silicon Valley startup, Dilbert finds that a boss's vague warning about culture clash was an understatement.

file: 1996/1996-09-20_column_click_menu_uderboy_reviewed draft_duh.gif
title: Tina's Insulting User Manual Draft

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tina the Technical Writer

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: To insert a column, click the column insert menu.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: But let's be honest, userboy, if you need to be told THAT, you're too stupid to use this product.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Have you reviewed the draft yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm up to the chapter titled "Duh."

situation: Tina, the technical writer, types software documentation that begins with an obvious instruction and then turns to insult the reader for needing it. She then asks Dilbert, who is reviewing the draft, how far he has gotten.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies the manual is so full of condescending, obvious statements that it contains an entire chapter called "Duh."
summary: A technical writer's manual mocks its own readers for needing basic instructions, and her reviewer deadpans that he has reached the chapter devoted to the obvious.

file: 1996/1996-08-01_supreme ruler_earth_landslide_low votor_benevolent ruler_caning_olympic event.gif
title: Dogbert Rigs Election, Rules Earth

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The votes are in. I've been elected to the position of Supreme Ruler of Earth.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I won in a landslide, thanks to low voter turnout and the fact that I voted for myself many times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope you'll be a benevolent ruler.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I'll make caning an Olympic event.

situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert, who sits at his computer, that he has been elected Supreme Ruler of Earth. He admits he won by stuffing the ballot box amid low turnout. When Dilbert hopes for a benevolent ruler, Dogbert replies that he plans to make caning an Olympic event.
punchline: Dogbert's answer to a plea for benevolence is to announce a cruel plan for his rule, revealing he will be a tyrant, after already admitting to rigging the election.
summary: A scheming dog declares himself planetary overlord after cheating at the polls and promptly hints at brutal plans for his reign.

file: 1996/1996-10-29_catbert_evil hr director_all employees_smell of popcron_unprofessional_banning popcorn_tobacco_perfum_wally.gif
title: Catbert Bans Popcorn, Targets Wally

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: To: All employees. The smell of popcorn in the office is unprofessional...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's banning popcorn! First it was tobacco, then perfume, now this... There's only one pollutant left.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: ...This brings me to the unpleasant subject of Wally...

setting: Office, Catbert's H.R. desk and a coworker's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, drafts a memo banning the smell of popcorn in the office. Alice and a coworker (Wally) read about it and note that tobacco and perfume were banned earlier, leaving only one pollutant. Catbert's next memo line turns to the unpleasant subject of Wally.
punchline: After banning smoke, perfume and popcorn smells, the only remaining office pollutant is Wally himself, implying he smells bad.
summary: A string of H.R. smell bans ends with the realization that the last remaining offender is a coworker's body odor.

file: 1996/1996-06-05_pond scum_nice to know_lower staus_brochures_vendor_hurts.gif
title: Tormenting the Vendor Below Us

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Although we are nothing but pond scum in this company...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's nice to know we can still find someone of lower status to torment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You call these brochures? How can I even consider buying products from a "ven-duh" such as you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tell me if this hurts.

setting: Office hallway and a conference room
situation: Dilbert and Wally walk through the office, admitting they are the lowest of the low at their company but happy to have someone even lower to bully. In a meeting, Dilbert sneers at a vendor's brochures and mocks him as a "ven-duh" while Wally leans in with a pointed remark.
punchline: Having no status themselves, Dilbert and Wally gleefully pass their mistreatment downhill by bullying a vendor, and Wally's "tell me if this hurts" shows they are about to turn the torment physical.
summary: Two low-ranking employees savor the chance to abuse a salesman who ranks beneath them by belittling his sales materials.

file: 1996/1996-06-08_all you can eat booth_since 1989_odd family_look like_burrito night_just kidding_woman_disbelief.gif
title: Dilbert's Dad Lives at Buffet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: I can't believe your father has been living in the "all you can eat" restaurant since 1989!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: You have the oddest family. What did he look like when you saw him after all these years?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I haven't seen him yet. I'm waiting for "burrito night."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: Now is when you should be saying "just kidding."

setting: Outdoors on a sidewalk, with Dilbert and a woman walking together
situation: Dilbert and a blonde woman walk along a sidewalk while she expresses disbelief that his father has been living in an all-you-can-eat restaurant since 1989. She asks what he looked like after all those years, and Dilbert reveals he hasn't even seen his father yet because he is waiting for burrito night. She replies that this is the moment he should say he was joking.
punchline: Dilbert is completely serious that his father lives at a buffet and is calmly waiting for the right themed night to visit him, which makes his date uncomfortable.
summary: A woman is aghast at the story of Dilbert's buffet-dwelling dad, only to learn Dilbert is bizarrely deadpan about the whole thing.

file: 1996/1996-07-28_budget trap_quick estimate_next project_rough estimate_wild guess_beudget_two million dollars_can't afford.gif
title: The Budget Trap Estimate

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The budget trap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a quick estimate for how much your next project will cost, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How should I know? You haven't even told me what my next project is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's okay. I only need a rough estimate for planning purposes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I see where this is going. You're going to turn my wild guess into a budget. Later I'll be blamed when it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, no. I won't hold you to these numbers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well... okay, let's say two million dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh... can't afford that. I'll put you down for twenty thousand dollars.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One year later...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're way over budget. Can you show me the cause?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It depends. Can mirrors reflect your image?

setting: Office cubicle and The Boss's office
situation: The Boss asks Wally for a rough, no-strings estimate for an unspecified project. Wally warns that the guess will become a binding budget, the Boss promises it won't, then slashes Wally's two-million-dollar figure to twenty thousand. A year later the project is over budget and the Boss asks Wally to show him the cause.
punchline: Wally's reply implies the Boss himself is the cause of the overrun, since he imposed an absurdly low budget, and he sarcastically suggests the Boss look in a mirror.
summary: A manager extracts a casual guess from an employee, turns it into an unrealistically tiny budget, then gets blamed to his face when the project overruns.

file: 1996/1996-08-04_incoming voicemail_email everyday_log onto network_boss bossy_print emails_get sandwhich_pre chew food_bubble bee costumes_engineers_tricked_hives_no emails.gif
title: Carol Gets Revenge With Bumblebee Costumes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, from now on I'd like you to type up all of my incoming voice mail so I can just read it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And print out all of my e-mail every day so I don't have to log onto the network.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And get me a sandwich from the cafeteria.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh, no cash. I'll pay you back.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Do you want me to prechew the sandwich or can you handle that on your own?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Listen up, you overpaid engineers...

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: By order of our reclusive boss, the new dress code for engineers is bumblebee costumes.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: If you don't believe me, send him voice mail and ask for yourself.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Oh, and he wants you to buy him a sandwich.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Still no messages this week? Is everybody out sick?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I heard they have hives.

situation: The Boss gives his secretary Carol a string of demeaning chores: transcribe his voice mail, print his e-mail, and fetch him a sandwich he won't pay for. Carol sarcastically offers to prechew it, then gets back at him by telling the engineers that he has ordered bumblebee costumes and sandwiches. Since the engineers stop sending him voice mail to verify, he later wonders why he has no messages while an engineer in a bee costume stands by.
punchline: Because the Boss has made himself unreachable by avoiding voice mail and the network, Carol can make up any order she likes in his name, and the engineers' bee costumes explain the silence as 'hives'.
summary: A lazy boss piles petty chores on his secretary, who retaliates by inventing a ridiculous dress code that exploits his own refusal to read his messages.

file: 1996/1996-08-15_dogbert_career counselor_contract employee_rehired_higher salary_downsized_dumb_hire third time_parable_ant and spider_both boring.gif
title: Dogbert's Boring Parable for Wally

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Career Counselor

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was fired once, but I came back as a contract employee. Later I was rehired at a higher salary.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I'm being downsized again. Do you think they'll be dumb enough to hire me a third time?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your story reminds me of the parable of the ant and the spider.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Really? How?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're both boring.

situation: Wally visits Dogbert, who works as a career counselor, and recounts how he was fired, brought back as a contract employee, and rehired at a higher salary. Now facing downsizing again, he hopes the company will be foolish enough to hire him a third time. Dogbert says the story reminds him of a parable, then reveals the only connection is that both are boring.
punchline: Dogbert sets up a wise-sounding parable comparison and then simply insults Wally's story as boring, offering no actual career advice.
summary: A man who gamed the system through repeated firings and rehirings asks a canine counselor for guidance and receives only a deadpan put-down.

file: 1996/1996-03-20_ask the intern_energency_crawl through wall_star trek_spank the intern_shut furnace.gif
title: Intern Stuck in the Jeffries Tube

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Asok the Intern

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, come quickly! It's an emergency!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You must crawl through the Jeffries tube and shut down the furnace before it fries us all!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today young Asok learns that life is not like "Star Trek."

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm stuck.

situation: Alice summons Asok the intern for an emergency and orders him to crawl through a Jeffries tube to shut down the furnace. Asok disappears into the vent and ends up stuck, with only his legs dangling out. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, comments that this is a lesson about real life versus Star Trek, while Alice holds a sign reading "Spank the intern 50 cents."
punchline: Asok is lured into a Star Trek-style maintenance crawlspace and gets stuck, serving as a cruel lesson that real life isn't like the TV show, and the coworkers exploit his predicament for sport.
summary: Coworkers send the gullible intern into a ventilation shaft under a sci-fi pretext, and he predictably gets wedged while they treat it as entertainment.

file: 1996/1996-10-27_new manager_keith_masters in business_motivating employees_hire good people_optional reading_finance and economics_alice.gif
title: MBA Grad Lacks Management Skills

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'd like you to meet the newest member of my management team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keith is highly qualified. He has a masters in business administration.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Very impressive. They must have taught you a lot about motivating employees.

transcript.speaker: Keith
transcript.text: No, not really.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well... you probably learned how to identify and hire good people, right?

transcript.speaker: Keith
transcript.text: That might have been optional reading.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you learn negotiation skills? Strategic thinking? Business writing?

transcript.speaker: Keith
transcript.text: No. No. No.

transcript.speaker: Keith
transcript.text: It was mostly finance and accounting.

transcript.speaker: Keith
transcript.text: And economics.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, you're a highly qualified leader because... you're good at math?

transcript.speaker: Keith
transcript.text: What should I do here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In these situations I like to use swearing.

situation: The Boss introduces Alice to Keith, a new manager whose qualification is an MBA. Alice politely quizzes him on motivating, hiring, negotiating, strategy and writing, and he admits his degree covered none of it, only finance, accounting and economics. Left with no answer to her skepticism, Keith asks the Boss what to do and is advised to swear.
punchline: An MBA-holding manager has learned none of the actual skills of managing people, and the Boss's only advice for handling this awkward exposure is to swear.
summary: A freshly minted business-school manager is revealed to have learned only number-crunching, leaving him unequipped for leading people and reliant on his boss's crude coping advice.

file: 1996/1996-10-12_humiliate employees_employee recognition_worthless award_pocket lint_better job.gif
title: Worthless Award for Employee Recognition

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: When I'm in a bad mood, I like to think of ways to humiliate the employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hmm... How about an employee recognition program with a thoroughly worthless award.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purrr purrr purrr

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's pocket lint from a vice president's trousers. He was wearing them on the day he left for a better job.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, sits at his desk and purrs as he dreams up ways to humiliate employees when he's in a bad mood. He settles on an employee recognition program with a worthless award. The Boss then presents Dilbert with the 'prize', a small box containing pocket lint from a departed vice president's trousers.
punchline: The company's employee recognition award is literally lint from the pants of an executive who escaped to a better job, making the 'honor' both worthless and a reminder that people leave.
summary: A malicious personnel chief invents a recognition scheme whose trophy turns out to be fluff from a former executive's pocket.

file: 1996/1996-03-24_analysis_worked all night_vital_meeting_excellent work_alice_backup material_performance review cycle_naked body threat to boss_cheap suit_fling_business_science.gif
title: Alice's All-Nighter Becomes Backup Material

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Here's the analysis you asked for... I worked all night.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But you said this was vital for your meeting today so I know it was worth the effort.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is excellent work, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A rare compliment; it was all worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Mmm

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll use it as backup material.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Backup?!! Nobody looks at backup material!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm going to grab your pointy hair, yank you out of that cheap suit and fling your naked body down the hall.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's always irritable the week before her performance review cycle.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Her distance improved this year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ow

setting: The Boss's office, then the hallway and cubicles outside
situation: Alice hands her boss an analysis she stayed up all night to finish, believing it was vital for his meeting. After he praises it, he reveals he will only use it as backup material that nobody reads. Furious, Alice threatens to strip him and throw him down the hall, and in the last panel his naked body lands in the corridor while coworkers comment on her mood.
punchline: Alice's nightlong effort is dismissed as backup material nobody reads, so she carries out a violent threat, and her coworkers shrug it off as normal pre-review irritability, noting only that she threw him farther this year.
summary: A tired employee's heroic overnight effort is casually downgraded to filler, prompting her to hurl her boss out of his clothes and down the corridor.

file: 1996/1996-05-08_career advice_career counselor_seek advice_sounds lazy_unhelpful_work hard_insecure people_self relaint.gif
title: Dogbert's Lazy Career Counseling Business

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to try my paw at being a career counselor.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Insecure people will seek my advice and I'll tell them to be more self-reliant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds lazy and unhelpful.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you want career advice from somebody who has to work hard?

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, with Dogbert lounging on the bed
situation: Dogbert, relaxing on Dilbert's bed, announces he will become a career counselor. His plan is to tell every insecure client to be more self-reliant. Dilbert, tying his tie, calls this lazy and unhelpful, and Dogbert replies that nobody should want advice from someone who has to work hard.
punchline: Dogbert justifies his effortless, useless advice by claiming that a counselor who works hard must not be successful, so laziness is actually a mark of credibility.
summary: A lounging Dogbert plans a career-counseling gig built on telling clients to fend for themselves, then spins his own laziness into a qualification.

file: 1996/1996-05-21_another company benefit_new policy forbids_permit_season_use of weapons_violence_workplace.gif
title: Workplace Violence Policy Previously Allowed Hunting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new policy forbids the use of weapons or any violence in the workplace.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Umm... What was the policy before this?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not sure... Maybe if you had a permit and it was in season.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: There goes another company benefit.

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: The Boss reads from a paper announcing a new policy banning weapons and violence at work. Dilbert asks what the policy was before, and the Boss vaguely answers that weapons might have been allowed with a permit and in season, like hunting. A bald coworker laments losing another company benefit.
punchline: The Boss's answer implies that weapons were previously tolerated like a hunting season, and the coworker sarcastically treats shooting people as a lost perk of the job.
summary: A new ban on workplace violence prompts a question about the old rules, and the vague reply treats shooting coworkers like hunting season.

file: 1996/1996-05-23_lying in sun spot_net worth_remains_laughter.gif
title: Cat Laughs at Dilbert's Net Worth

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yesterday I was lying in a sun spot thinking about how you work, work, work but your net worth remains constant.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Well... I guess you had to be there.

setting: Office cubicle, with Catbert perched on a filing cabinet
situation: Catbert sits on a filing cabinet and tells Dilbert about a thought he had while lying in a sunny spot: Dilbert works constantly yet never gets any richer. Catbert then bursts into long, loud laughter at his own observation while Dilbert scowls. He finishes by saying that the joke only works if you were there.
punchline: Catbert mocks Dilbert's futile hard work with a barbed observation, then undercuts his own laughter with the weak excuse that you had to be there, leaving Dilbert insulted and unamused.
summary: A smug cat cackles at his own insult about an employee's endless labor and stagnant wealth, then brushes off the lack of a reaction.

file: 1996/1996-10-06_special achievement award_does something good_don't think so_giving themselves awards_other departments_lower standards_standing in hallway_tried door knob.gif
title: Award for Trying the Door Knob

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nobody has nominated a co-worker for a special achievement award.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone in this group must have done something good this year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No... I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'd remember something like that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This looks bad. All the other departments are giving themselves awards.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We might have to lower our standards a bit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been proactive in that area.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are we standing in the hallway?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We think the room is locked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't have the key.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later that month

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This award goes to Alice for boldly trying the door knob.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When I find out who nominated me...

setting: Office hallway outside a locked meeting room, then an awards presentation
situation: The Boss complains that nobody in the group has been nominated for a special achievement award while other departments are giving themselves awards. After the team admits nobody has done anything notable, the Boss decides to lower standards. Later that month Alice receives an award for merely trying a locked door knob, and she is furious about being nominated.
punchline: With standards lowered far enough, the award goes to Alice for the trivial act of trying a locked door, which is hardly an achievement, and she is angry at the embarrassing recognition.
summary: A manager desperate to match other departments' honors ends up handing out an award for the most trivial act imaginable.

file: 1996/1996-02-08_one year project_boss three months_great confidence_padded estimate_hate guts_keep raises low_dip in motivation.gif
title: Multiple Choice Reasons for Impossible Deadline

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I told you this project would take a year. But on my objectives you say I must have it done in three months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which of these reasons best describes why:

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A. You have great confidence in me. B. You think I padded my estimate. C. You hate my guts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't really need the project. It's just a way to keep raises low.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just felt a little dip in my motivation.

situation: Dilbert points out to his boss that he estimated a project at one year, yet his objectives demand it be finished in three months. He offers the boss a multiple-choice list of possible explanations. The boss cheerfully admits the project isn't even needed and the impossible deadline exists only to deny Dilbert a raise.
punchline: The boss's real reason is none of Dilbert's flattering or paranoid guesses: the deadline is deliberately unachievable so that raises can be withheld, which understandably kills Dilbert's motivation.
summary: Offered a quiz about why his deadline is so unrealistic, an engineer learns the task is a sham designed to justify withholding pay increases.

file: 1996/1996-11-02_marketing dept._cubicle walls_sneak down_experimnet_forgets.gif
title: Shrinking a Cubicle, Quarter-Inch Weekly

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What are you doing in the marketing department?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's an experiment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I sneak down here once a week and move this guy's cubicle wall in by a quarter-inch.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What's this experiment going to prove?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I forget. It's been a long time.

situation: Carol catches Dilbert in the marketing department pushing against a cubicle wall. He explains that he secretly moves one man's cubicle wall inward by a quarter-inch every week as an experiment. When she asks what it is meant to prove, he admits he has forgotten because it has been going on so long, while the cramped occupant sits scowling in the foreground.
punchline: Dilbert has been slowly shrinking a coworker's cubicle for so long that he can no longer remember the purpose of the experiment, yet he keeps doing it.
summary: A prank-like experiment of gradually squeezing a coworker's workspace continues long after its original purpose has been forgotten.

file: 1996/1996-02-11_simple molecules_powerful chemicals_simple cells_powerful life forms_powerful comouters_less capable components_supreme being_future_god consciousness_files_web browser_fly.gif
title: God Is the Internet's Future

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Simple molecules combine to make powerful chemicals...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Simple cells combine to make powerful life-forms.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Simple electronics combine to make powerful computers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Logically, all things are created by a combination of simpler, less capable components.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Therefore, a supreme being must be our future, not our origin!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What if "God" is the consciousness that will be created when enough of us are connected by the Internet?!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would certainly limit the types of files I download.
