transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder what it would do to response times.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's so nice to spend time alone with my thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My web browser would fly!

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside at dusk
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert stroll across a hill while Dogbert builds a philosophical argument that complex things come from combining simpler parts. He concludes that God must be our future rather than our origin, emerging from a connected Internet. Dilbert responds only with practical concerns about his downloads and browser speed.
punchline: Faced with the idea of a God-like Internet consciousness, Dilbert only worries about how it would affect his file downloads and web browsing speed, trivializing a profound idea.
summary: A dog's grand theory that divinity will arise from a networked humanity gets reduced by his owner to concerns about download choices and browser performance.

file: 1996/1996-09-04_alice_email messages_melrose place_monkey love_strategic edits_total access_network administrator.gif
title: Network Admin Rewrites Emails Into Soap Opera

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Network Administrator

transcript.speaker: Network Administrator
transcript.text: I have total access to every employee's e-mail messages.

transcript.speaker: Network Administrator
transcript.text: With a few strategic edits I will transform the office into "Melrose Place."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, Alice... I will be your "monkey of love."

setting: Office cubicles and a network administrator's desk
situation: A network administrator realizes he can read every employee's e-mail and plans to edit the messages to turn the workplace into a soap opera. In the last panel a coworker, apparently reacting to a doctored message, tells Alice that he will be her "monkey of love," while she looks alarmed.
punchline: The network administrator's tampering with e-mail immediately produces absurd, awkward romantic confessions between coworkers, showing how little privacy and trust exist in corporate e-mail.
summary: A bored computer technician abuses his access to staff mail by rewriting messages so his colleagues start acting like characters in a prime-time drama.

file: 1996/1996-07-19_talc club_rise_next level shale_respect_aluminum.gif
title: Dilbert Climbs the Mohs Hardness Ladder

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you can see from my ring, I'm a member of the "Talc Club" at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With hard work and a bit of luck I will rise to the next level: Shale.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can honestly say my respect for you has never been higher.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Someday, God willing, I'll make it to aluminum.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch with Dogbert and proudly shows off his ring, which marks him as a member of the "Talc Club" at work. He explains that with hard work and luck he might advance to the next level, shale. Dogbert sarcastically says his respect for Dilbert has never been higher, while Dilbert dreams of someday reaching aluminum.
punchline: The company's status tiers are named after extremely soft minerals, so Dilbert's proud ambition to climb from talc to shale to aluminum is pathetically modest, and Dogbert's 'respect' is sarcastic.
summary: Dilbert earnestly brags about his low-ranking corporate status tier, which is named after the softest materials imaginable, while Dogbert mocks his meager aspirations.

file: 1996/1996-01-27_primary vendor_make a choice_impractical solution.gif
title: Boss Zones Out, Then Says Both

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...But our primary vendor can't deliver, so...

transcript.speaker: The Boss (thought)
transcript.text: I wonder what's on TV tonight.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Should we risk a lawsuit or build a a product that nobody on Earth wants?

transcript.speaker: The Boss (thought)
transcript.text: Did he ask me to make a choice?

transcript.speaker: The Boss (thought)
transcript.text: Will it be a request for information or an impractical solution?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's do both!

setting: Office, Dilbert and the Boss standing in conversation
situation: Dilbert explains that the company's primary vendor cannot deliver and asks his boss to choose between risking a lawsuit or building a product nobody wants. The Boss has been daydreaming about TV and only realizes late that a decision is expected. Unsure what kind of answer is wanted, he blurts out that they should do both.
punchline: The inattentive Boss, faced with a decision he didn't follow, picks the worst option of all by choosing both the lawsuit risk and the useless product.
summary: A manager who tuned out his employee's problem gets caught off guard by a request for a decision and answers with a reckless catch-all.

file: 1996/1996-02-04_never undertsnd_engineer_all day meetings_knowledge worker_prodcut_acronym_puntucal_dilbert's mother_engineering.gif
title: Mom Quizzes Dilbert's Knowledge Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I'll never understand what you do for a living.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I told you I'm an engineer, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: So you say. But you also say you spend all day in meetings. When do you do any engineering?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good point. Let's just say I'm what the experts call a "knowledge worker."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Which experts call it that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: What's the name of the product you're working on?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what the acronym stands for...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: What kind of market penetration and return on investment do you expect?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... I don't know...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Oh, dear...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Well, I'm sure you're very punctual.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ask me another question!! C'mon...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Why do they call you a "knowledge worker"?

setting: Dilbert's mother's living room, with a green couch and armchair
situation: Dilbert's mother, serving cookies, grills him about what he actually does for a living. He cannot explain his job, the product, or its market, and each answer is "I don't know." Embarrassed, she tries to compliment his punctuality, and he desperately begs for an easier question, only for her to repeat the original one.
punchline: Dilbert's title of "knowledge worker" is exposed as meaningless because he knows nothing about his own job, and his mother's polite attempt to find something praiseworthy only underscores it.
summary: A son who claims to be an engineer fails every question his mom asks about his work, revealing he knows surprisingly little about it.
keywords: what do you do for a living

file: 1996/1996-04-26_arbitrary clerical deadline_preserve integrity_time reporting system_time sheet_annoying.gif
title: Dilbert Honors the Timesheet Deadline

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my time sheet, including guesses for the next two days so I can meet your arbitrary clerical deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If anything important comes up, I'll ignore it to preserve the integrity of the time-reporting system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you finished annoying me yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to my timesheet I'll be here for another 14 minutes.

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss his time sheet, which already includes guesses for the next two days to meet a clerical deadline. He says he will ignore anything important that arises in order to keep the timesheet accurate. When the Boss asks if he is done being annoying, Dilbert says his timesheet says he will stay another 14 minutes.
punchline: Dilbert follows the time-reporting rules so literally that he lets his made-up timesheet dictate his behavior, using the pointless bureaucracy to needle his boss.
summary: An employee turns in a timesheet filled with predicted hours and then maliciously commits to following its fictional schedule, even at the expense of real work.

file: 1996/1996-02-05_project delays_piece of deadwood_contributor_waiting for information.gif
title: Dogbert Finds Literal Deadwood

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have discovered the cause of your project delays.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Somebody in this room is a piece of deadwood pretending to be a contributor!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It is you!

transcript.speaker: Tree stump employee
transcript.text: Hey, I made some calls and I'm waiting for information!

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the meeting attendees that he has found the cause of their project delays: someone who is deadwood pretending to contribute. He points at a coworker who turns out to be an actual tree stump wearing clothes, with a bird perched on it. The stump defends itself with the classic excuse of waiting on information from calls it made.
punchline: The 'deadwood' employee is literally a tree stump, yet it still offers the stock excuse of waiting for information, showing how unproductive staff hide behind plausible-sounding delays.
summary: A consultant exposes the team's slacker, who turns out to be a literal piece of wood making excuses.

file: 1996/1996-04-08_review board_fist of death_alice_wally no work_nostradamus_alice punches wally.gif
title: Alice Punches Smug Wally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Executive Review Board meeting is canceled. I hope you didn't work too hard preparing for it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control fist... of... death...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Unlike Alice, I saw it coming and did no work whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you see THAT coming, Nostradamus?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does this do to headcount?

situation: The Boss announces that the Executive Review Board meeting has been canceled and hopes nobody worked too hard preparing. Alice, who did prepare, seethes while Wally smugly says he anticipated the cancellation and did nothing. Alice punches Wally in the head, and Dilbert wonders what this does to headcount.
punchline: Alice's violent response to Wally's smugness could leave the company a person short, which Dilbert dryly frames as a headcount question.
summary: After a meeting is scrubbed at the last minute, the one coworker who skipped the prep gloats and gets knocked flat by the one who didn't.

file: 1996/1996-02-02_help shipping dept_fiscal year_no inventory.gif
title: Shipping Junk to Book Revenue

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need everybody to help in the shipping department today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every product that ships before the end of the month gets counted as revenue for the fiscal year. Unfortunately, we don't have inventory.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So we'll ship whatever is lying around, book it as revenue and sort it out later.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This one's getting gum.

setting: Office break area, then the shipping department
situation: The Boss recruits everyone to work in shipping because anything shipped before month-end counts as fiscal-year revenue. When he admits there is no inventory, he decides to ship whatever junk is lying around and record it as sales anyway. Wally cheerfully boxes up an item with gum.
punchline: The company is cooking its revenue numbers by shipping worthless stuff, and Wally's gum-filled package shows how little the product matters.
summary: With no real products to sell, management packs up random leftovers to inflate this year's sales figures and promises to deal with the fallout afterward.

file: 1996/1996-10-02_complaining_document_office supplies_out of ink_person who asked_requirement_supply cabinet.gif
title: Carol's Supply Cabinet Procedure Documented

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, I need to document your procedure for ordering office supplies. It's an ISO 9000 requirement.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: If someone asks for something, I check the supply cabinet first. Then I say, "There's one left. You can't have it because then we'd be all out."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Then I spend the rest of the day complaining about the person who asked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... I'm out of ink.

situation: Dilbert interviews Carol, the administrative assistant, so he can document her office supply ordering procedure for an ISO 9000 requirement. Carol explains that she refuses requests for the last item in the cabinet and then complains about the requester all day. Dilbert realizes he is out of ink and is now about to become that person.
punchline: Carol's 'procedure' is to never reorder anything and to badmouth whoever asks, which leaves Dilbert dreading the moment he has to request ink.
summary: An assistant describes her supply policy of hoarding the last item and gossiping about requesters, just as the man documenting it discovers he needs a refill.

file: 1996/1996-08-31_becoming annoying_misinterpret everything_asservtive_annoying not asservtive_clothes dryer.gif
title: Annoying Ratbert Climbs Into Dryer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear you're becoming an annoying person who misinterprets everything.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes, I'm more assertive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said annoying, not assertive.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Apology accepted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whatever you do, don't climb in this clothes dryer.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yeah, it does look cozy in there.

setting: Dilbert's home, living room and front doorway, then the laundry area
situation: Dilbert tells Ratbert he has heard Ratbert is becoming annoying and misinterprets everything. Ratbert keeps twisting Dilbert's words, mishearing 'annoying' as 'assertive' and then turning Dilbert's correction into an apology. Dilbert finally warns him not to climb into the clothes dryer, and Ratbert climbs in anyway.
punchline: Ratbert proves he really does misinterpret everything by treating Dilbert's warning as an invitation and climbing into the dryer.
summary: A pet who twists every remark into a compliment turns a stern warning about a dryer into a cozy suggestion.

file: 1996/1996-06-26_dogbert day care_progressive_duct tape_fortune.gif
title: Dogbert's Duct Tape Day Care

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What exactly is the Dogbert Day Care concept?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Progressive companies can provide day care without spending a bundle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wouldn't we spend a fortune on duct tape?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's reusable unless it gets slobbered on.

situation: The Boss asks Dogbert, who is pitching a consulting idea, to explain his cheap company day care concept. Dogbert says it lets progressive companies offer day care without spending much. When the Boss worries about the cost of duct tape, it becomes clear that the plan involves taping the children down.
punchline: Dogbert's low-cost day care plan quietly relies on restraining children with duct tape, and the only objection raised is the cost of the tape, not the cruelty.
summary: A consultant pitches a bargain childcare scheme to management, and the budget-minded worry turns out to be about the price of the tape used to restrain the kids.

file: 1996/1996-10-19_trade show_prodcuts_defective_stayed up_setting booth.gif
title: Exhausted Trade Show Rep's Insult

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the trade show

transcript.speaker: Trade Show Visitor
transcript.text: What can you tell me about your products?

transcript.speaker: Booth Rep
transcript.text: Our products are defective, much like yourself.

transcript.speaker: Booth Rep
transcript.text: I probably shouldn't have stayed up all night setting up the booth.

transcript.speaker: Trade Show Visitor
transcript.text: What are you doing later?

characters: Trade Show Visitor (man in yellow shirt)
setting: A company booth at a trade show
situation: A visitor asks a woman staffing a trade show booth about her company's products. Exhausted from setting up all night, she tells him the products are defective, just like him. She then admits she probably shouldn't have stayed up so late, and the visitor responds by asking her out.
punchline: Despite being openly insulted, the visitor is undeterred and treats her sleep-deprived rudeness as an opening to ask her on a date.
summary: A worn-out exhibitor blurts out an insult to a curious attendee, who somehow takes it as flirtation.

file: 1996/1996-03-22_slaving away_executive board meeting_work avoidance chromosome_avoiding it_be ready.gif
title: The Work Avoidance Chromosome

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why aren't you slaving away, preparing for the executive review board meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have the male "work avoidance chromosome." I can detect unnecessary work, thereby avoiding it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We ALL have to be ready to present something!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Could you hold it down? I'm trying to sleep.

situation: Alice, clutching papers, confronts Dilbert for lounging in his chair instead of preparing for an executive review board meeting. Dilbert claims he has a male 'work avoidance chromosome' that lets him detect and dodge unnecessary work. When Alice insists everyone must be ready to present, a coworker peeks over the cubicle wall and asks her to be quiet because he is trying to sleep.
punchline: Dilbert's pseudo-scientific excuse for slacking is undercut when a coworker reveals that the whole office is avoiding the work, and Alice is the only one bothered.
summary: A diligent employee scolds a reclining colleague for not preparing, only to find his genetic excuse for laziness is shared by a neighbor who is napping.

file: 1996/1996-08-09_prisoners dilemma_smal raise_rat  on_good times_no co ed prisons.gif
title: Peer Review Prisoner's Dilemma

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, these peer reviews are like the famous "Prisoner's Dilemma."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you rat on me but I say good things about you, you get the biggest raise. But if we praise each other we can both get a small raise.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, if you rat him out, I'll let you look at my "Victoria's Secret" catalog.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is exactly why there are no coed prisons.

situation: Dilbert peers over the cubicle wall at Wally and explains the prisoner's dilemma as it applies to peer reviews, proposing that mutual praise yields small raises for both. Alice then pops up from a neighboring cubicle and tempts Wally with her Victoria's Secret catalog if he betrays Dilbert.
punchline: Alice bribes Wally with a lingerie catalog to betray Dilbert, and Dilbert notes this is why prisons are not coed, since temptation would wreck any cooperation.
summary: A game-theory pact between coworkers is undermined when a third colleague offers a racy incentive for betrayal.

file: 1996/1996-08-24_bad grammar_common useage_entire language_grunting_pointing_ripped off_dog obedience.gif
title: Dogbert Plots Language Degradation Through Grunting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to use bad grammar more often.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My leadership will change the language through the principle of common usage.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I won't stop until the entire language is reduced to grunting and pointing! Buwahahaha!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I really got ripped off by that dog obedience school.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert reads a magazine on the couch while Dogbert announces he will deliberately use bad grammar, believing his leadership will change the language through common usage. He declares he will not stop until language is reduced to grunting and pointing. Dilbert, unmoved, complains that the dog obedience school he paid for was a rip-off.
punchline: Dogbert's plan to reduce language to grunting and pointing is exactly the kind of behavior obedience school was supposed to prevent, so Dilbert's complaint about being ripped off is a deadpan comment on his failed training of Dogbert.
summary: A scheming dog vows to wreck the English language one error at a time, while his owner bitterly concludes that his money for obedience training was wasted.

file: 1996/1996-01-15_entire pc industry_graphic metaphors_microsoft logo_pronounce differently_dogbert 2000.gif
title: Dogbert's Windows 95 Knockoff OS

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call my new operating system the "Dogbert 2000."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Soon I will dominate the entire PC industry! Heh-heh...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like "Windows 95."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I use some of the same graphic metaphors, but I pronounce them differently.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you pronounce the "Microsoft" logo?

situation: Dogbert sits at a computer and announces his new operating system, the Dogbert 2000, which he plans to use to dominate the PC industry. Dilbert, standing with a coffee mug, points out that it looks just like Windows 95. Dogbert claims it's different because he pronounces the graphics differently, and Dilbert asks how he pronounces the Microsoft logo.
punchline: Dogbert's defense that merely pronouncing the copied interface elements differently makes his product original is absurd, and the question about the logo exposes it as a blatant knockoff of Windows 95.
summary: A scheming dog unveils his supposedly original software that is plainly a clone of a famous rival's product, and defends it with a ridiculous excuse.

file: 1996/1996-01-31_critical code_air traffic control_gifted programmer_payroll system_dont fly_pay day.gif
title: Air Traffic Control Runs Payroll Code

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wally writes the critical code for our nation's new air traffic control system.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The crowd is silent.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Suddenly the gifted programmer employs a rarely seen strategy of "code reuse."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The crowd goes wild.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So you used code from the payroll system?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Here's a tip: Don't fly on pay day.

situation: Wally imagines himself as a heroic programmer writing the code for a national air traffic control system, to the cheers of an imaginary crowd when he applies code reuse. At lunch, Dilbert asks whether he simply copied code from the payroll system, and Wally cheerfully admits it and warns people not to fly on pay day.
punchline: Wally's celebrated 'code reuse' means he lazily pasted payroll software into a safety-critical air traffic system, so flying is only safe when no paychecks are being processed.
summary: A lazy programmer's heroic fantasy about reusing code collapses when he admits to recycling payroll software for air traffic control.

file: 1996/1996-04-29_catbert_hr director_employee oreinetation_glimmer_mandatory training video.gif
title: Catbert Orientation Crushes Wally's Hope

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I've come to give you "employee orientation," Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But I've worked here for years.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You still have a glimmer of hope. You'll have to watch this mandatory training video.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So, you still have hope...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Relax... let it go.

situation: Catbert, the H.R. Director, arrives to give Wally an employee orientation even though Wally has worked at the company for years. Catbert explains that Wally still has a glimmer of hope, so he must watch a mandatory training video, which is labeled "Hope." In the final panel Catbert sits on Wally's shoulder and tells him to relax and let his hope go.
punchline: The orientation is really a training program designed to eliminate an employee's hope, implying that a fully broken, hopeless worker is the company's ideal.
summary: An HR cat ambushes a veteran employee with a required video whose purpose is to drain away any remaining optimism.

file: 1996/1996-02-12_catbert_dierctor_eliminate sick days_evil human resources_too much time off_use vacation days_demons of darkness.gif
title: Catbert Invents the Time Bank

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert the evil Human Resources Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The employees have too much time off. It must be stopped.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I summon the demons of darkness to assist me!!!

transcript.speaker: Demon
transcript.text: ...Eliminate sick days. Make them use vacation days when they're ill. Call it a "time bank."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's playful... it's cruel... I like it.

setting: Catbert's Human Resources office, at his desk with a computer
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, decides employees have too much time off and summons demons of darkness to help him fix it. A demon suggests eliminating sick days so that ill employees must burn vacation days, and rebranding the policy as a "time bank." Catbert approves of its cruelty.
punchline: A policy that takes away employee benefits is dressed up with a friendly name, and the evil HR director admires it precisely because it is cruel.
summary: A malevolent personnel chief conjures a fiend who proposes making sick workers spend their holiday allowance, disguised under a cheerful label.

file: 1996/1996-09-14_dying comapny_fully understand_stock rose_boneheaded_competitive edge.gif
title: Stock Rises After Boneheaded Acquisition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In today's news, our company has decided to buy another dying company in a business we don't fully understand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our stock rose five points on the announcement.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why does our stock go up every time we do something boneheaded?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to think of it as our competitive advantage.

setting: Company meeting or announcement area in the office
situation: The Boss reads a news announcement that the company is acquiring a dying company in a business it doesn't understand, then notes that the stock price rose on the news. Wally asks why the stock goes up whenever the company does something foolish, and Dilbert sarcastically calls it their competitive advantage.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests that the company's reliable habit of making foolish decisions, which investors inexplicably reward, is its true competitive advantage.
summary: A boss announces a questionable takeover and the resulting stock bump, prompting a coworker's sarcastic theory about why foolishness pays off.

file: 1996/1996-10-09_strategic allaince_technical skill_endless supply_resistance is futile_assimilated.gif
title: Binders Steal Your Soul

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our strategic alliance is working well. My company provides amazing technical skill and your company...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...has a seemingly endless supply of three-ring binders.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Resistance is futile. You will be assimilated.

transcript.speaker: Spiky-haired partner
transcript.text: Is it true that if your name is written in a binder you lose your soul?

setting: Conference room during a meeting with a partner company
situation: Dilbert tells two visitors from a partner company that their strategic alliance is going well, with his side providing technical skill and theirs providing a huge supply of three-ring binders. In the last panel he ominously warns that resistance is futile and they will be assimilated. The spiky-haired visitor nervously asks whether having your name written in a binder costs you your soul.
punchline: Dilbert's Borg-style threat of assimilation turns the mundane partnership into something sinister, and the visitor's question implies that bureaucratic paperwork really does drain your soul.
summary: A boring corporate partnership is described in menacing sci-fi terms, leaving a visitor worried that office paperwork will consume his spirit.

file: 1996/1996-01-07_feeling of doom_room mate_dilbert_fiancee department_budget_square footage.gif
title: Cubicle Roommate Saves Budget Footage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do I have a feeling of impending doom?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You won't have to spend another lonely day in this tiny cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm getting an office?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Better! You're getting a roommate!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why??? We've got plenty of empty cubicles! Our company owns the whole building!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The finance department charges my budget for the square footage we use.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a false savings! You're hurting the company!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I hear is a faint buzzing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, well. How bad could it be?

transcript.speaker: Roommate
transcript.text: I hope you like baked beans and square-dancing as much as I do!

situation: The Boss cheerfully announces that Dilbert will be getting a roommate in his cubicle. Dilbert points out that the company owns the building and has many empty cubicles, but the Boss explains that the finance department charges his budget for the square footage he uses. Dilbert protests that it hurts the company, the Boss ignores him, and a cowboy-hatted roommate with a can of beans and a boombox arrives.
punchline: The Boss sacrifices his employee's comfort and the company's real interests to save on an internal budget charge, and Dilbert gets a terrible roommate as a result.
summary: A manager crams a new coworker into an employee's cubicle just to dodge an internal space charge, even though plenty of empty space exists.

file: 1996/1996-06-06_tormenting the bvendor_bidding economic future_buying decsion_performance measures_vendor challenge_nice t hsirts.gif
title: Vendor Jumps Through Hoops Literally

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tormenting the vendor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You must do our bidding, vendor. We control your economic future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course, our buying decision will be based solely on quantifiable performance measurements.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your competitor completed the "Vendor Challenge Course" in 37 seconds.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And he gave us very nice T-shirts.

setting: Conference room during a vendor sales meeting
situation: Dilbert and two coworkers sit across the table from a vendor trying to win their business. Dilbert declares that the vendor must do their bidding, then claims the decision rests on quantifiable measurements. In the last panel he holds up a hoop for the vendor, who is crawling on the table, and mentions a competitor finished the course in 37 seconds.
punchline: The supposedly objective purchasing process is really an excuse for the buyers to humiliate the vendor with silly stunts and extract free gifts.
summary: Buyers make a desperate supplier crawl through a hoop on the conference table in a mock obstacle course while claiming objectivity.

file: 1996/1996-07-12_ranking_rating system_salary depnds_bpss_defends_managers_ring a bell.gif
title: Boss Doesn't Know Dilbert's Raise

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: He's with the other managers in an employee ranking and rating session.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Your salary depends on how well your boss can defend your proposed raise to the other managers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sob

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I'm fairly sure this Dilbert guy works for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Doesn't ring a bell.

setting: Office reception area, then a management conference room
situation: Dilbert goes looking for his boss and is told by a secretary that the boss is in a ranking and rating session where managers decide raises. Dilbert learns his salary depends on his boss defending his raise, and he breaks down sobbing. In the meeting, another manager says Dilbert works for the boss, and the boss claims not to recognize the name.
punchline: Dilbert's raise depends on a boss who is so out of touch that he doesn't even know his own employee exists.
summary: An employee discovers his pay hinges on a supervisor who can't even recall who he is.

file: 1996/1996-05-20_supreme ruler_earth_wondering_dolts_worthy_leadership_ego.gif
title: Dogbert's Out-of-Control Ego

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It has always been my goal to become supreme ruler of Earth...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But lately I've been wondering if you dolts are worthy of my leadership.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think maybe your ego is out of control, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like it that way.

setting: Outdoor path and grassy hillside with a tree
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert walk outdoors while Dogbert announces his lifelong ambition to rule the Earth. He then declares that humanity may not deserve his leadership. Dilbert asks if his ego might be out of control, and Dogbert cheerfully says he likes it that way.
punchline: Dogbert, confronted about his runaway ego, doesn't deny it and instead happily embraces his arrogance.
summary: A would-be world dictator doubts that people merit his rule, then shrugs off the suggestion that his self-importance has gotten out of hand.

file: 1996/1996-03-08_new vp comig_demo_holographic inetrface_everything fine_product demos_loyal peon.gif
title: Dark Angel of Product Demos

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our new VP is coming. Is the demo of our holographic interface ready?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everything should be fine... unless we're suddenly visited by the dark angel of product demos...

transcript.speaker: Demon
transcript.text: Hello-o-o, Wally. Did somebody say "demo"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm Dilbert; loyal peon.

situation: Wally warns that the new VP is coming and asks whether the holographic interface demo is ready. Dilbert says all should be fine unless the dark angel of product demos appears, and a demon promptly shows up on the screen. Dilbert hastily introduces himself as a loyal peon.
punchline: Dilbert tempts fate by naming the dark angel of product demos, which summons it, and he then tries to appease the demon by presenting himself as a harmless, obedient underling.
summary: A cautious prediction that a product demo will go smoothly instantly conjures a mischievous demon from the computer screen.

file: 1996/1996-08-17_no downsizing_job is safe_quality good news_going downhill.gif
title: Good News: Everyone Else Quit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news, Wally. Most of our smart employees quit to get much better jobs elsewhere. Now we don't have to do any downsizing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job is safe. We need you to do the work of all the people who left.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it just me... or is the quality of "good news" really going downhill lately?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd have to say you're both going downhill.

setting: Office hallway, then a conference room table
situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Wally that most of the smart employees have quit for better jobs, so layoffs are unnecessary, and that Wally's job is safe because he must now cover the work of everyone who left. Later at a meeting table, Wally complains that the quality of good news is declining, and Dilbert replies that Wally and the Boss are both going downhill.
punchline: The supposed good news is really a bad deal, since keeping your job means doing the work of all the departed employees, and Dilbert sarcastically adds that Wally himself is part of the decline.
summary: A manager frames a mass exodus of talent as a happy alternative to layoffs, leaving one worker with a mountain of extra duties.

file: 1996/1996-05-10_career choices_dogbert_helpless people_insignificant insects_occupational preference_remove vital organs_serial killer_career counselor.gif
title: Career Test: Doctor or Serial Killer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Career Counselor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to your occupational preference test, you like to remove vital organs from helpless people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That narrows the career choices to doctor or serial killer. Do you get along with other people?

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Other people are insignificant insects.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll have to go to a tie-breaker question.

situation: Dogbert, working as a career counselor, reviews a client's occupational preference test results. The test shows the client likes removing vital organs from helpless people, which leaves only two possible careers. When Dogbert asks whether the client gets along with others, the answer fails to settle the question.
punchline: The client's contempt for other people fits a serial killer just as well as a doctor, so the career test cannot tell the two professions apart.
summary: A career test points a client toward either surgery or murder, and his low opinion of humanity leaves the decision unresolved.

file: 1996/1996-06-21_buns of steel_hardness_large magnets_not weight_video_ad campaign_work_gym_butt work.gif
title: Buns of Steel Means Hardness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was going to get the "Buns of Steel" video but I'm making excellent progress without it.

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: When they say steel, it refers to hardness, not weight.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I knew it seemed too easy.

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: Stay away from large magnets.

situation: Dilbert walks along a path with a little girl and brags that he is making great progress toward steel buns without buying the exercise video. The girl explains that 'steel' refers to firmness, not weight. Dilbert realizes his mistake, and she adds a dig about large magnets.
punchline: Dilbert thought 'buns of steel' meant heavy rear ends, so his 'progress' was just getting a bigger backside, which the girl mocks by warning him about magnets.
summary: A man proudly shares his fitness success, only to learn he misunderstood what the workout video's famous slogan actually promises.

file: 1996/1996-10-25_catbert_evil hr director_too busy_forty hours training.gif
title: Contract Worker Takes Wally's Training

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, you've been too busy to get the required forty hours of training this year.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So I hired a contract employee to help you out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When does he start?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yesterday. He already finished eight hours of your training.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells Wally he has fallen behind on his mandatory forty hours of annual training because he is too busy. Catbert says he hired a contract employee to help, and Wally assumes the helper will do his work. Instead the contractor has already been attending Wally's training sessions on his behalf.
punchline: The hired help was brought in to take Wally's training rather than his workload, so Wally still has all his work while someone else collects the training credit.
summary: An H.R. cat cheerfully solves a busy employee's training shortfall by hiring a stand-in to sit through the classes instead of lightening his workload.

file: 1996/1996-04-05_valuable experince_rodent_vice president of marketing_simple marketing plan_good press.gif
title: Rodent Marketing VP Clings to Columnists

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I had years of valuable experience as a rodent before I became vice president of marketing.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My marketing plan is simple. Each of you will cling to the leg of a technology columnist until we get some good press.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like you're full.

transcript.speaker: Technology Columnist
transcript.text: You can cling to the cat until a space opens.

setting: Conference room, then a columnist's office or elevator
situation: Ratbert, newly promoted to vice president of marketing, addresses a meeting and announces his plan: each employee will cling to a technology columnist's leg until the company gets good press. Dilbert goes to carry it out, but the columnist already has people clinging to his legs and tells Dilbert to hold onto the cat until a space opens up.
punchline: The ridiculous 'cling to the leg' marketing plan is so widespread among companies that the columnist's legs are already fully occupied, and Dilbert is told to wait by clinging to the cat.
summary: A rodent executive's absurd publicity plan has staff literally hugging a journalist's legs, only to find the journalist's legs are already taken.

file: 1996/1996-12-12_different religions_flexible_change relgion_whole religion_based on not dating_sunday_dogbert.gif
title: Religion Based On Not Dating Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Woman Coworker
transcript.text: I'm flattered. But I can't date you because we're different religions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm flexible. I'd change my religion to get a date.

transcript.speaker: Woman Coworker
transcript.text: It wouldn't work in this case.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know there's a whole religion based on not dating me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Where do you think I go every Sunday?

setting: Office cubicle, then Dilbert's living room couch
situation: Dilbert asks a female coworker out and she turns him down, citing different religions. He offers to convert, but she says that wouldn't work in this case. At home, Dilbert grumbles about a religion based on not dating him, and Dogbert says he attends its services every Sunday.
punchline: Dogbert quips that he practices the religion of not dating Dilbert, mocking how universally Dilbert gets rejected.
summary: A turned-down suitor learns that his romantic failure is so widespread it has practically become an organized faith.

file: 1996/1996-12-26_mail sent_bag_often flier status_seat upgrade_overhead bin_disaster averted_colicky baby convention_other passengers.gif
title: Junk Mail Bribe For Upgrade

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This bag contains all the mail you've sent me about my "often flier" status.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll trade everything in the bag for a seat upgrade. I'm currently assigned to an overhead bin.

transcript.speaker: Airline Agent
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whew! Disaster has been averted.

transcript.speaker: Man with Baby
transcript.text: Are you guys going to the colicky baby convention too?

setting: Airline check-in counter at an airport
situation: Dilbert hands a bag full of the airline's frequent flier mailings to the counter agent and offers to trade it for a seat upgrade, since he has been assigned to an overhead bin. The agent agrees, and Dilbert thinks he has avoided disaster. Then he sees that his new seats are surrounded by a man and a woman carrying crying babies, who are headed to a colicky baby convention.
punchline: Dilbert escapes a ridiculous seat assignment in the overhead bin only to land among a crowd of colicky babies, so the upgrade is no relief at all.
summary: A traveler barters a sack of junk mail for a better airline seat and ends up seated among fussy infants.

file: 1996/1996-11-20_first cigarette ever_smoking breaks_entitled_3x a day_smoking_chatting_fresh air_color coded end.gif
title: Nonsmoker Joins Smokers for Breaks

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Here's my first cigarette ever. I'm looking forward to the many smoking breaks I'm entitled to.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll probably see you three times a day, just smoking and chatting and enjoying the fresh air!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I assume you light the color-coded end, right?

transcript.speaker: Smoker
transcript.text: I quit.

characters: Smoker in white shirt and red tie
setting: Outdoor smoking area outside the office
situation: Wally proudly joins two coworkers who are smoking, holding the first cigarette of his life. He announces he's eager to take the frequent smoking breaks smokers get. After he asks which end of the cigarette to light, his coworkers are so appalled by the sight of a beginner that one of them immediately quits.
punchline: Wally's cluelessness about smoking is so extreme that it makes the veteran smokers quit, while he is only in it to exploit the extra breaks.
summary: A lazy coworker takes up smoking purely to get extra breaks, and his rookie mistakes persuade the real smokers to give it up.

file: 1996/1996-11-21_brand of ciagrette_mountain biking_sparkling waterfall_puff puff_smokers_cognitive disoonance_overrated_smoking.gif
title: Smoker's Cognitive Dissonance Over Cigarette Ads

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: According to the ads, this brand of cigarette will be like mountain biking past a sparkling waterfall.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Puff puff puff

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you getting that weird "smokers' cognitive dissonance" yet?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Man, this mountain biking is overrated.

setting: Office, against a plain blue background
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker tells Dilbert that the cigarette ads promise smoking will feel like mountain biking past a sparkling waterfall. He lights up and puffs away, and Dilbert asks whether he is experiencing cognitive dissonance yet. The coworker, surrounded by smoke, complains that mountain biking is overrated.
punchline: The smoker is so caught up in justifying his habit that he blames the idealized activity from the ad rather than admitting that smoking falls far short of the advertised experience.
summary: A man lights up expecting the outdoor bliss promised in a cigarette commercial and ends up disparaging the sport instead of acknowledging the ad was misleading.

file: 1996/1996-12-05_ratbert_corporate trainer_grim downsizer_stress reduction_budget cuts_class evaluation forms.gif
title: Grim Downsizer Sits In On Training

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert, Corporate Trainer

transcript.speaker: Grim Downsizer
transcript.text: Pssst!

transcript.speaker: Grim Downsizer
transcript.text: I'm the Grim Downsizer. Trainers are the first to go. I'll just hang around here until the next budget cuts.

transcript.speaker: Grim Downsizer
transcript.text: Do you mind if I sit in on your stress-reduction class?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I don't think I'll read the class evaluation forms from this one.

setting: A corporate training room with a flip chart
situation: Ratbert, working as a corporate trainer, is approached by a Grim Reaper figure who introduces himself as the Grim Downsizer. He explains that trainers are the first to be cut and that he plans to wait around until the next budget cuts, then asks to sit in on Ratbert's stress-reduction class.
punchline: Having Death himself in the audience would terrify any trainer, so Ratbert reasons the class evaluation forms will be too negative to bother reading.
summary: A hooded figure of doom lurks in a training session to wait for the next round of layoffs, making a stress-relief class decidedly stressful.

file: 1996/1996-12-24_marilyn vos savant_smartest human alive_often flier program_phone comapny_who saves most_brain scarred.gif
title: Smartest Human Stumped by Frequent Flier

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Marilyn vos Savant, the smartest human alive.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: She will help you understand your airline "often flier" program.

transcript.speaker: Marilyn vos Savant
transcript.text: I'm stumped.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After this, could you tell me which phone company saves me the most money?

transcript.speaker: Marilyn vos Savant
transcript.text: My brain's trying to escape; you scared it.

situation: Dogbert brings in Marilyn vos Savant, billed as the smartest human alive, to help Dilbert make sense of his airline frequent flier program. She reads the rules and admits she is stumped. Dilbert then asks her to also work out which phone company would save him the most money, and her brain tries to flee her head.
punchline: Even the smartest person in the world can't decipher airline frequent flier programs or phone company pricing, because they are deliberately convoluted.
summary: A celebrated genius is brought in to decode a loyalty program and is defeated by the confusing rules and the prospect of comparing phone plans.

file: 1996/1996-11-19_decided_start smoking_add interesting edge_personality_need help_personal magnetism_erase hard drive_psychology.gif
title: Smoking For Breaks And Personality

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've decided to start smoking. I'll be able to take more breaks that way.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And frankly, I'm hoping it will add an interesting edge to my personality and help me socially.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not that I need any help.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I can only pray that your personal magnetism won't erase my hard drive.

situation: Wally tells Tina, a coworker with big hair, that he plans to take up smoking so he can take more breaks. He adds that he hopes it will give his personality an interesting edge and help him socially, then boasts that he doesn't need help. Tina sarcastically replies that she hopes his supposed magnetic charm won't wipe her computer's hard drive.
punchline: Tina sarcastically mocks Wally's inflated opinion of his own charm by treating his 'personal magnetism' as a literal magnetic threat to her data.
summary: A lazy employee plans to pick up a cigarette habit for extra downtime and a cooler image, and a coworker answers his vanity with a dry magnet joke.

file: 1996/1996-12-22_10 year anniversary_service anniversary catalog_ceremony_speech_pick out gift_catalogue_golf ball_t shirt.gif
title: Wally's Meager Ten-Year Anniversary Gift

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Today is your ten-year service anniversary, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Pick a gift from the service anniversary catalog.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is there a ceremony?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yeah. We just had it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: May I say a few words?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Anywhere but here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The selection of gifts at the ten-year level is somewhat meager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The golf ball is nice.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm leaning toward the "I'm with stupid" shirt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I see is a blank shirt.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It comes with a fabric pen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can almost feel the love our company has for us.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What do you mean "us"?

situation: Alice tells Wally it's his ten-year service anniversary and sends him to pick a gift from a catalog. The 'ceremony' has already happened without him, and she shuts down his request to speak. Wally and Dilbert browse the catalog and find the gift choices pitifully cheap, ending with a blank shirt that comes with a pen.
punchline: The company's recognition of a decade of loyalty is so stingy that the best gift is a blank shirt you decorate yourself, and Wally's 'what do you mean us?' shows he feels no love at all, or perhaps that he assumes the company hates only Dilbert.
summary: A company marks a worker's decade of service with a skipped ceremony and a catalog of laughably cheap gifts.

file: 1996/1996-11-17_cubville_powerful leader_solution unique_brilliance_contribution_much better idea.gif
title: Boss's Useless Morale-Boosting Advice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The powerful leader enters Cubeville to inspire the wretched underlings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He spots one of the little people in desperate need of a morale boost.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The leader carefully assesses the situation. Every solution is unique.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try identifying the problem and then solving it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The leader waits while the brilliance of his contribution sinks in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a much better idea than what I was doing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been sitting here all day randomly pressing keys. But you've shown me a better way!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Suddenly the leader remembers why he rarely visits Cubeville.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My morale is soaring.

situation: The Boss wanders into Cubeville imagining himself as an inspiring leader and offers Dilbert the generic advice to identify a problem and then solve it. Dilbert responds with deadpan sarcasm, saying he has been randomly pressing keys all day and that the boss has shown him a better way. The Boss, narrating his own thoughts, realizes why he seldom visits and heads off.
punchline: The Boss's grand leadership gesture is empty, obvious advice, and Dilbert's sarcastic gratitude exposes it, leaving the Boss sarcastically claiming his morale is soaring.
summary: A self-important manager visits the cubicles to uplift his staff, but his platitude gets mocked by an employee and sends him scurrying away.

file: 1996/1996-12-10_dogcart the consultant_meet boss_dogcart talks_crud_crudibility_pointy haired wonder.gif
title: Dogbert Pitches Crud Plus Ability

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let me do the talking when we meet with your boss.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As you know, any idea from the Pointy-Haired Wonder is crud, but when you add my ability, what do you have?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Crudability?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And good looks too!

situation: Dogbert the consultant tells his client, The Boss, to let him do the talking in a meeting with the client's own boss. Dogbert then tells that executive that the Boss's ideas are crud, but combined with Dogbert's ability they become something better. The executive guesses 'crudability' and Dogbert adds that he has good looks too.
punchline: Dogbert openly insults his own client's ideas to the client's superior while smoothly selling himself, inventing a silly portmanteau and flattering himself in the process.
summary: A consultant brazenly insults his client's ideas in front of the client's superior, then credits himself with turning them into something worthwhile.

file: 1996/1996-12-30_pope showed up_hotel concierge_pay pope rate_pope in line.gif
title: Dilbert Demands the Pope's Hotel Room

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No rooms?? If the Pope showed up, would you have a room for HIM?

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, then give me HIS room!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am so clever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see you squirm out of THAT logic, weasel-girl.

situation: Dilbert is told by a hotel clerk that there are no rooms available, so he asks whether she would have a room if the Pope showed up. When she says yes, he demands the Pope's room, smugly congratulating himself on his logic. In the last panel the Pope himself, in his tall white mitre, has arrived and is standing right behind Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert's clever trap backfires because the Pope actually shows up, so the reserved room is about to be claimed by its rightful occupant and Dilbert's smug logic is moot.
summary: A traveler tries to outwit a hotel clerk with a hypothetical about a papal reservation, only to have the real Pope appear behind him.

file: 1996/1996-12-18_ratbert the consulatant_computers_highly exuberant_general protection_flying lessons.gif
title: Ratbert Consultant Blames General Protection

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I don't know much about computers so I compensate by being highly exuberant.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes!! Yes!! Computers!! Wahoo!!!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hey look! It's not my fault; it's some guy named "General Protection."

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: It's time for your flying lessons.

setting: Tina's office, at her desk with a computer
situation: Ratbert, working as a consultant, admits to a client that he knows little about computers and makes up for it with wild enthusiasm. When her computer shows an error, he cheerfully blames it on a person called "General Protection." Tina, fed up with his act, announces it is time for his flying lessons, implying she is about to throw him.
punchline: Ratbert misreads the "general protection fault" computer error as a person's name to dodge blame, and the client responds by threatening to hurl him through the air.
summary: An enthusiastic but clueless rodent consultant pins a computer crash on an imaginary culprit and earns a violent comeuppance from his exasperated client.

file: 1996/1996-12-08_pointy haired boss_speakerphone_important engineer training_talks back to speakerphone_boss heard insults.gif
title: Intern Insults Boss on Speakerphone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss will be joining us by speakerphone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is an important part of your engineering training, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What do I do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When Alice presses the mute button, you make witty and sarcastic remarks.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring ring

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hello, everyone. I'd like to talk about the new compensation plan.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Tell us some lies, you ugly, two-faced, hypocritical troll!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am Asok the intern and I spit on your feeble compensation plan!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I've found stuff on the bottom of my shoe that was smarter than you!! Ha ha ha !!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Next time, a bit wittier... and make sure Alice really presses the mute button.

setting: Conference room during a speakerphone meeting
situation: Dilbert tells the new intern Asok that his engineering training involves making witty, sarcastic remarks whenever Alice mutes the speakerphone. When the Boss calls in to discuss the compensation plan, Asok starts insulting him, but Alice never actually pressed mute, so the Boss hears everything.
punchline: Asok follows Dilbert's prank instructions, but the mute button was never pressed, so he insults the boss to his face and Dilbert only critiques his wit and the mute failure.
summary: A trusting intern is coached to mock the boss during a conference call, only to discover the line was never muted.

file: 1996/1996-11-14_resume_looks good_interested_brilliant engineer_pay cut_savings account.gif
title: Engineer Asked to Take Pay Cut

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your résumé looks good, but we could only pay half of what you're making now. Are you interested?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: So... you're looking for a brilliant engineer who is actively seeking a pay cut?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, you have to consider the many intangibles.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Such as my savings account if I worked here?

situation: Dilbert is interviewing a woman for an engineering job. He tells her the company can only pay half of her current salary and asks if she is interested. She points out how absurd it is to seek a brilliant engineer who wants a pay cut, and mocks his appeal to 'intangibles'.
punchline: The candidate sarcastically turns the vague 'intangible benefits' pitch against him by noting the only intangible effect would be the drain on her savings account.
summary: A job seeker coolly dismantles an interviewer's attempt to sell her on halving her salary.

file: 1996/1996-12-29_idiot boss_move mouse pad_mouse at end_cursor_moving desk_need 800 upgrade_dogbert tech support.gif
title: Dogbert's $800 Mousepad Upgrade

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert. How may I abuse you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to move my cursor to the right but my mouse is at the edge of the mousepad.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you tried rebooting without saving your files?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, several times.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you tried moving your desk?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It didn't work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need my $800 mousepad upgrade.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What account does this get charged to?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Idiot expense," just like everything else.

setting: Dogbert's tech support desk and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss calls Dogbert's tech support line because his mouse has reached the edge of the mousepad and he can't move the cursor further. Dogbert gives absurd advice, including rebooting without saving and moving the desk, which the Boss follows. Dogbert then sells him an $800 mousepad upgrade and bills it to an 'idiot expense' account.
punchline: Dogbert exploits the Boss's cluelessness by offering a ridiculously overpriced fix and openly admitting the cost goes to the 'idiot expense' account, which covers everything the Boss buys.
summary: A clueless manager gets ridiculous help from a predatory tech support dog who ends up selling him a wildly overpriced mousepad.

file: 1996/1996-12-06_ratbert_corporate trainer_class_sharing segment_grim downsizer.gif
title: Grim Downsizer Attends Training Class

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert: Corporate Trainer

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Let's go around the room and say who we are and what we hope to get out of the class.

transcript.speaker: Grim Downsizer
transcript.text: I'm the Grim Downsizer. I'm here to decruit the entire training department plus all of the people who have time to attend classes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My name is Dilbert. I'm here in place of Wally who is working hard to build a better tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nice try.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm somebody else too.

situation: Ratbert, working as a corporate trainer, asks attendees to introduce themselves and say what they hope to get from the class. The Grim Reaper-style Grim Downsizer announces he is there to lay off the training department and anyone with time to attend classes. Dilbert and the others hurriedly claim to be someone else, standing in for colleagues who are supposedly busy working.
punchline: Anyone with time to attend training is a layoff target, so the attendees all frantically pretend to be absent coworkers to avoid being cut.
summary: A death-cloaked layoff specialist crashes a training session and sends the participants scrambling to disown their own identities.

file: 1996/1996-12-14_quality school_quality black master_title metaphoric_breakout session_pre course reading.gif
title: Quality Black-Belt Master Beating Question

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: After I graduate from "Quality School" I'll be a Quality Black-Belt Master.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is the title metaphoric, or is there a chance you'll be beaten senseless during a breakout session?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Zip zip zip zip.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was that necessary?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not sure. I haven't done the pre-course reading yet.

situation: The Boss announces that after finishing "Quality School" he will become a Quality Black-Belt Master. Dilbert asks whether the title is just a metaphor or whether people get beaten up in breakout sessions. The Boss imagines karate-chopping moves, and in the last panel Dilbert is apparently knocked down after asking if that was necessary.
punchline: The Boss physically attacks Dilbert for asking a sarcastic question about the martial-arts title, then admits he doesn't know if it was warranted because he hasn't done the pre-course reading, mocking jargon-heavy corporate quality training.
summary: A boss training to be a quality martial-arts master gets asked if the title is figurative and answers with a violent demonstration he isn't even sure was appropriate.

file: 1996/1996-11-24_serious threat_competitors_consultants_eat our lunch_executive comapny_hired security guard_lunches_safe_figure of speech_better than usuaal_cafeteria.gif
title: Boss Guards Cafeteria Against Competitors

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Last week our consultants warned us about a serious threat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They said our competitors would "eat our lunch."

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Eat our lunch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm happy to tell the executive committee that I leapt into action.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a security guard to protect the cafeteria.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our lunches are safe.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I always thought that was just a figure of speech.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Fool! Give me your department!

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Let go of my hair!!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slap

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Ouch!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is going better than usual.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is the cafeteria closed?

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Someone ate all the lunches.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Burp

setting: Executive committee meeting room and the company cafeteria
situation: The Boss proudly reports to the executive committee that after consultants warned competitors would 'eat our lunch,' he hired a security guard to protect the cafeteria. An executive explains it was only a figure of speech and attacks him, taking his department. Afterward, the cafeteria is closed because the security guard himself ate all the lunches.
punchline: The Boss takes a business metaphor literally and guards the actual lunches, and the hired guard is the one who eats them.
summary: A manager responds to a competitive warning by posting a guard over the cafeteria food, only for the guard to devour it.

file: 1996/1996-11-25_effective raise_evil_mr catbert_moving_slow motion.gif
title: Raise Effective When You're Not

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When will my raise be effective?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The same time you are.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The evil Mr. Catbert, Director of H.R., is feeling "in the zone."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's as if all the employees are moving in slow motion.

situation: Wally asks the H.R. director when his promised raise will take effect. Catbert, speaking from off-panel, replies with a dig at Wally's lack of productivity. In the last panel, Catbert sits at his desk, feeling 'in the zone' and thinking everyone else is moving in slow motion.
punchline: Catbert implies Wally's raise will only become effective when Wally himself becomes effective, i.e. never, since Wally is notoriously unproductive.
summary: An employee asks about the start date of his pay increase and gets an insulting answer from the cruel human resources cat.

file: 1996/1996-12-02_metric_project_growth rate_time zone_favorable_working smater_not harder_new paradignm.gif
title: Meaningless Metrics Prove Smarter Working

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This metric shows an excellent trend in the number of days since the beginning of my project.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That growth rate compares favorably with the best companies in our time zone.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm working smarter, not harder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a whole new paradigm.

situation: Wally presents a chart to the Boss, who sits at his desk with Dilbert beside him, claiming that the passing of days since his project began is an excellent trend. He adds that the growth rate beats the best companies in his time zone. Dilbert then remarks on the 'new paradigm' of working smarter, not harder.
punchline: Wally dresses up the mere passage of time as impressive performance data, mocking how buzzwords and meaningless metrics can pass as productivity.
summary: An employee shows off a chart that merely tracks elapsed days as if it were proof of stellar progress, while a coworker sarcastically applauds the clever new approach.

file: 1996/1996-11-23_warning label_cigarette box_kill you right away_come to your house_wally.gif
title: Menacing Warning Label and Air Freshener Printer

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I never noticed this warning label on my cigarettes before.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "If this product doesn't kill you right away, the executives of our company will drive over to your house and finish the job. We know where you live, Wally. Quit now!"

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why am I paying for a color printer?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's also an air freshener if you know how to use it.

situation: Wally studies a warning label on his cigarette pack and reads aloud a threat that company executives will come to his house and kill him if the cigarettes don't. In the final panel, the Boss holds a paper and asks Dilbert why the company is paying for a color printer. Dilbert deadpans that it doubles as an air freshener.
punchline: Wally's cigarette label is absurdly personalized and threatening, and Dilbert sarcastically answers the Boss's question about the color printer's value by claiming it works as an air freshener.
summary: A cigarette pack unexpectedly addresses Wally by name with a murderous ultimatum, followed by a sarcastic quip about an overpriced printer.

file: 1996/1996-12-07_downsized artbert_generous retirement plan_employment_calendar_when done.gif
title: Generous Retirement Plan: Used Calendar

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're being downsized, Ratbert. Fortunately, there's a generous retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see... for your length of employment, at your grade level... you get a wall calendar.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: When do I get it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As soon as I'm done with it.

situation: The Boss informs Ratbert that he is being laid off and touts a generous retirement plan. Reading from a sheet, he reveals the entire package is a wall calendar. When Ratbert asks when he will receive it, the Boss says he'll hand it over once he has finished using it himself.
punchline: The supposedly generous retirement package is just a wall calendar, and the Boss is so stingy he intends to keep using it himself before handing over the leftover.
summary: A manager lays off a small rodent employee and presents a laughably cheap farewell gift that he still wants to use first.

file: 1996/1996-12-16_elbonian database_payroll_accounts receivable_golf balls.gif
title: Golf Balls Close the Software Deal

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Salesman
transcript.text: Our Elbonian database product can replace every one of your current systems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No thanks.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Salesman
transcript.text: It can do payroll, accounts receivable, inventory, sales...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No thanks.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Salesman
transcript.text: And I'll throw in some golf balls.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a deal! Just toss them in the lake with all my other ones.

setting: Conference room during a vendor sales pitch
situation: An Elbonian salesman pitches a database product that could replace all of the company's systems. Dilbert and Alice each turn him down flat, even as he lists its features. When he offers free golf balls, the Boss immediately accepts the deal.
punchline: Technical staff reject the product on its merits, but the Boss makes the purchasing decision based solely on a trivial freebie, showing how vendor gifts sway management more than functionality.
summary: A vendor's feature list leaves the engineers cold, but a bonus gift is enough to win over the one person who signs the contract.

file: 1996/1996-12-03_enter profession_huge difference_self esteem_corporate trainer_downsizing.gif
title: Lowering Self-Esteem Through Corporate Training

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm going to enter a profession that will make a huge difference in my self-esteem.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll be a corporate trainer in a company that's downsizing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure that will raise your self-esteem?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Why would I want to raise it?

situation: Ratbert sits on Dilbert's desk while Dilbert types and later reads a document. Ratbert announces he will become a corporate trainer at a downsizing company to change his self-esteem. When Dilbert asks whether that will raise it, Ratbert reveals he actually wants to lower it.
punchline: Ratbert's goal is to deliberately lower his self-esteem, implying that training employees at a downsizing company is a thoroughly demoralizing job.
summary: A little lab rat plans a career in a shrinking company's training department, and it turns out he's chasing misery rather than confidence.

file: 1996/1996-12-19_consultant_highly paid_150 per hour_ideal career_unproductive_business.gif
title: Ratbert Wiggles for Consulting Fees

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: As a consultant, I earn $150 per hour even when I'm unproductive.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I can earn 42 cents by wiggling my furry little behind for ten seconds.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: C'mon, count with me!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I imagine my ideal career, it's never like this.

setting: Office cubicle area, with Ratbert perched on a computer monitor
situation: Ratbert sits on top of a computer monitor and boasts that as a consultant he earns $150 an hour even when he is unproductive. He then wiggles his rear end, calculating that ten seconds of it earns him 42 cents, and invites his coworkers to count along. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, comments that this is not what he pictured for his ideal career.
punchline: The highly paid consultant is literally wiggling his behind for money, showing how absurd and undignified consulting pay can be, while the salaried employees are left disillusioned.
summary: A small rodent consultant gleefully shakes his tail end to demonstrate how much money he makes per second, much to a coworker's dismay.

file: 1996/1996-11-10_offered pormotion_another department_snail crud_fantasy_reality_current assignment_too valuable_comapny_raise_valuable assignment_why low morale_breath.gif
title: Promotion Fantasy Versus Reality

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been offered a promotion in another department.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Fantasy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm outta here, you worthless piece of snail crud!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Reality

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I meekly request to be released from my current assignment.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Fantasy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I would never stand in your way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Reality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't release you. You're too valuable.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Fantasy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I'm so valuable, explain my last raise!!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Reality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In fact, I have another valuable assignment for you.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stunned silence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm doing a survey to find out why morale is so low.
