transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think it's your breath.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert at a coworker's cubicle
situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has been offered a promotion in another department. Alternating panels show what he fantasizes saying and the boss responding versus the meek reality, where the boss refuses to release him because he is too valuable and piles on more work. In the last panel Dilbert surveys a coworker about low morale.
punchline: Dilbert's survey about why morale is low gets the blunt answer that the problem is his breath, ignoring the obvious cause of his boss blocking his promotion and overworking him.
summary: A worker imagines triumphantly quitting for a better job but meekly gets denied by a boss who calls him too valuable to lose.

file: 1996/1996-11-12_catbert_evil hr dierctor_resumes_highly qualified_applicants_don't pay enough_hire qualified applicants.gif
title: Catbert Mocks Low Pay, Bad Resumes

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Here are the résumés of highly qualified applicants for your opening.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's too bad we don't pay enough to hire qualified applicants. Ha ha ha ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zip

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Let's see... We've got résumés in pencil... crayon... pencil... eyeliner...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey! Dot matrix!

setting: Office, Catbert's desk and a hiring review table
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, hands over a stack of résumés for highly qualified applicants, then snatches them away while laughing that the company doesn't pay enough to attract anyone qualified. The people doing the hiring are left sorting through résumés written in pencil, crayon and eyeliner, and Dilbert is thrilled to find one that is dot matrix printed.
punchline: Because the salary is so low, the only applicants are unqualified, so a résumé printed on an old dot matrix printer counts as an impressive find.
summary: Stingy pay guarantees a pool of hopeless job candidates, and the hiring team is reduced to celebrating the one résumé that was actually printed.

file: 1996/1996-11-28_computer screen_drivers side window_interpersonal skills_stupid person_windshield gone_without rolling eyes_yugo.gif
title: Listening To Stupid Without Eye-Rolling

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This lesson in interpersonal skills involves listening to a stupid person without rolling your eyes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My computer screen says, "Press any key to continue." Can I borrow your keys? Mine are locked in my Yugo.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must focus... must... focus...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I could break the driver's side window... but it's bad enough that the windshield is gone.

situation: Dogbert, perched on a stool, teaches Dilbert an interpersonal skills lesson about listening to a stupid person without rolling his eyes. A coworker then arrives and delivers a series of absurdly dim remarks, taking his computer's 'press any key' message literally and asking for keys to a car he has locked himself out of. Dilbert holds his head and strains to keep his composure.
punchline: The coworker is so spectacularly dense that Dilbert must struggle to apply the lesson, and the coworker's missing windshield makes his locked-out car problem even more absurd.
summary: A lesson on patiently enduring fools is put to the test the moment a clueless colleague starts rambling about keys and his battered car.

file: 1996/1996-12-27_hotel_tip door man_bell hop_hotel zombies_bag losing_reservation.gif
title: Dilbert Runs Hotel Bellhop Gauntlet

transcript.speaker: Bellhop
transcript.text: Welcome to the hotel. Allow me to touch your bag so you'll feel obligated to tip me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got to make it through the gauntlet of bag-losing hotel zombies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No room?!!! I have a reservation!!!

transcript.speaker: Desk Clerk
transcript.text: Oh, that's original.

setting: Outside and inside a hotel, beside a yellow taxi
situation: Dilbert arrives at a hotel by taxi, where a bellhop announces he will touch Dilbert's bag purely to guilt him into a tip. Dilbert clutches his bag and dodges a pair of grasping bellhops to reach the lobby. At the front desk he is told there is no room despite his reservation, and the clerk dismisses his complaint as an unoriginal one.
punchline: Hotels combine tip-hungry bellhops with desks that routinely lose reservations, and the clerk's sarcastic reply shows she has heard every complaint before.
summary: A weary traveler fights off aggressive luggage handlers only to be told at reception that his booking has vanished.

file: 1996/1996-11-15_long range career goal_arm wrestle_have job in six months_working for her_women college_confident and assertive.gif
title: Interview Candidate Challenges Dilbert to Arm Wrestle

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you were hired, what would be your long-range career goal?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'd have your job in six months. In a year you'd be working for me, you big pile of dinosaur dung.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see you attended an all women's college. Does that experience really make you more confident and assertive?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Either arm. Let's go.

situation: Dilbert interviews a job candidate and asks about her long-range career goal. She answers aggressively, saying she would take his job in six months and be his boss within a year. Dilbert then asks whether her all women's college made her confident and assertive, and she responds by rolling up her sleeve and challenging him to an arm wrestle.
punchline: Dilbert's condescending question about assertiveness is answered with an aggressive physical challenge, proving the candidate is more than confident enough and implying he has just insulted the wrong person.
summary: A candidate who has just threatened to take over her interviewer's career responds to a patronizing question about her education by offering to fight him.

file: 1996/1996-11-11_catbert_evil hr director_get extra engineer_project_transfer_loser_comapny_misplaced optimism.gif
title: Catbert Savors Crushing Dilbert's Optimism

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There are two ways to get an extra engineer for your project.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You can transfer some unqualified loser from within the company...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Not so fast. I like to savor the moment before I crush your misplaced optimism.

situation: Dilbert visits Catbert, the evil H.R. director, to request an extra engineer for his project. Catbert says there are two ways to get one, the first being to transfer an unqualified loser from elsewhere in the company. When Dilbert asks about the second option, Catbert delays, gleefully enjoying the moment before dashing Dilbert's hopes.
punchline: Catbert implies the second option will be even worse, and he sadistically relishes building up Dilbert's hope before destroying it.
summary: An H.R. cat dangles a staffing solution in front of a hopeful engineer purely so he can enjoy ruining it.

file: 1996/1996-11-16_brian_work for comapny_job interview_practice interview_done here_lunch time_don't see sandwhiches.gif
title: Practice Interview Meets Lunch Demands

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So tell me... Brian... why do you want to work for this company?

transcript.speaker: Brian
transcript.text: Well, to be honest, I don't. I'm using this as a practice interview.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess we're done here.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Hello-o-o!!! It's lunch time and I don't see sandwiches.

setting: Interview room with a conference table
situation: Dilbert is interviewing a job candidate named Brian and asks why he wants to work for the company. Brian frankly admits he doesn't and is only using the session as practice for other interviews. Dilbert ends the interview, and another interviewer on the panel loudly complains that no sandwiches have been provided for lunch.
punchline: The interviewer is upset not that the candidate has no interest in the job, but that the interview didn't come with free sandwiches.
summary: A candidate admits he's only there for interview practice, but the real grievance in the room turns out to be the missing lunch.
keywords: why do you want to work here

file: 1996/1996-12-17_computer support_elbonian data base_expensive consultant_five hundred dollars_meeting_business.gif
title: Outrageously Expensive Consultant Joins Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to replace our computer support systems with the Elbonian database product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's risky, but don't worry. I've hired an outrageously expensive consultant who has never done this before.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I earned five hundred dollars just coming to this meeting. How's your day going?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It won't make my top ten.

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that the company will replace its computer support systems with an Elbonian database product. He admits it is risky but reassures everyone by saying he has hired a very costly consultant with no experience in this kind of project. The consultant boasts about earning $500 just for showing up, and Wally deadpans a reply.
punchline: Wally's sarcastic reply shows how little a day spent watching a pricey, inexperienced consultant pocket money appeals to him, while the Boss treats the consultant's lack of experience as reassurance.
summary: A manager tries to soothe worries about an untested software switch by pointing to a pricey consultant who has never done the job, and the consultant's bragging draws a dry remark from a coworker.

file: 1996/1996-12-04_new corporate trainer_teach classes_stress reduction_teamwork_burn in hell_filthy weasel_hired you_subject matter expert.gif
title: Hostile Trainer Teaches Teamwork

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: I'm looking for a new corporate trainer to help me teach classes in stress reduction, conflict resolution, and teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll burn in hell before I'll do your work plus my own, you filthy weasel!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And they hired you?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: A good trainer doesn't have to be a subject matter expert.

situation: A voice off-panel asks for a corporate trainer to help teach classes on stress reduction, conflict resolution and teamwork. Ratbert, the new trainer, responds with an angry, hostile outburst. Dilbert asks how he got hired, and Ratbert says a trainer doesn't need to be an expert in the subject.
punchline: The corporate trainer hired to teach stress reduction, conflict resolution and teamwork is hostile and uncooperative himself, and he claims expertise in the subject isn't required for training.
summary: A rodent hired to teach workplace harmony responds to a request for help with furious abuse, then shrugs off his lack of qualifications.

file: 1996/1996-11-18_catbert_monitor_stressed out_strategy_downsizing_big wuss.gif
title: Catbert Recommends Smoking for Stress

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Are you stressed out, Wally? I have a solution.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Start smoking. That way you'll have frequent company-sanctioned breaks throughout the day.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is your strategy for downsizing, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try it, you big wuss.

setting: Wally's cubicle, with Catbert perched on his computer monitor
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, sits on Wally's monitor and offers a cure for his stress: take up smoking so he gets regular sanctioned breaks. Wally suspects this is really a scheme to thin out the workforce, and Catbert dismisses his worry and taunts him.
punchline: Catbert's wellness advice is a disguised downsizing tactic, since encouraging employees to smoke will eventually kill off staff, and he mocks Wally for being too timid to try it.
summary: An evil personnel cat pitches a health-damaging habit as stress relief, and the intended victim realizes it is a cull in disguise.

file: 1996/1996-11-30_improvement_document_errors_huge blinking red lights_ambulance as warning.gif
title: Intern Critiques Alice, Gets Insulted Back

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I found many areas for improvement in your document, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I'm only an intern, but these errors stand out like huge, red, blinking lights.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: You could put this on top of an ambulance as a warning.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was thinking the same thing about you.

situation: An eager intern approaches Alice at her desk with a marked-up copy of her document and enthusiastically lists its many errors, comparing them to flashing warning lights. After he cheerfully suggests the document could be mounted on an ambulance as a warning, Alice coldly turns the insult around on him.
punchline: The intern's smug, over-the-top criticism of Alice's work earns him a sharp retort that his own obnoxious presence is the real warning sign.
summary: A cheerful junior hire tears apart a senior colleague's paperwork with a flashy metaphor and promptly gets a taste of her own sharp-tongued medicine.

file: 1996/1996-12-15_upgarde_product design_overheat_big picture_no benefits_over heating_sales are strong_end civilization.gif
title: Boss's Upgrade Destroys Civilization

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I made an upgrade to your product design.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This would make the product overheat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's try to look at the big picture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay... Let's see... Your upgrade has no benefits and it costs more.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The overheating would start office fires and put all of our customers out of business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If our sales are strong, we could create economic chaos and a global firestorm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your "upgrade" would destroy civilization as we know it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep me informed.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So you're going to end civilization as we know it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think I'll miss it, frankly.

setting: Office cubicle, then Dilbert's home couch
situation: The Boss proudly announces he has made an upgrade to Dilbert's product design. Dilbert points out it would overheat, and when told to look at the big picture, he escalates the consequences from no benefits and higher cost to office fires, economic chaos and global destruction. The Boss's only reaction is to ask to be kept informed, and Dilbert later tells Dogbert he wouldn't mind civilization ending.
punchline: Even when told his meddling would destroy civilization, the clueless Boss shrugs it off, leaving Dilbert so fed up that he welcomes the apocalypse.
summary: A manager's careless tweak to a product would trigger worldwide catastrophe, yet he responds with indifference, driving his engineer to despair.

file: 1996/1996-12-09_unpaid overtime_immoral_quality of life_designed stockholder value_human resources_business.gif
title: HR Director Isn't Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The mandatory unpaid overtime is immoral. It's destroying the quality of my life.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Alice, Alice, Alice... Companies are designed to maximize stockholder value, not employee happiness.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe the head of human resources should be a human.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Privately I refer to myself as the director of disgruntled cat toys.

situation: Alice complains to Catbert, the evil HR director, that mandatory unpaid overtime is immoral and ruining her quality of life. Catbert calmly replies that companies exist to maximize stockholder value rather than employee happiness. Alice suggests the head of HR should be a human, and Catbert responds that he privately thinks of himself as the director of disgruntled cat toys.
punchline: Catbert dismisses Alice's complaint about employee welfare and, when she points out he isn't human, reveals he sees employees as playthings to torment like a cat's toys.
summary: An overworked employee appeals to the feline head of personnel about her unpaid hours and learns he regards staff as his playthings.
keywords: head of hr should be human

file: 1996/1996-11-09_move slowly_online relationships_yipe_madam cruella.gif
title: Dilbert's Online Date Madame Cruella

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have to move slowly with these online relationships. I'll ask her what she likes to do for fun.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yipe!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'd think that a woman named Madame Cruella would compensate by being extra nice.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer, planning to take things slowly with an online romantic prospect by asking what she likes to do for fun. Her reply makes him recoil in alarm. He then remarks that someone named Madame Cruella should have been extra nice to compensate for her name.
punchline: Dilbert's online date is clearly a dominatrix-type whose answer about her idea of fun is alarming, and Dilbert is naively surprised that someone named Madame Cruella isn't sweet.
summary: A cautious Dilbert gets a shocking answer from his internet romance interest and wryly laments her ominous name.
keywords: what do you like to do for fun

file: 1996/1996-12-25_decoy suitcase_airline distracted_lose decoy_sneak_emergency carry on_eat their food.gif
title: Dilbert Outwits Airline With Decoy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This suitcase is the decoy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: While the airline is distracted trying to lose the decoy, I'll sneak aboard with this emergency carry-on bag.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What if they try to make you eat their food?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fake vomit. They'll think I already ate.

setting: Dilbert's home, while he packs for a flight
situation: Dilbert packs a suitcase and explains his plan to Dogbert: the big suitcase is a decoy for the airline to lose, while he boards with a small emergency carry-on bag. Dogbert asks what happens if they try to make him eat the airline food, and Dilbert pulls out a lump of fake vomit to make them think he has already eaten.
punchline: Dilbert's elaborate plan to beat the airline ends with him carrying fake vomit to avoid eating airline food, a sarcastic jab at how bad airline meals are and the absurd lengths travelers go to for dodging them.
summary: A traveler plans to game the airline with a sacrificial suitcase and a prop designed to get him out of eating the in-flight meal.

file: 1996/1996-11-29_presentation package_worked 12 hrs_creative_stupor_dementia_worse.gif
title: Don't Circulate This Presentation For Comments

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Here's my presentation package. I worked twelve straight hours on it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That includes three hours of creativity followed by nine hours of stupor, senseless twiddling and outright dementia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I suppose there's only one thing that could make this presentation worse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Send it around for comments.

situation: Alice, her hair wildly frizzed from overwork, hands her boss a presentation she spent twelve straight hours on. She candidly admits that only three of those hours were creative and the other nine were mindless dementia. The boss dryly says the one thing that could make it worse is circulating it for comments, then does exactly that.
punchline: The boss claims that sending the presentation around for comments would make it worse, yet immediately orders that very thing, showing that group review is a dreaded ordeal that managers impose anyway.
summary: After a sleepless marathon of work, an exhausted employee delivers a presentation and her manager responds by condemning it to the dreaded committee review process.

file: 1996/1996-12-23_direct flight_aisle seat_upgrade_first class_overhead bin_north korea_non smoking_anti aircraft fire.gif
title: Travel Agent Books Dilbert Terrible Flight

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like a direct flight... aisle seat... and an upgrade to first class if possible.

transcript.speaker: Travel Agent
transcript.text: The best I can do is to put you in an overhead luggage bin... with one stop in North Korea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it non-smoking?

transcript.speaker: Travel Agent
transcript.text: That depends on how accurate the anti-aircraft fire is.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the travel agent's desk, connected by a phone call
situation: Dilbert phones a travel agent and requests a comfortable trip with a direct flight, aisle seat and a first class upgrade. The agent offers him a spot in an overhead luggage bin with a stopover in North Korea. Dilbert calmly asks about smoking, and the agent replies that it depends on anti-aircraft fire.
punchline: The travel agent's dark sarcasm turns a routine booking into a dangerous trip, and the joke lands when Dilbert's deadpan smoking question gets an answer about being shot at.
summary: A traveler's modest airline wishes are met with a deadpan offer of cargo-hold-style transport through a hostile country, and his follow-up question gets an even grimmer reply.

file: 1996/1996-11-26_yelling_boss_diagree_oor interpersonal skills_class_improve them_snarky remarks_dilbert_boss projects.gif
title: Boss Sends Dilbert to Etiquette Class

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whenever we disagree, I always end up yelling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's an indication that you have poor interpersonal skills. I'm sending you to a class to improve them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like you've gained weight. Would it help if I started jogging?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is exactly what I'm talking about.

situation: Dilbert admits to the Boss that he ends up yelling whenever they disagree. The Boss concludes Dilbert has poor interpersonal skills and announces he is being sent to a class. Dilbert then makes a snide remark about the Boss's weight, offering to start jogging, which the Boss cites as proof of the problem.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic jab about the Boss's weight, disguised as a helpful offer, perfectly demonstrates the poor interpersonal skills the Boss was accusing him of.
summary: After being told he needs training to fix his people skills, an employee proves the point by insulting his manager's waistline in the guise of a polite offer.

file: 1996/1996-12-01_be competetive_carpets_catbert_evil director_evil policies_foot sizing program_no compalints_reduce wear and tear_tail twitching_wear shoes smaller.gif
title: Catbert's Smaller-Shoes Policy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert the Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My tail is twitching...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That can only mean it's time to write some more evil policies.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: To: All employees. Subject: New policy

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Employees must wear shoes that are one size smaller than their feet.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This will reduce wear and tear on carpets by 5%

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This is my favorite part.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We must do this to be competitive.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: I'm a reporter for "Evil HR Policies Weekly." Do you have any success stories?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purr. Purr.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This is how industry practices are born

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Has anyone complained about the "footsizing" program?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I haven't listened to a single complaint.

setting: Catbert's HR office and employee workstations
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, feels his tail twitch and writes a new company policy requiring employees to wear shoes one size too small. He justifies it as a way to cut carpet wear by 5% and to stay competitive. A reporter from a trade publication later asks if anyone has complained, and Catbert says he hasn't listened to a single complaint.
punchline: Catbert gleefully imposes a painful, absurd policy, then claims success by simply ignoring all complaints, showing how bad corporate practices spread across industries.
summary: A malicious HR cat invents a painful tight-shoe rule for flimsy cost reasons and brags to the press that nobody objected because he never listened.

file: 1996/1996-11-13_ask applicants sone questions_see how think_five gallon_bucket_holds water_job interview.gif
title: Interview Question Backfires: Bucket Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We like to ask our applicants some questions that will allow us to see how you think.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you have a five-gallon bucket and a fifty-gallon bucket, how can you tell which one holds more water?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I said, "See how you think," what I meant was...

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow!

setting: Interview room with a conference table
situation: Dilbert interviews a job applicant and explains that he asks questions to reveal how candidates think. He poses a puzzle about which of two buckets holds more water. The applicant responds by apparently hitting himself on the head with a bucket, causing him to yelp in pain.
punchline: The applicant takes the bucket question literally and tests it by physically putting a bucket over his head, showing that the interview question was a bad way to judge thinking.
summary: A hiring puzzle about buckets ends in pain when the candidate answers it with a hands-on experiment.

file: 1996/1996-11-22_new smoking habit_teeth turned yellow_social outcast_going broke_house burned down_going to quit_long term view.gif
title: Smoking Habit's Long Term View

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: How do you like your new smoking habit?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: My teeth turned yellow, my breath is putrid, I'm a social outcast, I'm going broke, and my house burned down.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: So you're going to quit?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: No, I'm trying to take a long term view of it.

situation: Carol asks a bald, bespectacled coworker how he likes his new smoking habit. He lists a string of terrible consequences, including yellow teeth, bad breath, financial ruin and a house fire. When she assumes he will quit, he says he is instead trying to take a long term view of it.
punchline: Despite every awful outcome, he refuses to quit and uses the corporate cliche of 'taking a long term view' to rationalize persisting with a clearly failing choice.
summary: A man recites the ruinous results of taking up smoking, then dodges quitting by calling his stubbornness a long-range outlook.

file: 1996/1996-12-21_ntern_elbonian data base_installing_bad movies_password.gif
title: Intern Fixes System, Suggests Hacking NATO

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I am only an intern, but may I make a suggestion?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The Elbonian database system you're installing for our company will never work... unless I rewrite the entire thing with just six keystrokes...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought this was only possible in bad movies.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hey, let's hack into NATO's system. I can guess their password in three tries.

situation: Ratbert, working as an intern, sits at Dilbert's computer and offers to fix the Elbonian database system the company is installing. He rewrites the whole thing with six keystrokes. Dilbert is amazed that this only happens in bad movies, and Ratbert cheerfully proposes hacking into NATO's system next.
punchline: After pulling off a movie-style miracle fix, the tiny intern casually suggests committing an international cyber-crime, showing he is happy to keep living out Hollywood hacking clichés.
summary: A small lab-rat intern effortlessly repairs a hopeless software installation in moments, then eagerly proposes breaking into a military alliance's computers.

file: 1996/1996-12-13_culture of cycnicism_cynicism_happiness commitee_improve morale_negativism.gif
title: Happiness Committee Brainstorms Terrible Perks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must change our culture of cynicism and negativism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You two will be the "Happiness Committee." Come up with some ideas to improve morale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So far we've got: 1) Raises, 2) Slap-the-boss day and 3) Nude Fridays.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I feel my cynicism melting away already.

situation: The Boss announces that the company must fix its culture of cynicism and appoints Dilbert and Wally as the Happiness Committee to come up with morale-boosting ideas. Dilbert and Wally later report their brainstormed list, which consists of raises, a slap-the-boss day, and nude Fridays.
punchline: Wally's claim that his cynicism is melting away is sarcastic, since the committee's ideas are self-serving fantasies that management would never approve, showing the cynicism is fully intact.
summary: Two employees assigned to boost workplace happiness respond with a wish list of absurd and unrealistic perks while sarcastically pretending it's working.

file: 1996/1996-12-31_business traveler_wrinkle free_the wrapper_wrinkled suit.gif
title: Wrinkle-Free Suit Claim Wrinkled

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Business Traveler

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I bought this suit, it said "wrinkle-free" on the wrapper.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The wrapper?

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Dilbert sits at a meeting table with two colleagues, wearing a badly crumpled red suit after traveling. He explains that the suit was advertised as wrinkle-free when he bought it. A coworker questions the odd detail that the claim was on the wrapper.
punchline: The 'wrinkle-free' promise applied only to the packaging, not the suit itself, so Dilbert's suit is hopelessly rumpled and his purchase relied on misleading labeling.
summary: A traveling Dilbert shows up to a meeting in a crushed suit and blames a product label that apparently promised more than the garment could deliver.

file: 1996/1996-12-11_tina_tech writer_first draft_boring_presence of genius.gif
title: Exclamation Points Rescue Technical Document

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your first draft was boring, so I added a bunch of exclamation points.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Wow! Those exclamation points make this technical document come alive!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This might be that sarcasm thing I keep hearing about.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm in the presence of genius! I beg you to father my children!

situation: The Boss hands Tina, the technical writer, her document back and explains that he improved her boring draft by adding exclamation points. Tina responds with gushing, over-the-top praise, and the Boss wonders whether he is witnessing sarcasm.
punchline: Tina's absurdly effusive flattery is clearly sarcastic, but the clueless Boss can only vaguely suspect it, since he has merely heard of sarcasm rather than recognised it.
summary: A manager who thinks punctuation can fix dull writing receives such extravagant praise from his technical writer that he dimly suspects he is being mocked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't fault your efficiency, though.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whump

transcript.speaker: Sound effect

setting: A curbside taxi stand, then inside a moving taxi
situation: A uniformed officer hands Dilbert a written description of how his assigned taxi driver will try to cheat him, and Dilbert reads it aloud to the grinning driver. As the driver speeds off, he runs over pedestrians and objects, with debris and a flailing hand flying past the car.
punchline: Dilbert dryly admits that even though the driver is a cheat, he is at least efficient, while the driver is plowing through pedestrians without slowing down.
summary: A traveler is handed a printed list of his taxi driver's scams, then watches the driver barrel through the street flattening everything in his way.

file: 1996/1996-11-27_school for interpersonal skills_dogbert_good relationships_huge phony_three fundamentals_loud_simple_smiley_low pressure system_weather.gif
title: Dogbert Teaches Phony Small Talk

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's School for Interpersonal Skills

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The secret to good relationships is to be a huge phony.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's practice the three fundamentals.

transcript.speaker: Whiteboard
transcript.text: Loud. Simple. Smiley.

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: Hey, how about that low-pressure system, huh?!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Again, but this time say "weather."

setting: A classroom at Dogbert's School for Interpersonal Skills
situation: Dogbert runs a class on interpersonal skills and tells his students the secret to good relationships is being a huge phony. He drills them on three fundamentals: loud, simple and smiley. A student then loudly and cheerfully comments on a low-pressure system, and Dogbert asks him to repeat it using the word "weather."
punchline: The student follows the loud, smiley small-talk advice so literally that he uses obscure jargon instead of the simple word "weather," and Dogbert has to correct him.
summary: A dog instructor coaches his class on faking friendliness, and a student's enthusiastic small talk still manages to miss the point of keeping it simple.
